Discriminator Briefs

What actually decides the question, and how else they can ask it. Every entry names the fork, tables the mimics, and banks the variants.

112 topics 37 board-style 12 systems 10 named trap species Last updated September 2026

How to Use This

The clinical content is downstream of the method. Read this section once, then let the briefs reinforce it.

Method guide — the three habits, question verbs & the trap speciestap to expand

The three habits

  1. The assassin scan. For each answer choice, find the sentence in the stem that makes it impossible. When every option but one has an assassin, the question is finished — no forward reasoning required. A stem's "normal" findings are eliminations, not filler.
  2. The switch rule. Change an answer only when rereading reveals a misread fact — never when it reveals a new possibility. A detail that is merely compatible with another diagnosis is flavor. Incompatibility, not plausibility.
  3. Store the discriminator, not the outcome. Learn "limping child → score Kocher," never "limping child → aspirate." Rules stored as outcomes fire on the benign mirror-twin stem and get you twice.

Read the verb before the choices

  1. "Most likely diagnosis" → the diagnosis that explains all findings, not the most findings.
  2. "Most sensitive / screening" → lowest detection threshold. "Most accurate / definitive / confirms" → tissue, or the gold-standard test.
  3. "Next step in management" → the next rung on the ladder. "Next step in diagnosis" → the test whose result changes what you do tonight.
  4. "Most beneficial / reduces mortality" → match the intervention's time-to-benefit to the outcome's time horizon. Lipids = years. BP, volume, GDMT = weeks to months.
  5. "Underlying cause" → the trunk of the causal tree, not a branch.
The ten trap species
SpeciesHow it worksAntidote
Salient decoyA vivid, concrete detail — occupation, travel, family history — that is compatible with the right answer but suggests a wrong one. Camping in Georgia → Lyme, when the answer is rheumatic fever.Ask what job the detail is doing. If it's making you nervous rather than deciding anything, it's bait.
Treat-the-numberAn abnormal lab planted so you medicate the value instead of the outcome. Low HDL → niacin. High A1c → metformin. High Hct → phlebotomy.Ask which intervention changes the outcome named in the question.
Trump-card inversionA risk calculator offered when a categorical indication already decides it. 10-year risk 4.9% in a diabetic — diabetes already earned the statin.Check trump cards before calculators: prior event, LDL ≥190, diabetes 40–75.
True-fact-wrong-slotA real association placed where the timeline or findings forbid it. Post-URI in a 12-month history. Fibroids causing postmenopausal bleeding.Verify the interval and the physiologic state before you use the association.
Mirror twinThe benign version of a stem you just learned the dangerous version of. Transient synovitis right after septic arthritis.Store the scoring rule, not the action.
Sequencing trapA correct action offered one step out of order. MRI before conservative therapy. Antibiotics before aspiration. Imaging before airway.Name the ladder out loud before choosing a rung.
Uniform-answer doubtAn "all yes" or "no further testing" option rejected because it feels too easy. HIV vaccine grid — the answer really was yes to all four.Reject it only with a named disqualifying criterion you can say out loud.
Test-overrides-findingsA normal or discordant test offered against classic findings. Negative scaphoid film. Negative nitrite. Negative Phalen. Normal creatinine in early nephropathy. A nonfocal neuro exam in brain abscess.A negative test rules out only when its sensitivity exceeds your pretest probability.
Unchecked attributeThe right category is retrieved and then never checked against the one attribute that separates its members — direction, age, duration, grade, timing, or kind. The option is the correct disease family with the wrong value on the deciding axis.Name the attribute the stem specified, out loud, before choosing: which direction, at what age, over how long, at which grade.
Class-vs-memberThe right drug class represented by the wrong member, making a keyed answer look like it contradicts a guideline. "NSAIDs are first-line for OA" — but the only NSAID offered is ketorolac, a 5-day drug, so acetaminophen wins.Read which specific agent represents each class before rejecting the class.
The recurring failure mode Fast-and-wrong misses cluster where the deciding fact lives in the background — the past medical history, the gestational age, the menopausal status, the duration — rather than in the foreground finding. Recognition speed is not the problem; the missing step is a deliberate 10-second completion pass: read the entire lab panel and the entire PMH before locking.

Musculoskeletal & Rheumatology 19 topics + 4 board-style

The shelf's densest system. Nearly every stem is decided by a maneuver, a time course, or a red flag hiding in the past medical history.

Polymyalgia Rheumatica

Elderly · proximal stiffness · ESR

The decision point

Age >50 + bilateral proximal girdle aching with morning stiffness + systemic symptoms + ESR ≥50, with no true weakness and no muscle tenderness. The trap is confusing "can't get out of bed" (pain and stiffness) with weakness (myositis). Treatment is low-dose prednisone ~15 mg; a dramatic response within days is nearly diagnostic.

Defining criteria Diagnosis — age >50, bilateral proximal girdle aching with morning stiffness, ESR ≥50, with normal strength and no muscle tenderness · Response criterion — dramatic improvement on prednisone ~15 mg within days is nearly diagnostic · Rules out polymyositis — PMR is pain with normal CK; polymyositis is weakness with elevated CK
Proximal pain & stiffness — the differential
DiagnosisKey discriminatorLabsTreatment
Polymyalgia rheumaticaProximal pain/stiffness, strength normalESR/CRP ↑, CK normalLow-dose prednisone
Giant cell arteritis EmergencyHeadache, jaw claudication, vision loss; coexists with PMR in ~50%ESR often >50–100High-dose prednisone; don't wait for biopsy if vision is threatened
PolymyositisProximal weakness > painCK ↑, anti-Jo-1High-dose steroids
Elderly-onset RASmall-joint synovitis (MCP/PIP), erosionsRF / anti-CCP +Methotrexate
FibromyalgiaDiffuse tender points, younger womenNormal ESR/CRPExercise, duloxetine, amitriptyline
Hypothyroid myopathyFatigue, weight gain, bradycardiaTSH ↑, CK ↑Levothyroxine
Statin myopathyStatin exposureCK ↑Stop the statin
Scenario bank
  1. 72 yo F, bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching, morning stiffness 90 min, ESR 62, strength 5/5 → polymyalgia rheumatica → prednisone 15 mg daily
  2. 72 yo F with known PMR, new jaw claudication and temporal tenderness → giant cell arteritis → high-dose prednisone immediately, biopsy after
  3. 68 yo M, progressive proximal weakness, CK 4,000, normal ESR → polymyositis → EMG and muscle biopsy
  4. 70 yo F on atorvastatin, proximal aching, CK 900 → statin myopathy → stop the statin and recheck CK
  5. 66 yo F, proximal aching, ESR 12, TSH 14 → hypothyroid myopathy → levothyroxine
  6. 74 yo F with presumed PMR, no response after a week of prednisone 15 mg → reconsider the diagnosis — PMR responds within days
  7. 63 yo F, widespread pain, non-restorative sleep, normal ESR and CK → fibromyalgia
Pearls PMR = pain with normal CK; polymyositis = weakness with high CK · PMR responds to low-dose steroids, GCA needs high dose · every PMR diagnosis gets a GCA symptom screen, and ~50% of GCA patients have PMR · NSAIDs fail in PMR — that's the "close but inadequate therapy" distractor.
Sequencing trapTreat-the-number

Shoulder Pain: the Range-of-Motion Rule

Aquifer FM 25 · rotator cuff · impingement

The decision point

One rule sorts every shoulder stem: active ROM lost with passive preserved = muscle/tendon (rotator cuff tendinopathy or tear, biceps tendinitis, impingement). Both active and passive lost = joint (adhesive capsulitis, glenohumeral OA, septic joint). Then the maneuvers map one-to-one onto muscles.

Shoulder pain — the differentialsorted by the range-of-motion rule
DiagnosisWhat is driving itThe NBME tell
Cuff tendinopathy / impingementOverhead use; painful arc; active ROM ↓ onlyEmpty can (Jobe) +, Neer / Hawkins +
Full-thickness cuff tearWeakness > pain; can't raise arm overheadDrop arm +; traumatic in young, degenerative in old
Biceps tendinitisAnterior pain, bicipital groove tendernessPain on resisted flexion–supination
Adhesive capsulitisActive and passive ROM ↓; DM, hypothyroidFollows immobilization — the sling trap
Glenohumeral OAActive + passive ↓ + crepitus, olderPrior dislocation is the risk factor
Septic arthritis / bursitis EmergencyFever, red, swollen; IVDU, DM, RAAspirate first — never blind antibiotics
C5–C6 radiculopathyNeck → shoulder pain, numbnessShoulder exam NORMAL; Spurling +
Referred cardiac / diaphragmaticExertional or visceral patternNormal shoulder exam → get the ECG
Maneuver → muscle
  • Empty can (Jobe) → supraspinatus (abduction)
  • Resisted external rotation → infraspinatus / teres minor
  • Resisted internal rotation → subscapularis
  • Drop arm → full-thickness tear
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo M, painful arc, active abduction limited, passive abduction full → rotator cuff tendinopathy → relative rest and physical therapy
  2. 62 yo F with diabetes, both active and passive ROM lost in every plane → adhesive capsulitis
  3. 70 yo M cannot initiate abduction, positive drop-arm test → full-thickness rotator cuff tear → MRI
  4. 55 yo M, shoulder pain with fever, refuses all movement, effusion → septic arthritis → aspirate before antibiotics
  5. 48 yo M, shoulder pain radiating below the elbow with thumb numbness → C5–C6 radiculopathy
  6. 60 yo M, shoulder pain on exertion relieved by rest, with diaphoresis → referred cardiac pain → ECG
  7. 58 yo M given a sling for cuff tendinopathy, still wearing it at 3 weeks → immobilization risks adhesive capsulitis → stop the sling, start PT now
Management ladder & the sling trap First-line is relative rest + physical therapy — strengthen the cuff and scapular stabilizers to open the subacromial space. "Rest" must never be communicated as immobilize: a sling causes atrophy and adhesive capsulitis, and slings are for dislocation and fracture only. No reflex MRI — X-ray only for trauma or failed therapy, and older adults have asymptomatic cuff tears on MRI. Subacromial steroid injection gives short-term relief only, and never through suspected infection.
Nerve one-liners Anterior dislocation → axillary nerve (lateral deltoid numbness, weak abduction) · scapular winging → long thoracic · supraspinatus + infraspinatus atrophy → suprascapular.
Transferable rule The exam answer is usually the boring next rung: activity modification beats PT beats injection beats MRI beats surgery.

Biceps Tendinitis

Overuse tendinopathy · initial management

The decision point

Anterior shoulder pain + bicipital groove tenderness + pain on resisted elbow flexion/supination in someone still doing the offending activity. "Initial step" questions reward the least-intensive appropriate intervention: activity modification (stop the throwing and lifting) → NSAIDs → PT if not improving in 2–4 weeks → injection → imaging.

Scenario bank
  1. 26 yo M pitcher, anterior shoulder pain, bicipital groove tenderness, still throwing weekly → activity modification plus NSAIDs
  2. 26 yo M, still painful after 6 weeks of activity modification and NSAIDs → physical therapy
  3. 62 yo M, sudden pop while lifting, bulge in the mid upper arm → long head of biceps rupture → non-operative in older adults
  4. 26 yo M, pain reproduced by resisted supination with the elbow flexed → biceps tendinitis
  5. 45 yo M, anterior shoulder pain with a positive Hawkins test → subacromial impingement
  6. 26 yo M with biceps tendinitis; the question asks the least intensive appropriate step → activity modification
Exam logic vs. clinic reality On the exam, PT is not wrong — it's not initial when the patient is still throwing every weekend. In clinic, modern tendinopathy management is relative rest plus progressive loading, and the two aren't really opposed. What matters at the bedside: say the words "do not wear a sling." Patients hear "rest" and immobilize, and the shoulder is uniquely punished for immobilization — adhesive capsulitis can set in within weeks.
Transferable rule Give patients a positive instruction (what to do), not just a negative one (what to avoid), or they will invent their own version of rest.

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

Median neuropathy at the wrist

The decision point

Read the verb. "Confirm the diagnosis" → nerve conduction studies. "Next step in management" → nocturnal neutral wrist splint. "Next step" with thenar atrophy → surgical release. Phalen and Tinel are ~50–60% sensitive, so negative maneuvers cannot overturn a classic history.

The anatomy fact they build questions on CTS spares sensation over the thenar eminence, because the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the tunnel and runs over the retinaculum. Numbness that includes the thenar eminence means a proximal lesion — pronator teres syndrome. Motor loss is late: LOAF (Lumbricals 1–2, Opponens, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis).

Anterior interosseousNone — pure motorCan't make the "OK" sign
C6 radiculopathyThumb / index + neckDiminished brachioradialis reflex → cervical MRI
C7 radiculopathyMiddle fingerDiminished triceps reflex
Ulnar — cubital tunnel4th–5th digitsWorse with elbow flexion; Froment sign, claw hand
Ulnar — Guyon canal4th–5th digits, volar onlyCyclists; hook of hamate fracture
Radial at spiral grooveDorsal web spaceWrist drop — "Saturday night palsy"

  2. New bilateral CTS + enlarging ring size, coarse features → acromegaly → IGF-1

De Quervain Tendinopathy

First dorsal compartment · APL + EPB

The decision point

Radial styloid tenderness + positive Finkelstein/Eichhoff (thumb flexed, wrist ulnar-deviated) is a clinical diagnosis. No imaging, no labs. Treatment: thumb spica splint + NSAIDs → corticosteroid injection → first dorsal compartment release.

The restraint answer "No additional testing," "reassurance," "proceed with the procedure," and "continue current management" are a family of correct answers. They win when the diagnosis is clinical, a provocative test is positive, and there are no red flags. The instinct to "get an X-ray to be safe" adds only incidental findings.
Radial wrist pain — the differential
DiagnosisLocationThe tell
De QuervainRadial styloidFinkelstein +; jars, lifting infants, repetitive gripping
Scaphoid fractureAnatomic snuffboxFOOSH trauma
1st CMC (basal) OAThumb baseGrind test +, squared joint, older
Intersection syndrome~4 cm proximal, dorsalCrepitus; rowers, weightlifters
Trigger fingerA1 pulley, palmCatching / locking + nodule
Ganglion cystDorsal wristSoft, transilluminates, fluctuates
DupuytrenPalmar fascia, 4th/5thCord + contracture; alcohol, diabetes
Disseminated gonococcal Can't missMultiple tendon sheathsFever + migratory polyarthralgia + pustules → NAAT + ceftriaxone
Scenario bank
  1. 32 yo F, new mother, radial wrist pain, positive Finkelstein test → De Quervain tendinopathy → thumb spica splint and NSAIDs
  2. 28 yo M after a FOOSH, snuffbox tenderness, normal initial X-ray → occult scaphoid fracture → thumb spica cast, re-image in 2–3 weeks
  3. 65 yo F, thumb base pain, positive grind test, joint space narrowing on X-ray → first CMC osteoarthritis
  4. 24 yo F, sexually active, wrist tenosynovitis with a pustular rash → disseminated gonococcal infection → NAAT and blood cultures
  5. 32 yo F with De Quervain still symptomatic after 6 weeks of splinting and NSAIDs → corticosteroid injection
  6. 40 yo M rower, forearm pain with crepitus a few centimetres proximal to the wrist → intersection syndrome
Hand arthritis distribution — pure recall RA = MCP and PIP, symmetric, spares DIP · OA = DIP (Heberden) and PIP (Bouchard) · Psoriatic = DIP, dactylitis, nail pitting, "pencil-in-cup." DIP involvement essentially rules out RA.

Meralgia Paresthetica

Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve · L2–L3

The decision point

The LFCN is purely sensory — compressed under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS. No motor fibers means no weakness is possible, so 5/5 strength is confirmatory, not reassuring incidental data. Clinical diagnosis; conservative management resolves >90%.

Thigh sensory symptoms — the differential
DiagnosisSensoryMotorThe tell
Meralgia parestheticaUpper lateral thigh patchNoneTight belts, straining, obesity, pregnancy
L2–L3 radiculopathyDermatomal + backHip flexion weaknessBack pain, femoral stretch test +
Femoral neuropathyAnterior thigh + medial legQuadriceps weakness↓ patellar reflex
Diabetic amyotrophyVariableProximal weakness, wastingSevere pain + weight loss, asymmetric
Diabetic polyneuropathyStocking-glove, feet firstLateBilateral, symmetric; ↓ vibration first
Trochanteric bursitisNoneNonePoint tenderness over greater trochanter
Scenario bank
  1. 44 yo M, obese, burning numbness over the upper lateral thigh, strength 5/5 → meralgia paresthetica → weight loss and loosen restrictive belts
  2. 44 yo M with lateral thigh numbness and weak knee extension → femoral neuropathy
  3. 60 yo M with diabetes, severe thigh pain, proximal weakness and weight loss → diabetic amyotrophy
  4. 44 yo M, lateral thigh numbness with back pain to the knee and a reduced patellar reflex → L2–L3 radiculopathy
  5. 44 yo M with point tenderness over the greater trochanter and no numbness → trochanteric bursitis
  6. 44 yo M with classic meralgia paresthetica asking what workup is needed → none — it is a clinical diagnosis
Pearls Other pure sensory entrapments: sural (lateral foot), superficial peroneal (foot dorsum), saphenous (medial leg), digital → Morton neuroma (3rd/4th interspace, Mulder click) · metformin causes B12 deficiency over years, producing a distal symmetric neuropathy — never a focal thigh patch · foot drop after leg-crossing or rapid weight loss = common peroneal at the fibular head.
Transferable rule A nerve's motor content determines what a lesion can look like. If the candidate nerve has no motor fibers, a normal exam confirms rather than refutes.

Scaphoid Fracture

FOOSH · the negative film

The decision point

FOOSH + anatomic snuffbox tenderness = scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise, and a negative initial X-ray proves nothing — up to 20–25% are radiographically occult in week one. Answer: thumb spica cast anyway, re-image in 2–3 weeks (or MRI now, if offered).

Scenario bank
  1. 22 yo M after a FOOSH, snuffbox tenderness, X-ray negative → thumb spica cast and re-image in 2–3 weeks
  2. 22 yo M, same presentation, with MRI among the options → MRI now
  3. 22 yo M with a missed scaphoid fracture presenting 6 months later with wrist pain → avascular necrosis and nonunion
  4. 22 yo M after a FOOSH with distal radius tenderness and dorsal angulation → Colles fracture
  5. Which scaphoid fracture site carries the highest avascular necrosis risk → proximal pole
  6. 22 yo M with a displaced scaphoid waist fracture on X-ray → surgical fixation
Why the stakes justify casting on suspicion The scaphoid's blood supply enters distally and runs retrograde to the proximal pole. A missed fracture means avascular necrosis and nonunion. Highest AVN risk = proximal pole. The AVN club worth memorizing: femoral head, scaphoid proximal pole, talus, humeral head — all retrograde or tenuous supply.
Transferable rule The D-dimer principle in orthopedic clothing: a negative test cannot rule out disease when pretest probability is high. High-probability PE → CTA regardless of dimer; high-probability scaphoid → cast regardless of film.
Test-overrides-findings

Low Back Pain: Red Flags

When to image · when not to

The decision point

Acute low back pain (<4 weeks) gets no imaging — unless a red flag fires. Red flags for malignancy do not require a neurologic deficit; early vertebral metastasis is neurologically silent. A normal exam only rules out when its sensitivity exceeds your pretest probability, and that probability is set by the past medical history.

Defining criteria Imaging gate — acute low back pain <4 weeks → no imaging unless a red flag fires · Malignancy red flags — do not require a neurologic deficit; early vertebral metastasis is neurologically silent
Low back pain — red flags by category
CategoryRed flagsImaging
MalignancyPrior cancer, age >50, weight loss, night / rest pain, pain >4–6 wksMRI with contrast; X-ray + ESR/CRP if suspicion moderate
InfectionFever, IVDU, recent bacteremia, immunosuppression, recent spinal procedureMRI with contrast + blood cultures
FractureAge >70, osteoporosis, chronic steroids, traumaX-ray first
Cauda equina EmergencyUrinary retention (most sensitive), saddle anesthesia, bilateral sciatica, ↓ anal toneEmergent MRI + decompression
Cord compression EmergencyUMN signs, hyperreflexia, sensory levelDexamethasone first, then whole-spine MRI
Inflammatory (AS)Age <40, >3 months, better with exercise, worse with rest, HLA-B27SI joint X-ray → MRI
AAAAge >60, atherosclerosis, pulsatile mass, tearing painUltrasound / CTA
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo M, back pain, prior prostate cancer, night pain, normal neurologic exam → malignancy → MRI with contrast
  2. 34 yo M who injects drugs, back pain with fever and focal spinal tenderness → vertebral osteomyelitis → MRI plus blood cultures
  3. 70 yo F on chronic prednisone, acute back pain after a minor fall → vertebral compression fracture → lumbar X-ray
  4. 48 yo M, back pain with urinary retention and saddle anesthesia → cauda equina syndrome → emergent MRI and decompression
  5. 72 yo M, back pain with a pulsatile abdominal mass and hypotension → ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm → immediate surgical evaluation
  6. 40 yo M, acute low back pain under 4 weeks, no red flags, normal exam → no imaging → NSAIDs and stay active
Pearls Vertebral mets seed the vertebral body first via Batson's valveless venous plexus · pedicle destruction = "winking owl" sign · bone-seeking primaries: "BLT with a Kosher Pickle" — Breast, Lung, Thyroid, Kidney, Prostate · give dexamethasone before imaging when cord compression is suspected with deficits — the one place treatment precedes diagnosis · plain films miss 30–50% of bone loss.
Transferable rule In any "most patients don't need X" topic, the question is never whether the base rate is low — it's whether this patient is the exception. Scan the PMH before applying the population rule.
Test-overrides-findingsTrue-fact-wrong-slot

Hip Positioning: Fracture vs. Dislocation

Free points, frequently reversed

The decision point

Shortened + externally rotated + abducted = hip fracture (femoral neck / intertrochanteric). Shortened + internally rotated + adducted + flexed = posterior hip dislocation — the dashboard injury, ~90% of hip dislocations, with the sciatic nerve at risk.

Mnemonic and the shoulder mirror Fracture = Falls outward (external). Posterior dislocation = Points inward (internal). The shoulder mirrors it: anterior dislocation (95%) = abducted + externally rotated; posterior dislocation (seizures, electrocution) = adducted + internally rotated. In both joints the common and rare forms are mirror images.
Scenario bank
  1. 78 yo F after a fall, leg shortened and externally rotated → femoral neck fracture → X-ray, then arthroplasty
  2. 28 yo M after a head-on collision, leg shortened, internally rotated, adducted and flexed → posterior hip dislocation → reduction within 6 hours
  3. 28 yo M with foot drop after a posterior hip dislocation → sciatic nerve injury
  4. 78 yo F with a displaced femoral neck fracture → arthroplasty → retinacular vessel disruption risks AVN
  5. 28 yo M whose hip dislocation was reduced at 10 hours → increased risk of femoral head osteonecrosis
  6. 70 yo M after a fall, leg shortened and externally rotated but abducted, groin pain → intertrochanteric fracture
Time-critical Posterior dislocation needs reduction within ~6 hours to avoid femoral head AVN. Femoral neck fracture in the elderly → AVN risk from retinacular vessel disruption → arthroplasty.

Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome

Findings beat pain descriptors

The decision point

Point tenderness over the greater trochanter with a normal neurologic exam. Stems plant "burning," which sounds neuropathic and pulls toward meralgia paresthetica — but burning is a quality descriptor, while tenderness and a normal neuro exam are findings. GTPS is a tendinopathy; meralgia is a neuropathy.

The location rule that organizes all hip pain: groin → the joint itself (OA, AVN, fracture, labral tear) · lateral → trochanter and its tendons, or the LFCN · posterior/buttock → spine, SI joint, or piriformis.

Lateral hip pain — the differential
DiagnosisLocationExamThe tell
GTPSLateral hip over the trochanterPoint tenderness over the greater trochanter; ROM normalWorse lying on that side; stairs, uphill, getting out of a car
Meralgia parestheticaUpper lateral thigh patchSensory loss; no bony tenderness; strength normalLFCN is purely sensory
Hip osteoarthritisGroin/medial, radiates to thigh or knee↓ internal rotation, groin pain on FABERCrepitus, morning stiffness <30 min
Femoral neck stress fractureGroin/anteriorPain with hopping and log-rollRunner or military recruit; female athlete triad → MRI
IT band syndromeLateral KNEETenderness at the femoral condyle; Noble testA knee diagnosis, not a hip one
Gluteal tendon tearLateral hipAbductor weakness, Trendelenburg gaitSevere end of the GTPS spectrum → MRI
Osteoid osteomaProximal femurOften no focal finding in adultsNight pain dramatically relieved by NSAIDs; children/young adults
AVN of the femoral headGroin↓ ROM in all planesSteroids, alcohol, sickle cell → MRI
GTPS essentials An overuse tendinopathy of the gluteus medius and minimus at the greater trochanter — "trochanteric bursitis" is a misnomer, since the bursa usually isn't the source. Risk factors: age ≥50, women > men, obesity, and lower-limb or low-back disorders. Clinical diagnosis; X-ray excludes hip joint disease rather than confirming GTPS. Ladder: activity modification + NSAIDs + physical therapy (abductor strengthening) → corticosteroid injection if refractory.
Scenario bank
  1. Abductor weakness and Trendelenburg gait → gluteus medius tendon tear → MRI
  2. Groin pain with reduced internal rotation and crepitus → hip OA → X-ray
  3. Marathon runner, groin pain, pain on hopping, normal X-ray → femoral neck stress fracture → MRI
  4. Lateral knee pain in a cyclist → IT band syndrome
  5. Upper lateral thigh numbness, normal strength, no tenderness → meralgia paresthetica
  6. Adolescent with night pain relieved by NSAIDs → osteoid osteoma → CT shows the nidus
  7. Chronic steroids or heavy alcohol, progressive groin pain, normal X-ray → AVN → MRI
  8. Buttock pain radiating down the leg, worse sitting → piriformis syndrome or lumbar radiculopathy
  9. Still symptomatic after 6+ weeks of PT and NSAIDs → corticosteroid injection
Transferable rule When a stem gives a pain quality suggesting one mechanism and physical findings suggesting another, the findings win. "Burning" and "shooting" are how patients describe pain, not how you localize a lesion.

Inflammatory Back Pain & Spondyloarthritis

Two causes of night pain, opposite behavior

The decision point

Inflammatory back pain is defined by its relationship to rest and activity: age <40, insidious onset >3 months, worse at night and with rest, better with movement — the exact inverse of mechanical pain. The mechanism is enthesitis: inflammation where tendons and ligaments insert into bone, as opposed to RA's synovitis.

Inflammatory vs mechanical back pain
InflammatoryMechanical
Age of onset<40Any
OnsetInsidious, >3 monthsOften acute, identifiable event
Night painYes — second half of the nightUsually absent
Morning stiffness>30 minutes<30 minutes
Rest / activityWorse with rest, better with movementBetter with rest, worse with activity
NSAID responseDramaticVariable
The discriminator worth extracting Both inflammatory back pain and malignancy wake patients at night. The separator: inflammatory pain improves once you get up and move; malignant pain is unrelieved, and comes with age >50, prior cancer, or weight loss. Same symptom, opposite response to activity.
The spondyloarthritis family — "PAIR" Psoriatic arthritis · Ankylosing spondylitis · IBD-associated · Reactive arthritis. All seronegative (RF-negative), HLA-B27-associated, sharing enthesitis, dactylitis, and uveitis.
Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Young men; HLA-B27 ~90% (supportive, not diagnostic)
  • Sacroiliitis is the earliest finding → X-ray of the SI joints first; MRI if the X-ray is normal and suspicion is high
  • Exam: reduced Schober test, reduced chest expansion, loss of lumbar lordosis; late bamboo spine
  • Extra-articular: anterior uveitis (25–40%), aortitis → aortic regurgitation, AV block, apical pulmonary fibrosis, IgA nephropathy, and a rigid spine that fractures with minor trauma
  • Treatment: NSAIDs + exercise first-line → TNF-α or IL-17 inhibitors. Methotrexate and sulfasalazine work for peripheral disease but not axial. Screen for latent TB before a TNF inhibitor.
Scenario bank
  1. Normal SI joint X-ray with high suspicion → MRI of the SI joints
  2. Develops a red painful eye with photophobia → anterior uveitis → topical steroid + cycloplegic
  3. New diastolic murmur → aortic regurgitation from aortitis
  4. New neck pain after a minor fall → spinal fracture — a rigid spine is brittle → CT
  5. Age 55, prior breast cancer, night pain not relieved by moving, weight loss → metastasis → MRI
  6. Age >60, leg pain walking, relieved leaning on a shopping cart → spinal stenosis
  7. Radiation below the knee with a positive straight-leg raise → radiculopathy
  8. Young man 2 weeks after dysentery with asymmetric lower-limb arthritis, conjunctivitis, urethritis → reactive arthritis
  9. Older diabetic with flowing anterior spinal ossification and spared SI joints → DISH, not spondyloarthritis
Transferable rule When a symptom appears in two categories, find the modifier that separates them — here, what happens when the patient gets up. Symptoms rarely discriminate; symptom behavior does.

Osteoarthritis Pharmacotherapy

Class vs. member

The decision point

A keyed answer can look like it contradicts a guideline when the right class is represented by the wrong member. "NSAIDs are first-line for knee OA" is correct — but if the only NSAID offered is ketorolac, a drug with a hard 5-day maximum because of GI, renal, and bleeding risk, then it is disqualified for a 6-month condition in a 72-year-old, and acetaminophen wins by default.

Guideline currency ACR/Arthritis Foundation 2019 strongly recommends topical NSAIDs for knee OA (upgraded from conditional in 2012) and strongly recommends oral NSAIDs, while acetaminophen was downgraded to conditional — framed for patients unable to take NSAIDs, with small effect sizes in trials. Older NBME items still key acetaminophen. Patient factors here also favor it: age 72 (GI, renal, CV risk) and pain rated 3/10.
Osteoarthritis pharmacotherapy ladder
TierIntervention
AlwaysExercise (strongly recommended) · weight loss — with BMI 35, the highest-value intervention · self-management programs
First-line drug, kneeTopical NSAIDs — preferred in the elderly, minimal systemic exposure
NextOral NSAIDs — lowest effective dose, add a PPI if GI risk
ConditionalAcetaminophen (limited efficacy) · duloxetine · topical capsaicin
AdjunctIntra-articular glucocorticoid injection
Recommended againstOpioids · hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate (strongly against) · glucosamine · oral glucocorticoids (strongly against)
DefinitiveJoint replacement for refractory disease
How the stem pre-excludes inflammatory arthritis No fever, no morning stiffness, no synovitis, crepitus present — that is mechanical, not inflammatory, which kills hydroxychloroquine and prednisone before you weigh them. Oral steroids are strongly recommended against in OA; the accepted steroid route is intra-articular.
Scenario bank
  1. Same patient with topical diclofenac among the choices → that becomes the answer
  2. Knee OA with CKD or prior GI bleed → topical NSAID or acetaminophen, avoid systemic NSAIDs
  3. Refractory pain despite NSAIDs and PT → intra-articular glucocorticoid
  4. Morning stiffness >1 hour with symmetric MCP/PIP synovitis → this is RA, not OA → RF/anti-CCP, DMARDs
  5. Acute monoarticular knee with warmth and effusion → arthrocentesis before any pharmacotherapy
  6. End-stage disease, failed all conservative measures → joint replacement
Transferable rule When a question asks for "initial pharmacotherapy," read which specific agent represents each class. A class can be right while the offered member is wrong — ketorolac for chronic OA, gentamicin for simple cystitis, chloramphenicol for otitis. Don't reject a guideline; check the drug.
Class-vs-member

Septic Bursitis

Prepatellar & subacromial · aspirate the bursa, not the joint

The decision point

Localized bursal swelling with erythema and warmth, but preserved joint range of motion = the pathology is extraarticular. That single exam finding separates septic bursitis from septic arthritis and decides which space gets the needle. When infection is plausible — erythema, warmth, fever (~40%), or worsening pain days after an injection — aspirate the bursal fluid (cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystals) before any empiric therapy.

Defining criteria Bursitis vs arthritis — bursal infection spares the joint: ROM preserved, swelling localized over the bursa · Aspiration gate — erythema/warmth, fever, or post-procedure worsening → bursal fluid analysis · Drainage gate — failure to improve after ~2 days of antibiotics · Timing tell — post-injection steroid flare starts fast and resolves within 48 h; infection worsens over several days
Septic bursitis — quick reference
AxisFindings
Risk factorsLocal cellulitis, abrasions, penetrating trauma, bursal injection/instrumentation; diabetes and immunocompromise raise risk
PresentationPainful localized bursal swelling with erythema & warmth; fever in ~40%, less prominent age ≥65
OrganismsSkin flora — S aureus most common; S pyogenes
DiagnosisBursal fluid aspiration — cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystal analysis; x-ray only for suspected fracture or foreign body
TreatmentSystemic antibiotics; drainage if not improving after ~2 days
Scenario bank
  1. 45 yo M floor installer, boggy prepatellar swelling, erythema, warmth, knee ROM intact → aspirate the bursal fluid → infection must be excluded before gout or overuse bursitis is presumed
  2. 52 yo M, red, hot, tender prepatellar swelling with fever; full painless passive knee motion → septic prepatellar bursitis
  3. 58 yo F, worsening shoulder pain, fever, and myalgias 4 days after a subacromial corticosteroid injection → image-guided aspiration of the bursa → iatrogenic inoculation of skin flora
  4. 60 yo M, severe shoulder pain 6 hours after a corticosteroid injection, afebrile, resolving by the next day → post-injection steroid flare → chemical synovitis, self-limited within 48 h
  5. 49 yo M with septic prepatellar bursitis, no improvement after 3 days of antibiotics → incision and drainage of the bursa
  6. 70 yo M, diffusely swollen knee, severe pain with any passive motion, fever → septic arthritis → aspirate the joint
Pearls Serum uric acid never rules infection in or out — even a high level cannot replace aspiration · corticosteroid injection is contraindicated when infection is suspected · subacromial bursa can communicate with the glenohumeral joint, so bursal infection may become septic arthritis · fever is absent in most elderly patients with septic bursitis.
Pairs with Part II The Acute Hot Joint (adult) — same rule, different space: any hot fluid collection is aspirated before treatment. Store the discriminator: "is joint motion preserved?"
Transferable rule The needle goes where the infection is: preserved joint motion moves the aspiration from the joint to the bursa — and no empiric therapy (antibiotics, colchicine, steroids) precedes the fluid.
Mirror twinSteroid flare is the benign twin of iatrogenic infection — the discriminator is the clock, not the severity.
Sequencing trapAntibiotics, colchicine, or a repeat injection offered before the bursal fluid has been sampled.

Septic Arthritis of the Hip

Surgical emergency · Kocher criteria

The decision point

Score the Kocher criteria: fever >38.5 °C, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40, WBC >12,000 (CRP >2.0 often added as a fifth). Three criteria ≈ 93% probability, four ≈ 99% → arthrocentesis. Hip held flexed, abducted, externally rotated maximizes capsular volume — but that position occurs in transient synovitis too and discriminates nothing.

Defining criteria Kocher criteria — fever >38.5 °C, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40, WBC >12,000 (CRP >2.0 often added as a fifth) · Scoring — one point per criterion present, unweighted; probability climbs with the count (ladder below) · Aspiration gate — ≥3 of 4 → arthrocentesis · Septic fluid — synovial WBC >50,000, PMN-predominant
Kocher score ladderprobability of septic arthritis by predictor count
Predictors presentProbability of septic arthritisAction
0<0.2%Consistent with transient synovitis — observe, re-examine
1~3%Observation with close follow-up
2~40%Gray zone — ultrasound ± aspiration by clinical picture; 2/4 alone sits below the aspiration gate
3≈93%Arthrocentesis
4≈99.6%Arthrocentesis — surgical urgency Kocher, JBJS 1999 derivation (n=282)
Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo M, T 39.1, refuses to bear weight, ESR 62, WBC 15,000 → arthrocentesis → 4/4 Kocher predictors (≈99.6%); cultures before antibiotics
  2. 3 yo M, febrile, hip held flexed, abducted and externally rotated → septic arthritis of the hip → urgent aspiration
  3. 3 yo M, afebrile and walking with a limp 10 days after a URI; ultrasound shows a small hip effusion → transient synovitis → effusion occurs in both conditions and discriminates nothing; NSAIDs and re-examination
  4. 3 yo M with culture-confirmed septic arthritis of the hip → surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics
  5. 2 yo M with sickle cell disease, fever, refuses to bear weight; beyond S aureus, empiric coverage must include → Salmonella
  6. 10 mo F, afebrile, asymmetric thigh folds, positive Ortolani → developmental dysplasia of the hip → ultrasound
  7. 3 yo M with a septic hip; why delay is dangerous → femoral head osteonecrosis from raised intracapsular pressure
Sequencing Aspirate before antibiotics. Synovial fluid >50,000 WBC (PMN-predominant) confirms it. Septic hip is a surgical emergency — delayed drainage causes femoral head AVN and growth arrest. Organisms: S. aureus overall, Kingella <4 years, gonococcus in adolescents, Salmonella in sickle cell disease.
Septic joint vs. osteomyelitis Septic joint = passive ROM excruciating. Osteomyelitis = ROM relatively preserved with point tenderness over the metaphysis.

Transient Synovitis Mirror twin

The benign version of the same stem

The decision point

Kocher 0–1 of 4. Well-appearing, afebrile, limps but walks, post-viral URI 1–2 weeks prior. A small effusion on ultrasound is a decoy — it is present in both twins. Management is NSAIDs and follow-up.

Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M, well-appearing, afebrile, limps but walks, URI 10 days ago, ESR 18 → transient synovitis → NSAIDs and follow-up
  2. 5 yo M limping after a URI, but T 39.0 and refusing to bear weight → arthrocentesis → ≥3 of 4 Kocher predictors; the febrile twin, not the benign one
  3. 5 yo M, afebrile and well-appearing with a limp; ultrasound shows a small hip effusion → transient synovitis → effusion occurs in both conditions and discriminates nothing — the Kocher score decides
  4. 5 yo M with transient synovitis still limping at 4 weeks → re-image — synovitis should have resolved
  5. 6 yo M, insidious limp over 2 months, afebrile, normal labs → Legg-Calvé-Perthes → hip X-ray
  6. 5 yo M with a limp plus night pain waking him and easy bruising → CBC with smear → evaluate for leukemia
Why this one gets people It arrives right after you learn septic arthritis. The lesson you should store from a septic-hip miss is never "limping child → aspirate"; it is "limping child → score Kocher." A rule stored as an outcome fires indiscriminately; stored as a test, it self-corrects.
Mirror twin

The Limping Child — Master Table

Sick or well → acute or chronic → age

The limping child — the differential
DiagnosisThe pictureThe NBME tell
Septic arthritis EmergencyAcute, febrile, toxic, refuses to bear weightKocher 3–4/4 → aspirate before antibiotics
Transient synovitis3–8 yrPost-viral URI; afebrile, well, walks with a limpKocher 0–1/4; effusion is a decoy
OsteomyelitisSubacute fever + bone pain; ROM preservedPoint tenderness over metaphysis → MRI
LCPLegg-Calvé-Perthes, boys 4–9Insidious limp over weeks–months, afebrileChronic + normal labs → X-ray/MRI; ↓ abduction and internal rotation
SCFEslipped capital femoral epiphysis · growth spurt, girls 11–13, boys 13–15 · obesity is a risk factor, NOT a requirement — also occurs in tall, thin adolescentsInsidious thigh or KNEE pain (obturator referral) + limp; minor trauma often prompts the visit but did not cause itLoss of internal rotation; obligate external rotation on flexion → frog-leg X-ray of BOTH hips → pin in situ
DDHdevelopmental dysplasia, infantBreech, female, family historyBarlow / Ortolani → US if <4–6 mo → Pavlik harness
Toddler's fracture1–3 yrNew limp after a minor, often unwitnessed twistSpiral tibia on X-ray; metaphyseal corner / bucket-handle = abuse
JIAjuvenile idiopathic arthritis>6 weeks of symptoms, morning stiffnessDuration IS the diagnosis; ± ANA → slit-lamp for uveitis
Acute rheumatic feverMigratory arthritis 2–4 wks post-pharyngitisJONES + ASO; a new murmur seals it
Leukemia / bone tumor Can't missNight pain that wakes from sleep, fatigue, bruisingCytopenias — CBC + smear before calling anything benign
Psoas abscess / appendicitis"Hip pain" with a normal hip jointPain on hip extension (psoas sign)
Decision spine 1. Sick or well? 2. Acute (days = infection/synovitis/fracture) or chronic (weeks–months = LCP, SCFE, JIA, tumor)? 3. Age picks the disease: infant DDH · 1–3 toddler's fracture · 3–8 synovitis/LCP · 10–16 SCFE (any body habitus — obesity raises risk but is not required). 4. Night pain, weight loss, or bruising overrides everything → CBC. 5. Knee pain in a child = examine the hip.
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo M, fever 39, non-weight-bearing, ESR 55, WBC 14,000 → septic arthritis → aspirate before antibiotics
  2. 12 mo F, breech delivery, asymmetric thigh folds, positive Barlow → developmental dysplasia of the hip
  3. 2 yo M, limp after an unwitnessed fall, tibial tenderness, afebrile → toddler's fracture
  4. 13 yo M with obesity, knee pain and reduced hip internal rotation → slipped capital femoral epiphysis → frog-leg lateral of both hips
  5. 10 yo M with 8 weeks of joint symptoms and morning stiffness → juvenile idiopathic arthritis → slit-lamp exam for uveitis
  6. 8 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis 3 weeks after pharyngitis → acute rheumatic fever
  7. 6 yo M with night pain that wakes him, bruising and fatigue → leukemia → CBC with smear
Correction worth internalizing "SCFE = obese teenager" is a stereotype stored as a rule, and stems defeat it deliberately. The physis is weak during any rapid growth spurt, so tall, thin adolescents get SCFE too. The real discriminators are age at the growth spurt, loss of internal rotation, and obligate external rotation on passive flexion — not body habitus. And when SCFE appears in an atypical patient (age <10 or >16, short stature, very thin), screen for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, panhypopituitarism, hypogonadism, or renal osteodystrophy.

Systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

Still disease · the three-category matrix

The decision point

Chronic arthritis + quotidian fever + evanescent salmon rash. The subtle confirmatory detail: quotidian fever spikes once or twice daily and returns to normal or subnormal between spikes — so being afebrile in clinic supports sJIA. Infection doesn't do that.

Systemic JIA vs infection vs malignancy
InfectiousInflammatoryNeoplastic
OnsetAcuteSubacute / chronicSubacute / chronic
Pain timingConstantWorse in the morningWorse at night, wakes from sleep
Bears weight?NoYesVariable
Labs↑WBC, ↑plt, ↑↑ESR↑WBC, ↑plt, ↑↑ESR, ↓RBC↓WBC, ↓plt (cytopenias)
Criteria and complications
  • Quotidian fever ≥2 weeks + arthritis ≥6 weeks + salmon-pink macular rash with fever spikes (± Koebner)
  • Hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, serositis/pericarditis
  • Labs: leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, anemia of inflammation, very high ferritin; ANA and RF typically negative
  • Treatment: NSAIDs, steroids, IL-1 blockade (anakinra, canakinumab) or IL-6 blockade (tocilizumab)
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo F, 3 weeks of fever spiking once daily to 39.5 and returning to normal, salmon rash, arthritis → systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
  2. 5 yo F with 2 weeks of daily fever spikes and an evanescent rash, afebrile at the afternoon visit → continue the sJIA evaluation → quotidian fever returns to baseline between spikes; a normal clinic temperature excludes nothing
  3. 5 yo F with sJIA, now falling ESR with cytopenias, high ferritin and triglycerides → macrophage activation syndrome
  4. 5 yo F with fever, rash and arthritis; ANA positive, RF negative → systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
  5. 5 yo F whose joint symptoms have lasted only 3 weeks → JIA requires 6 weeks of symptoms
  6. 5 yo F with oligoarticular JIA and a positive ANA → slit-lamp exam for asymptomatic uveitis
Macrophage activation syndrome A systemic JIA patient who suddenly deteriorates with cytopenias, ferritin in the thousands, hypertriglyceridemia, liver dysfunction, DIC — and a paradoxically FALLING ESR (fibrinogen consumed). That inverted ESR is the pathognomonic tell. Treat with high-dose steroids ± anakinra.
Uveitis rule Oligoarticular (≤4 joints, young girls, ANA+) = highest uveitis risk → slit-lamp every 3–4 months. Systemic (Still) = lowest. Enthesitis-related (HLA-B27, older boys) = acute symptomatic uveitis.
True-fact-wrong-slot

Nursemaid's Elbow

Radial head subluxation · reading the exam block

The decision point

In the newer "Patient Information" format, the treatment is often buried inside the physical exam section. "When the forearm is supinated and the elbow flexed… she begins to reach for toys 15 minutes later" is the reduction and is the confirmation it worked. The answer is what comes after a successful reduction: nothing.

  • Mechanism: axial traction on an extended, pronated arm; peak ages 1–4, rare after 5
  • Pathology: annular ligament slips over the radial head into the radiocapitellar joint
  • Exam: arm held extended and pronated, with no swelling, no deformity, no point tenderness — those three absences permit a clinical diagnosis
  • Reduction: hyperpronation, or supination + flexion; use returns within minutes
  • After success: no imaging, no sling, no NSAIDs, no restrictions. Recurrence ~25%
  • If reduction fails (two attempts) → X-ray for occult fracture
Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo F pulled up by the wrist, holds the arm pronated, refuses to use it, no swelling → radial head subluxation → supination-flexion reduction
  2. 3 yo F reaching for toys 15 minutes after the manoeuvre → no further intervention → the manoeuvre was both the treatment and the confirmation of reduction
  3. 3 yo F with elbow swelling and refusal to move it after a fall onto an outstretched hand → supracondylar fracture → elbow X-ray
  4. 3 yo F with a supracondylar fracture and an absent radial pulse → brachial artery injury → urgent orthopedic evaluation
  5. 3 yo F with a second episode of nursemaid's elbow this year → counsel against axial traction — recurrence is common
  6. 10 mo M with a spiral humerus fracture and an inconsistent history → non-accidental trauma → skeletal survey
When it is NOT nursemaid's Swelling, ecchymosis, or deformity · point tenderness over bone · age >5 · a mechanism that doesn't fit the injury, or no mechanism at all → consider non-accidental trauma. Any fracture in a non-ambulatory infant → skeletal survey (<2 yrs) and report. Abuse patterns: metaphyseal corner / bucket-handle, posterior rib fractures, multiple fractures at different healing stages.
Pediatric elbow neighbors Supracondylar humerus fracture — 5–8 yrs, FOOSH hyperextension, posterior fat pad sign; check the anterior interosseous nerve ("OK sign") and brachial artery; watch for Volkmann ischemic contracture · newborn not moving an arm after shoulder dystocia with an asymmetric Moro → clavicle fracture or brachial plexus injury (Erb C5–C6 "waiter's tip"; Klumpke C8–T1 claw hand).

Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

The stereotype that stems are built to defeat

The decision point

"SCFE = obese teenager" is a stereotype stored as a rule, and question-writers defeat it deliberately. The physis is mechanically weak during any rapid growth spurt, so tall, thin adolescents get SCFE too. The real discriminators are age at the growth spurt (girls 11–13, boys 13–15), loss of internal rotation, and obligate external rotation on passive flexion — not body habitus.

Defining criteria Age window — the growth spurt: girls 11–13, boys 13–15 · Exam criteria — loss of internal rotation, obligate external rotation on passive hip flexion · Imaging — AP + frog-leg lateral of both hips
Two familiar decoys "Runny nose last week" — the post-URI transient synovitis bait, planted where the age and a 3-week course forbid it. "Fell while skateboarding" — the fracture bait; minor trauma exacerbating a weeks-long insidious problem is classic SCFE, whereas a pediatric femoral neck fracture needs high-impact trauma and shows a fracture line.
  • Pathology: the epiphysis displaces posteroinferiorly through the hypertrophic zone of the physis — "ice cream slipping off the cone"
  • Imaging: AP + frog-leg lateral of BOTH hips. Klein's line along the superior femoral neck should intersect the epiphysis — it fails to in SCFE
  • Stable vs. unstable: can bear weight vs. cannot bear weight — unstable carries AVN risk approaching 50%
  • Treatment: immediate non-weight-bearing (do not let the patient walk) plus urgent in situ screw fixation. Never attempt reduction — it increases AVN
  • Bilateral in 20–40% — image the other hip; some pin it prophylactically
  • Complications: AVN, chondrolysis, early osteoarthritis
Scenario bank
  1. SCFE in a short, thin 9-year-old → screen for hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, panhypopituitarism, renal osteodystrophy
  2. Cannot bear weight at all → unstable SCFE → highest AVN risk → urgent fixation, no reduction
  3. Contralateral hip asymptomatic → still image it; 20–40% bilateral
  4. Knee pain with a completely normal knee exam in an adolescent → examine the hip
  5. Boy 5–7, insidious limp, normal labs, femoral head fragmentation → Legg-Calvé-Perthes
  6. Same age with fever, refusal to bear weight, ESR 90 → septic arthritis → aspirate
  7. Well-appearing 5-year-old post-URI, limps but walks, normal X-ray → transient synovitis
  8. Months after fixation, new groin pain with joint space narrowing → chondrolysis or AVN
  9. Adolescent athlete, groin pain, normal X-ray, pain on hopping → femoral neck stress fracture → MRI
Transferable rule Demographic stereotypes are priors with exceptions, and exceptions are what question-writers write. When a patient violates the classic demographic but matches the exam findings, the findings win — and an atypical demographic is itself a prompt to ask why.
Mirror twinTrue-fact-wrong-slot
4 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Musculoskeletal & Rheumatology

The Acute Hot Joint (adult)

Aspirate before you treat

The decision point

An acute hot, swollen, erythematous joint with severe pain on passive range of motion and fever gets aspirated — and the reason is stronger than "this looks septic." Nothing on exam can exclude infection, gout and septic arthritis overlap completely, and a missed septic joint destroys cartilage in days. Aspiration is diagnostic and therapeutic.

The comorbidities point the opposite way from how they read. Obesity, hypertension, and diabetes feel like "metabolic → gout" — but diabetes is a septic arthritis risk factor, and joint space narrowing on x-ray means preexisting joint disease, another one.

Synovial fluid analysisWBC & PMN interpretation
Synovial fluidWBCPMNInterpretation
Non-inflammatory (OA)200–2,000 ⚠︎<25%Degenerative
Inflammatory (gout, RA)2,000–50,000 ⚠︎>50%Crystal or autoimmune
Septic>50,000, often >100k>75%Drain + IV antibiotics
Crystals Gout — negatively birefringent needles (monosodium urate). Pseudogout — positively birefringent rhomboids (CPPD), with chondrocalcinosis on x-ray. Serum uric acid is useless acutely — often normal during a flare (urate shifts into the joint) and elevated in many who never flare.
Management ladder — the acute hot joint
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Arthrocentesis — cell count + differential, Gram stain, culture, crystalsAlways, for any acute hot joint
2Empiric IV antibiotics after cultures drawn — vancomycin ± ceftriaxone/cefepimePurulent fluid or >50,000 WBC; do not wait for culture
3Joint drainage — serial aspiration, arthroscopic, or open washoutConfirmed septic arthritis
Scenario bank
  1. 47 yo F, hot knee, aspirate 68,000 WBC, 85% PMN, no crystals → septic arthritis → vancomycin + drainage
  2. 55 yo M, acute first-MTP pain after a steak dinner, aspirate 12,000 WBC, negatively birefringent needles → gout → NSAID or colchicine
  3. 72 yo F, hot knee, x-ray shows chondrocalcinosis, positively birefringent rhomboids → pseudogout
  4. 47 yo F, aspirate shows crystals AND 60,000 WBC → treat as septic — crystals do not exclude coexisting infection
  5. 68 yo M with a knee prosthesis, aspirate 3,000 WBC, 70% PMN → prosthetic joint infection — the 50,000 threshold does not apply ⚠︎
  6. 24 yo F, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, pustular rash → disseminated gonococcal → NAAT + cultures
  7. 47 yo F with cellulitis overlying the knee → don't pass a needle through infected skin → image-guided or alternate approach
  8. 60 yo M with sickle cell, hot joint → add Salmonella to coverage
Trap autopsy Naproxen — skipped tier; treats an unestablished diagnosis and delays drainage. Serum uric acid — wrong parameter; neither rules in nor out. Intra-articular corticosteroid — actively contraindicated into a possibly infected joint. MRI — redundant; the x-ray is done and there's no trauma.
Pairs with Part I Septic Arthritis of the Hip, Transient Synovitis (pediatric), and Septic Bursitis — the extraarticular mimic, where preserved joint motion moves the needle from joint to bursa. Note the asymmetry: tier 1 has no fork in adults — every acute hot joint aspirates. The pediatric twin is the only place the answer diverges, and it diverges on toxicity and inflammatory signs, not on the presence of fluid.
Transferable rule When a test is both diagnostic and therapeutic and the disease it excludes is time-destructive, it precedes every treatment option — even one that would be right for the more likely diagnosis. You don't aspirate because it's probably septic; you aspirate because you can't prove it isn't.
Skipped tierWrong parameter

Acute Low Back Pain with No Red Flags

A wall of negatives is permission to do less

The decision point

Acute (<4–6 weeks) back pain with a clear mechanical trigger and a completely normal neurologic exam, in a stem that spends its sentences deleting red flags. Nothing licenses imaging or escalation → NSAIDs + stay active.

Stem findings → options ruled out
Stem lineWhat it kills
"no fever, chills"Osteomyelitis, discitis, epidural abscess
"no constipation or urinary incontinence"Cauda equina
"no tenderness over the spine" (paraspinal only)Fracture, malignancy, infection
"DTRs normal, strength intact, sensation normal"Radiculopathy with objective deficit
"began 1 day after moving furniture"Supplies the mechanical cause
Management ladder — acute low back pain
TierInterventionEscalate when
1NSAIDs + stay active (avoid bed rest); ± heat, ± short muscle relaxantNo improvement at 4–6 weeks, or a red flag appears
2Physical therapy; MRI if radicular symptoms persistRadicular symptoms ≥6 weeks
3Epidural steroid injectionFailed conservative therapy
4Surgical referralProgressive deficit, cauda equina, refractory pain
Trap autopsy Bed rest — actively harmful; bed rest delays recovery. A reversed-teaching item: the old advice is now the wrong answer. CT lumbosacral spine — wrong twice: no indication at 1 week, and wrong modality (MRI images disc and nerve root). Epidural injection — skipped tier, needs ≥4–6 weeks of failed conservative care. Oral prednisone — systemic steroids do not improve outcomes in acute sciatica.
Why the no-imaging rule exists Early imaging leads to more surgery without better outcomes. Asymptomatic disc bulges and degenerative change are near-universal by middle age, so a scan mostly generates incidental findings that invite intervention. Also: ~90% of acute low back pain and ~90% of sciatica resolve within 6 weeks.
Scenario bank
  1. 47 yo F, same pain now at 8 weeks with persistent L5 symptoms, normal strength → MRI, PT, consider epidural
  2. 47 yo F, new urinary retention and saddle anesthesia → emergent MRI + decompression
  3. 47 yo F, new foot drop → progressive deficit → urgent MRI
  4. 62 yo F with prior breast cancer, pain worse at night, unrelieved by rest → MRI for metastasis
  5. 34 yo M, 3 months, better with activity, worse with rest, morning stiffness >30 min → inflammatory → SI joint imaging, HLA-B27
  6. 68 yo M, leg pain walking, relieved leaning forward → spinal stenosis
  7. 28 yo M who injects drugs, back pain with fever and focal spinal tenderness → MRI + blood cultures
  8. 72 yo F on chronic prednisone, pain after a minor fall → X-ray for compression fracture
  9. 47 yo F with CKD and prior GI bleed, same presentation → same tier, different agent: acetaminophen or topical NSAID
Pairs with Part I Low Back Pain Red Flags and Inflammatory Back Pain. This is the third member of the family and the one with no red flags. Store the discriminator as a question: "Any red flag, and is the neuro exam normal?"
Transferable rule When a stem spends most of its sentences on what the patient doesn't have, it is building a case for doing less. A dense list of pertinent negatives is permission for conservative management.
Skipped tierClass-vs-member

Transient Synovitis: Management

A completed investigation closes its tier

The decision point

The ultrasound was already performed and answered its question — small effusion, joint characterized. Ordering an X-ray after a completed, diagnostic ultrasound in a child with no trauma and no bony tenderness is redundant workup. Imaging tier closed; treatment tier empty; lowest untried rung is ibuprofen.

"Results of laboratory studies are pending" is itself a ledger entry — it means the answer doesn't depend on them. If labs decided this question, the examiner would have given the values.

The stem ledgerdone / normal / elapsed — and what each entry rules out
LedgerEntryKills
DoneUltrasonography → small effusionX-ray, MRI
Normal"appears well," vitals normal, no tenderness, no traumaBoth antibiotics; fracture; osteomyelitis
Elapsed1 day of pain; URI 10 days ago—
BotheredLimping, ROM limited by painPure observation
Kocher, with what you have Fever >38.5 no · non-weight-bearing no (he walks with a limp) · ESR >40 pending · WBC >12,000 pending. Two known criteria negative; even if both pending values returned positive that's 2/4 — below the aspiration threshold. Kocher is clinic-ledger — not stated in the bank explanation for either this or the septic-arthritis stem.
Management ladder — the limping child after workup
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Rest + NSAIDs, activity as toleratedFever develops · refuses to bear weight · no improvement in 24–48 h ⚠︎
2CBC, ESR, CRP + re-examine → score Kocher≥3 criteria or deterioration
3ArthrocentesisKocher 3–4/4, or effusion with toxicity
4Surgical drainage + IV antibioticsPurulent fluid, >50,000 WBC
Exit ramps & stop criteria Fever → septic pathway · refuses to bear weight → Kocher climbs · point tenderness over bone → osteomyelitis → MRI · not resolving past 1–2 weeks ⚠︎ → Legg-Calvé-Perthes → X-ray · age 10–16 → SCFE → frog-leg lateral · night pain, bruising, weight loss → CBC with smear.
Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo M, post-URI limp, T 39.2, refuses to bear weight, ESR 78 → Kocher 3+/4 → arthrocentesis before antibiotics
  2. 4 yo M, well-appearing, point tenderness over the femoral metaphysis → osteomyelitis → MRI
  3. 6 yo M, insidious limp over 6 weeks, normal labs → Legg-Calvé-Perthes → X-ray becomes correct when the timeline is chronic
  4. 13 yo M, 95th %ile height, 3 weeks of thigh pain, ↓ internal rotation → SCFE → frog-leg lateral of both hips
  5. 4 yo M, limp with night pain waking him, bruising → CBC with smear
  6. 2 yo M, limp after unwitnessed fall, tibial tenderness → toddler's fracture → tibia X-ray
  7. 4 yo M on ibuprofen, still limping at 3 weeks → re-image; synovitis should have resolved
  8. 4 yo M, aspirate 80,000 WBC, PMN-predominant → septic arthritis → drainage + IV antibiotics
Warning about the common mnemonic "Post-viral limp = ibuprofen, not imaging" is an outcome, not a discriminator — and it fails on bank item 1, where a post-viral limp with fever is septic arthritis. Store the question instead: "Is he toxic, and has the joint already been imaged?"
Pairs with Part I Transient Synovitis and Septic Arthritis of the Hip. Part I settles which disease; this settles what to do.
Transferable rule A completed, reported investigation closes its tier. When the stem hands you a result, every option that re-opens that tier in a different modality is dead — and the discomfort you feel choosing treatment over one more test is the trap working.
Redundant workupMirror twin

Congenital Muscular Torticollis and Plagiocephaly

Tilt toward the mass, chin away · UWorld · the ear tells you which flat head

The decision point

Torticollis has a direction, and the direction is the diagnosis. The sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the opposite side, so a shortened left muscle pulls the left ear toward the left shoulder and swings the chin right — exactly the geometry described, with the mass in the left sternocleidomastoid. The flat head is downstream: she can only look one way, so she lies on one spot.

The etiology is in the delivery note. Breech presentation means intrauterine crowding, the same mechanism that produces developmental dysplasia of the hip, metatarsus adductus and clubfoot. The non-transilluminating mass is the sentence written to stop you answering the neck lump instead of the syndrome.

Defining criteria Congenital muscular torticollis — head tilts toward the tight sternocleidomastoid, chin rotates away from it · Positional plagiocephaly — flat occiput with the ipsilateral ear and forehead displaced anteriorly, a parallelogram skull · Lambdoid craniosynostosis — flat occiput with the ipsilateral ear displaced posteriorly, a trapezoid skull with a palpable ridge
The infant with a neck mass or flat head — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Congenital muscular torticollisIntrauterine crowding — breech, twins, oligohydramniosTilt toward, chin away, firm non-transilluminating sternocleidomastoid mass
Positional plagiocephalySupine sleep, car seats, limited neck rotationIpsilateral ear pushed forward; parallelogram
CraniosynostosisPremature suture closureIpsilateral ear pushed backward, palpable ridge, no neck mass
Cystic hygromaCongenital lymphatic malformation, aneuploidy associationFluctuant and transilluminates, posterior triangle
Clavicle fractureShoulder dystociaCrepitus and arm pseudoparalysis, not a neck tilt
Posterior fossa tumor Can't missAcquired tilt in an older childCranial nerve palsies and papilledema, no neck mass
Scenario bank
  1. 2 mo F, right occipital flattening with the right ear pushed forward, tilts left with chin right, firm left sternocleidomastoid mass, breech delivery → congenital muscular torticollis → repositioning, tummy time and physical therapy
  2. 3 mo F, flat right occiput with the right ear anterior, full neck range of motion, sleeps supine → positional plagiocephaly → repositioning and tummy time
  3. 4 mo M, flat right occiput with the right ear displaced posteriorly, a palpable ridge, no neck mass → craniosynostosis → head CT and craniofacial referral
  4. Newborn F with a soft, fluctuant posterior-triangle neck mass that transilluminates → cystic hygroma → karyotype and imaging
  5. Newborn after shoulder dystocia, not moving the right arm, with crepitus over the clavicle → clavicle fracture → reassurance and gentle immobilization
  6. 8 yo M with a new head tilt, morning vomiting, papilledema and a sixth nerve palsy → posterior fossa tumor → MRI of the brain
  7. 3 wk M with a painless firm neck mass who tilts toward it, delivered breech → congenital muscular torticollis
  8. 2 mo F with congenital muscular torticollis, what else must be examined for → developmental dysplasia of the hip → hip ultrasound
  9. 2 mo F with torticollis and a positive Ortolani and Barlow maneuver → developmental dysplasia of the hip → Pavlik harness
  10. 6 mo F with congenital muscular torticollis and no improvement after 3 months of stretching → refer to pediatric orthopedics
Crowding is a package deal Breech, oligohydramnios and multiple gestation produce congenital muscular torticollis, developmental dysplasia of the hip, metatarsus adductus and clubfoot together. Find one and examine for the rest — the stem's explicit note that the hips are stable is the examiner confirming they know this.
Pearls Cystic hygroma is soft, fluctuant and transilluminates; the torticollis mass is firm and does not · Missed or delayed treatment leads to permanent craniofacial asymmetry · Treatment is positioning, tummy time, passive stretching and physical therapy, with helmets reserved for severe or refractory plagiocephaly · An acquired head tilt in an older child with any neurologic sign is a posterior fossa tumour until imaged
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves shares the constraint physiology — absent amniotic fluid produces clubfeet and flat facies by the same mechanism that produces torticollis in a breech infant.
Transferable rule When a stem asks for the underlying cause, the answer explains every finding rather than the most alarming one, so count the findings your choice leaves orphaned and reject any option that leaves one behind.
Salient decoyBirth trauma sells the clavicle fracture, which affects the arm rather than the neck.
Mirror twinCraniosynostosis is the other flat-head diagnosis, separated only by which way the ear points.
True-fact-wrong-slotA posterior fossa tumour causes acquired tilt with cranial nerve findings, not a neonatal neck mass.

Pediatrics 3 topics + 6 board-style

Growth, development and the general-paediatric board questions that belong to no single organ. Everything else paediatric is filed under its organ system and reachable from the Pediatrics shelf — age is a filter here, not a category.

Growth & Developmental Milestones

Derive, don't memorize

The decision point

Growth: birth weight is regained by 10–14 days, doubles by 4–6 months, triples by 1 year, quadruples by 2. When numbers match a milestone rule and the exam is normal, the answer is the reassurance option and every distractor is an unnecessary intervention.

The four developmental laws
  • Motor descends the body — 2 mo lifts head · 4 mo head steady + forearms · 6 mo rolls / props on hands · 9 mo sits alone · 12 mo pulls to stand and cruises
  • Grasp moves pinky-side → thumb-side — 4 mo midline · 6 mo whole-hand reach · 9 mo raking · 12 mo pincer
  • Language: vowels → consonants → meaning — 4 mo "ooo" · 6 mo raspberries/squeals · 9 mo "mamama" · 12 mo "mama" meaning mama
  • Social: everyone → someone — 2 mo social smile at anyone · 6 mo familiar faces · 9 mo stranger and separation anxiety · 12 mo social games, object permanence
Age anchors
AgeImageHook
2 moThe Greeter — lifts head, tracks you, smiles, coosTWO eyes track, TWO lips smile
4 moThe Sphinx — head steady on forearms, hands to midline and mouthFOUR = everything to the FORE
6 moThe Roller — rolls, sits propped, mouths toys, laughsSIX: Sits, Squeals, raSpberries
9 moThe Anxious Sitter — sits alone, rakes, babbles, cries at strangersNINE = "No! Not you!"
12 moThe Little Person — cruises, pinches a Cheerio, first wordONE year = ONE word, ONE-finger pinch
Scenario bank
  1. 4 mo M, birth weight 3.2 kg, now 6.6 kg, normal exam → normal — weight doubles by 4 to 6 months → reassurance
  2. 12 mo M whose weight has tripled since birth → normal → reassurance
  3. 10 day M who has not yet regained his birth weight → normal — birth weight is regained by 10 to 14 days → reassurance
  4. 2 mo M who lifts his head and smiles socially → age-appropriate development
  5. 9 mo M who cannot sit without support → gross motor delay → developmental evaluation
  6. 6 mo M who does not babble and does not respond to sound → audiology evaluation
Red flags — worth more points than the milestones No social smile by 3 mo · no babbling by 9 mo · no words by 15 mo · not walking by 18 mo · hand preference before 12 months (suggests hemiparesis) · loss of any acquired milestone at any age — regression is always pathologic (Rett, autistic regression, metabolic disease, leukodystrophy).
Primitive reflexes must leave before the skill arrives Palmar grasp gone 3–6 mo (enables voluntary grasp) · Moro by 6 mo · rooting by 4 mo · ATNR by 4–6 mo · parachute appears 6–8 mo and stays for life · Babinski normal until 12–24 mo. Persistence beyond these windows = UMN lesion / cerebral palsy. Note: the CDC 2022 revision moved milestones from the 50th to the 75th percentile — that's why "sits without support" now sits at 9 months where older sources say 6.
Pairs with Part I Toddler Food Refusal owns the case where growth falters because of how the child eats rather than how much.

Maternal Carryover in Newborn Labs

separate maternal carryover from the baby's own disease · board question · Is the infant voiding, growing and normal on exam — and does the mother's chart explain the number?

The decision point

Creatinine crosses the placenta freely, so a value drawn at 23 hours is a two-patient result — and this mother has end-stage renal disease on regular hemodialysis. The infant's own ledger says the kidneys are working: two voids (the floor is one void per day of life), 3% weight loss (expected is under 10%), normotensive, no edema, no dysmorphism. With no red flag and a maternal source sitting in the history, the number needs no renal explanation of its own.

Defining criteria Neonatal creatinine at birth — equals the mother's value; it falls over the first 2 postnatal weeks to a nadir set by the infant's muscle mass · Urine output floor — at least one void per day of life · Expected weight loss — under 10% of birth weight in the first days · Red flags that make it the baby's kidney — oliguria, edema, or hypertension; any of the three earns a renal ultrasound and a trended creatinine, especially with nephrotoxic drugs or perinatal hypoxia
Pertinent positives & negatives Mother with ESRD on hemodialysis — her creatinine is high and it crosses the placenta; this is the explanation · Two voids at 23 hours — meets the one-void-per-day-of-life floor; excludes renal agenesis and argues against oliguric injury · 3% weight loss — within expected; excludes dehydration and breastfeeding failure as the cause of the number · Apgars 8 and 9 — excludes perinatal asphyxia, and with it hypoxic-ischemic renal injury · Examination otherwise unremarkable — normotensive, no edema, no Potter facies or limb deformity; no red flag, so no imaging is indicated · Total bilirubin 4.3 at 23 hours — normal for age; the jaundice explains why a panel exists, not why the creatinine is high · Intraamniotic infection with ampicillin and cefotaxime — the reason chemistries were drawn at all; neither drug is nephrotoxic, which removes a named risk factor ⚠︎ · Maternal SLE — inert for the creatinine, but it is the setup for the transplacental antibody diseases the same axis generates ⚠︎
An abnormal newborn laboratory value — the differential
ExplanationIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Maternal renal failure (carryover)Creatinine crosses the placenta; the day-1 value is the mother's and falls over 2 weeksA well infant with normal output and a mother with renal disease— (the answer)
Bilateral renal agenesis Can't missOligohydramnios sequence; pulmonary hypoplasiaNo or minimal urine output, respiratory distress, Potter facies and limb deformitiesVoided twice; no distress; normal exam
Hypoxic-ischemic renal injuryPerinatal asphyxia injures the tubules; creatinine rises abnormally over daysLow Apgars and an abnormal neurologic examApgars 8 and 9; exam normal
Dehydration (prerenal)Inadequate intake while feeding is established; prerenal azotemiaWeight loss ≥10% with reduced voids3% loss; two voids
Breastfeeding jaundiceInadequate intake early; explains hyperbilirubinemia, and only reaches creatinine through dehydrationIt answers the bilirubin, not the creatinineBilirubin normal for age; no dehydration
Tier fingerprint done — chemistry and bilirubin drawn as part of the sepsis workup · normal — urine output, weight, blood pressure, examination · elapsed — 23 hours, which is exactly when a maternal value has not yet cleared.
Management ladder — newborn maternal carryover
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Well infant, output and exam normal, maternal source in the chart: document voids and repeat the creatinine in 24–48 hours ⚠︎Oliguria (fewer voids than days of life), edema, hypertension, or a creatinine that fails to fall
2Any red flag, or a risk factor (nephrotoxic drug, perinatal hypoxia): renal ultrasound and trend the creatinine; review the medication listAnuria, a rising creatinine, or electrolyte or fluid derangement
3Nephrology involvement; renal replacement therapy for refractory derangement ⚠︎—
Numbers that gate & exit ramps the one-void-per-day-of-life floor, the 10% weight-loss limit, and the 2-week normalization window — all in-context. · no void by 24 hours with respiratory distress → obstructive uropathy or agenesis, image now · maternal anti-Ro/SSA with fetal or neonatal bradycardia → congenital heart block ⚠︎ · maternal Graves → transplacental TSI and neonatal thyrotoxicosis ⚠︎ · maternal ITP → transplacental antiplatelet IgG and neonatal thrombocytopenia ⚠︎.
Decision spine What was actually asked? — The creatinine — not the jaundice that brought her in · Is the baby making urine? — Two voids at 23 hours → the floor is met · Is she dry? — 3% loss → no · Was there an insult? — Apgars 8 and 9 → no · Does the mother's chart contain the number? — ESRD on hemodialysis → yes, and creatinine crosses the placenta
Scenario bank
  1. 23-hour-old, well, 2 voids, 3% weight loss, creatinine 4.2, mother on hemodialysis for ESRD → Maternal creatinine crossing the placenta → Repeat the value rather than image
  2. Day 4, creatinine still 4.2, one void in 24 hours, mother on hemodialysis → Renal ultrasound and a trended creatinine → The value should have been falling
  3. Day 1, no void in 26 hours, respiratory distress, flat facies and limb deformities → Bilateral renal agenesis → Potter sequence from oligohydramnios
  4. Term infant, Apgars 2 and 4, encephalopathic at 4 hours, creatinine rising on day 2 with oliguria → Therapeutic hypothermia with supportive renal care → Hypoxic-ischemic injury
  5. Day 5, breastfeeding, 12% weight loss, one void in 24 hours, sodium 152, sunken fontanelle → Supervised feeding with supplementation and rehydration → Breastfeeding failure with prerenal azotemia
  6. Day 3, mother with immune thrombocytopenia, infant platelets 40,000, well with no bleeding → Observe with serial platelet counts → Transplacental antiplatelet IgG
  7. Day 5, mother with Graves disease, infant tachycardic and irritable with a goiter → Methimazole with a beta-blocker → Transplacental thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin
  8. Mother with systemic lupus erythematosus; fetal heart rate 55 at 22 weeks, persisting after birth → Maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies crossing the placenta → Congenital complete heart block
  9. 23-hour-old, well, creatinine 4.2 explained by maternal ESRD; which intervention is inappropriate → Initiate neonatal renal replacement therapy → The number is not the infant's
  10. Day 1 creatinine 4.2 from maternal ESRD; which test establishes the infant's own renal function → A repeat serum creatinine over the next 1-2 weeks → The nadir reflects infant muscle mass
Decoy note The delivery paragraph is the whole trap: infection, arrest of labor, cesarean — three details that are compatible with the right answer and suggestive of the wrong one, disarmed by the Apgars two sentences later. The jaundice is a second decoy of a different kind — it is the reason the panel was drawn, so it feels like the thing to explain, and the question deliberately asks about a different value in the same panel. Maternal SLE is inert for the creatinine but not for the topic: it is the entry point to the antibody-mediated members of this same family.
Pearls Day-one creatinine is the mother's; it falls to the infant's own nadir over two weeks, and normal urine output proves the kidneys work. · Creatinine, IgG antibodies, and thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin all cross the placenta, so all three can produce a "neonatal" finding that is really maternal — IgM and TSH do not. · Normal urine output is the cheapest renal function test in a newborn: at least one void per day of life, so two voids on day one is normal and none by 24 hours is not. · Up to 10% weight loss in the first days is expected; beyond that, look for feeding failure with hypernatremia and prerenal azotemia. · Ampicillin and cefotaxime are the non-nephrotoxic sepsis pair; when gentamicin is in the stem instead, a rising creatinine acquires a named risk factor ⚠︎. · The maternal antibody diseases run on one sentence of history each: anti-Ro/SSA → congenital heart block; Graves → neonatal thyrotoxicosis; ITP → neonatal thrombocytopenia; all transient as maternal IgG clears ⚠︎.
Pairs with Verified: Part II Posterior Urethral Valves and Potter Sequence owns the obstructed, oliguric end of this differential — the infant whose creatinine really is his own. Store the discriminator as a question: is the baby making urine, and does the mother's chart contain the number? Candidate twin — confirm: a brief on maternal-antibody neonatal disease (anti-Ro, TSI, antiplatelet) does not exist yet; this brief wants it.
Transferable rule A newborn's laboratory value in the first days belongs to two patients — read the maternal history as part of the panel before attributing anything to the infant, and when a number and a ledger disagree, the ledger of output, growth and examination decides.
Salient decoyHypoxic-ischemic renal injury — Apgars 8 and 9 with a normal examination; asphyxia leaves a mark the stem does not have
True-fact-wrong-slotDehydration — 3% weight loss and two voids; the stem's own numbers exclude it
Salient decoyBreastfeeding jaundice — It answers the bilirubin; the question asked about the creatinine, and it reaches creatinine only through a dehydration that is absent
