Cardiovascular

Murmur Man and Post-ToF Pulmonic Regurgitation

Shape first, then breathing · UWorld · every distractor gets one coordinate right

The decision point

Murmur Man puts you on a body part and breathing picks the tenant. Decrescendo diastolic is the right arm — the tail falling away from S2 — and that arm holds exactly two valves, aortic and pulmonic regurgitation. Six options collapse to two. Then increases with inspiration means right heart: pulmonic regurgitation.

Everything else corroborates. Single S2 means a component is gone, here P2, because the pulmonic valve is incompetent. The parasternal heave is the dilated right ventricle carrying the volume load. And the etiology is in the history: repairing tetralogy of Fallot requires enlarging the outflow tract, which disrupts the pulmonic annulus.

Defining criteria Diamond head — crescendo-decrescendo ejection: aortic stenosis, pulmonic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy · Flat body — holosystolic from S1 to S2: mitral regurgitation, tricuspid regurgitation, ventricular septal defect · Left arm — late diastolic rumble into S1: mitral stenosis, tricuspid stenosis · Right arm — early diastolic decrescendo off S2: aortic regurgitation, pulmonic regurgitation · RILE — right-sided murmurs louder on inspiration, left-sided on expiration
Murmur Man - splitting the tenants of each shape
Body partTenantsWhat separates them
Diamond headAS, PS, HOCMHOCM louder with Valsalva and standing, AS softer; PS louder on inspiration
Flat bodyMR, TR, VSDTR louder on inspiration; MR radiates to the axilla; VSD harsh at the lower sternal border
Left armMS, TSTS louder on inspiration, MS on expiration with an opening snap at the apex
Right armAR, PRPR louder on inspiration, AR on expiration with a wide pulse pressure
Late systolic with a clickMitral valve prolapseClick moves earlier with standing and Valsalva
Crossing S2Patent ductus arteriosusContinuous machine-like, the only murmur that crosses a heart sound
Scenario bank
  1. 30 yo M, tetralogy of Fallot repaired at age 3, exertional dyspnea, decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border increasing with inspiration, single S2, parasternal heave → pulmonic regurgitation → serial echocardiography
  2. 45 yo M, decrescendo diastolic murmur that decreases with inspiration, wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses → aortic regurgitation → echocardiography
  3. 38 yo F, mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap, loud S1 and atrial fibrillation → mitral stenosis
  4. 55 yo F, positional dyspnea, a tumor plop, a rumble that varies with body position, fever and weight loss → left atrial myxoma
  5. 17 yo M, harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border that gets louder with Valsalva and on standing, family history of sudden death → hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → echocardiography
  6. 78 yo M, crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids that softens with Valsalva, delayed carotid upstroke, syncope → aortic stenosis → echocardiography
  7. 28 yo F with a mid-systolic click followed by a murmur, the click moving earlier on standing → mitral valve prolapse
  8. 22 yo F with a systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border and fixed splitting of S2 → atrial septal defect
  9. 60 yo M with a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border increasing with inspiration, large jugular v waves and a pulsatile liver → tricuspid regurgitation
  10. Preterm infant with a continuous murmur below the left clavicle, bounding pulses and a widened pulse pressure → patent ductus arteriosus → indomethacin or ibuprofen
  11. 30 yo M with a decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, a loud P2 and pulmonary hypertension → Graham Steell murmur → treat the pulmonary hypertension
  12. 28 yo M with repaired tetralogy of Fallot presenting with palpitations and syncope → ventricular arrhythmia → ECG, Holter and electrophysiology referral
  13. 30 yo M with severe pulmonic regurgitation after tetralogy of Fallot repair, progressive right ventricular dilation and symptoms → pulmonic valve replacement
Name the operation, then name what it breaks A repaired congenital lesion in a young adult is the etiology, not the background. Tetralogy of Fallot repair gives pulmonic regurgitation, right ventricular dilation, ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death. Aortic valvotomy gives aortic regurgitation. Coarctation repair gives re-coarctation and persistent hypertension. Fontan gives protein-losing enteropathy and arrhythmia. Mustard or Senning gives baffle obstruction and systemic right ventricular failure.
Pearls Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and augments right-heart filling, which is the whole mechanism behind RILE · Mitral valve prolapse and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy both get louder with reduced preload, and aortic stenosis gets softer · Single S2 — severe pulmonic regurgitation, pulmonary atresia, severe aortic stenosis, transposition, truncus · Fixed split S2 — atrial septal defect · Paradoxical split — left bundle branch block or severe aortic stenosis · Graham Steell is pulmonic regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension, with a loud P2 rather than an absent one
Pairs with Part II Congenital Shunts and the Transitional Clock owns when a murmur appears and why; this brief owns what the murmur is. Store the discriminator as a question: am I asking what the murmur is, or why it is here now?
Transferable rule A murmur has two coordinates and every distractor gets exactly one of them right, so fix the phase and the side before you name a valve.
Mirror twinAortic regurgitation is the other tenant of the same arm, right shape and wrong side.
Class-vs-memberTricuspid regurgitation is the right side with the wrong phase.
True-fact-wrong-slotAtrial septal defect gives fixed splitting; the stem says single.

Congenital Shunts and the Transitional Clock

Falling resistance opens the gradient · Aquifer · weeks for shunts, days for the ductus

The decision point

A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border in an acyanotic infant is a ventricular septal defect, and a VSD murmur is generated by flow across a pressure gradient. At birth there is no gradient: pulmonary vascular resistance is still near systemic, so almost nothing crosses the defect and the newborn exam is normal.

Over the following weeks pulmonary vascular resistance falls, the gradient opens, shunt flow rises, and the murmur appears at 2 to 4 weeks. The same falling resistance explains the tachypnea and poor feeding, because increasing left-to-right shunt means pulmonary overcirculation. The normal two-week visit brackets the onset precisely, and the ductus was already closed by then.

Defining criteria Transitional circulation — pulmonary vascular resistance falls from near-systemic at birth to its nadir at roughly 6 to 8 weeks · Ductal closure — functional in 50% by 24 hours, 90% by 48 hours, essentially all by 72 hours · Left-to-right shunt murmur — appears at 2 to 4 weeks as resistance falls; heart failure at 4 to 6 weeks
Congenital lesions - when each declares and why
LesionThe NBME tellWhen it declares, and what to do
Ventricular septal defectHolosystolic at the lower sternal border; a louder murmur means a smaller defect2 to 4 weeks as resistance falls; diurese and feed, close if failure persists
Atrial septal defectFixed split S2 with a soft pulmonic flow murmurOften not until childhood, because the atrial gradient is low throughout
Patent ductus arteriosusContinuous machine-like murmur, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressureDays to weeks; the murmur disappears on closure. Indomethacin closes it
Coarctation of the aorta Can't missUpper to lower extremity blood pressure gap, weak femoral pulsesDays, on ductal closure. Prostaglandin E1 reopens it
Ductal-dependent cyanotic lesions Can't missCyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, failed pulse oximetry screenDays; prostaglandin E1 and echocardiography
Tetralogy of FallotHarsh systolic murmur that softens during a spellVariable; squatting raises systemic resistance and reduces the shunt
Scenario bank
  1. 5 wk old, acyanotic, tachypneic, with a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that was absent on the newborn exam, why now → pulmonary vascular resistance has fallen → the gradient across the defect has opened
  2. Term infant with a normal 2-week visit, now 5 weeks old with poor feeding, RR 70 and a new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border → falling pulmonary vascular resistance has opened the interventricular gradient → the murmur and the symptoms share one cause
  3. 3 wk old with fixed splitting of S2 and a soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, thriving → atrial septal defect → often silent into childhood
  4. 2 day old with weak femoral pulses, an upper extremity blood pressure 30 mmHg above the lower, and shock → start prostaglandin E1 → coarctation of the aorta
  5. 3 day old with cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen, a single S2, and now weak pulses with poor perfusion → start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiography → the duct is closing, so instability licenses the drug before the picture
  6. 6 wk old with a large ventricular septal defect, poor weight gain, RR 70 and hepatomegaly → diuretics, afterload reduction and caloric fortification → surgical closure if medical therapy fails
  7. Preterm infant with a continuous murmur below the left clavicle, bounding pulses and a widened pulse pressure → indomethacin or ibuprofen → patent ductus arteriosus
  8. 4 mo old with an unrepaired large ventricular septal defect whose murmur has softened and who now desaturates with crying → urgent cardiology referral → rising resistance with Eisenmenger physiology
  9. Why a louder ventricular septal defect murmur predicts a better prognosis → a small defect produces high-velocity turbulent flow → large defects are quieter and shunt more
  10. Newborn with a normal pre-discharge examination who fails pulse oximetry screening at 24 hours → echocardiography → critical congenital heart disease screening
Prostaglandin opens, indomethacin closes Which drug you want depends entirely on whether the ductus is the patient's lifeline or their problem. Ductal-dependent lesions — coarctation, pulmonary atresia, transposition, hypoplastic left heart — decompensate when it closes, so you reopen it. A preterm PDA shunting into the lungs is the problem, so you close it. And a softening murmur in an unrepaired large shunt is a warning, not an improvement.
Pearls Falling resistance is the clock for left-to-right shunts, ductal closure is the clock for ductal-dependent lesions — weeks versus days · Louder VSD murmur means smaller defect, so murmur intensity runs opposite to severity here · Cyanosis that does not improve on 100% oxygen is a shunt rather than a lung · Failure to thrive is the infant's exercise intolerance, because feeding is their exertion
Pairs with Part II Murmur Man and Post-ToF Pulmonic Regurgitation owns murmur shape and location; this brief owns when the murmur appears. Also adjacent to Part II Neonatal Respiratory Distress, where the fork is lung versus heart.
Transferable rule A murmur requires flow across a pressure gradient, so when a stem asks why a murmur appeared or disappeared, ask what changed about the gradient rather than what changed about the heart.
True-fact-wrong-slotDuctal closure removes a continuous infraclavicular murmur; it cannot create a holosystolic one.
Trump-card inversionRising pulmonary pressure is the opposite direction and would soften the murmur.

Pulmonary 14 topics + 1 board-style

Occupational and exposure histories dominate here — and they are as often bait as they are the answer. Check the lobe and the pleura before trusting the resume.

COPD: Which Interventions Improve Survival

Mortality vs. symptoms

The decision point

"Maximum impact on survival" asks you to rank by outcome, not to treat the disease. Only a handful of things reduce mortality in COPD — and stems often preemptively remove smoking cessation (patient already quit) to force you into the second tier.

Reduce mortality
  • Smoking cessation
  • Long-term oxygen therapy — if criteria met
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation
  • Vaccination (influenza, COVID; pneumococcal)
  • Lung volume reduction surgery / transplant in selected patients
  • Nocturnal NIV for chronic daytime hypercapnia

Everything else — LAMA/LABA, ICS, macrolides, roflumilast, chest physiotherapy — improves symptoms and/or exacerbations with no demonstrated survival benefit.

Long-term oxygen therapy criteria
LTOT thresholdApplies when
PaO₂ ≤55 mm Hg or SaO₂ ≤88%Standard — at rest, with exertion, or during sleep
PaO₂ ≤59 mm Hg or SaO₂ ≤89%If cor pulmonale or secondary polycythemia (Hct >55%)
Scenario bank
  1. 68 yo M with COPD, PaO₂ 52 mm Hg at rest on room air → long-term oxygen therapy
  2. 68 yo M with COPD who has already quit; what else reduces mortality → long-term oxygen if hypoxemic
  3. 68 yo M with COPD, PaO₂ 57 with cor pulmonale and hematocrit 57% → start long-term oxygen → cor pulmonale or Hct >55 lowers the gate to PaO₂ ≤59 / SaO₂ ≤89
  4. 68 yo M with COPD who still smokes a pack a day → smoking cessation → the largest mortality benefit available
  5. 68 yo M with COPD asking what pulmonary rehabilitation achieves → improved symptoms and quality of life → not mortality, not lung function
  6. 68 yo M with COPD, frequent exacerbations and eosinophils 340 → add an inhaled corticosteroid
The two-step catch A saturation of 89% fails the standard threshold by one point — the hematocrit of 58% is what qualifies the patient under the second criterion. The "ruddy and plethoric" face is the same finding in physical-exam form. Titrate to SaO₂ 90–94%, ≥15 hrs/day. Mechanism: reversing chronic hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction prevents pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
Why phlebotomy is wrong The polycythemia is appropriate compensation for hypoxemia; removing it reduces oxygen delivery. Phlebotomy is only for symptomatic hyperviscosity (blurred vision, confusion), typically Hct >65. Correct the hypoxemia and the Hct falls. And normal WBC and platelets make this secondary polycythemia — polycythemia vera would elevate all three lines with low EPO and JAK2 V617F.
Treat-the-number

Asthma vs. COPD

Objective measurement beats subjective report

The decision point

Asthma and COPD are defined apart by reversibility of airflow obstruction — and reversibility is a measurement, not an impression. That is why spirometry before and after a bronchodilator beats "symptomatic response to a trial of albuterol," even though both involve the same drug: subjective relief does not correlate with the spirometric bronchodilator response.

Notice these stems are deliberately unresolvable clinically — asthma features (seasonal, episodic, eczema, family history) stacked against COPD features (age, pack-years). When the history cannot settle it, the answer must be a test that measures the defining variable, not a proxy marker.

Asthma vs COPD
AsthmaCOPD
OnsetChildhood or early adulthood>40, after years of smoking
CourseEpisodic, variable, trigger-drivenProgressive, persistent
AtopyCommon — eczema, rhinitis, family historyNot typical
FEV₁/FVC↓, reversible↓, post-BD <0.70, largely fixed
DLCONormal or ↑ (bronchial hyperemia)↓ in emphysema; normal in chronic bronchitis
Controller therapyInhaled corticosteroid ± LABALAMA/LABA; ICS only for eosinophilic exacerbators
The numbers Significant bronchodilator response: FEV₁ increases ≥12% AND ≥200 mL. Asthma often normalizes (post-BD FEV₁/FVC ≥0.70). COPD is defined by a POST-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.70 — obstruction persists even if some improvement occurs.
When the other tests ARE the answer
  • Methacholine challenge → symptoms suggest asthma but spirometry is normal; a negative test rules out asthma
  • Peak flow diary → >20% diurnal variability supports asthma
  • DLCO → separates emphysema (low) from chronic bronchitis and asthma
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin → COPD under ~45, minimal smoking, lower-lobe panacinar emphysema, or unexplained liver disease
  • Serum IgE → ABPA: refractory asthma, brown mucus plugs, central bronchiectasis, Aspergillus precipitins
  • Blood/sputum eosinophils → guides adding ICS in COPD (eos ≥300), not diagnostic
Scenario bank
  1. Classic episodic symptoms but normal spirometry → methacholine challenge
  2. Post-BD FEV₁/FVC 0.62 with 6% improvement → COPD → LAMA/LABA
  3. Post-BD ratio normalizes to 0.78 with 18% improvement → asthma → ICS
  4. Emphysema at age 40 with minimal smoking, lower-lobe predominance → alpha-1 antitrypsin level
  5. Refractory asthma with brown mucus plugs and central bronchiectasis → ABPA → steroids + itraconazole
  6. COPD with frequent exacerbations and eosinophils ≥300 → add ICS
  7. Isolated cough worse at night and with cold air, normal spirometry → cough-variant asthma
  8. Long-standing asthmatic who smokes, now with fixed obstruction → asthma-COPD overlap → the regimen must include ICS
  9. Distinguishing emphysema from chronic bronchitis → DLCO
Pairs with Part I When Antibiotics Fail in a Structural Lung expands the allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis line of this brief's test-selection block.
Transferable rules When two choices test the same physiologic variable, pick the one that yields a number over the one that yields an impression — "symptomatic response to a trial of X" is nearly always a distractor when objective measurement is available. And separately: an association is not a discriminator — a finding common in disease A but also present in disease B cannot separate them, however classic.
Test-overrides-findings

Chronic Cough

Treatment failures are eliminations

The decision point

Chronic cough (>8 weeks) with a normal chest X-ray comes down to three causes: upper airway cough syndrome, asthma, and GERD. A completed empiric trial is a diagnostic test — "did not respond to antihistamines and decongestants" is the diagnostic trial for UACS, and failure effectively excludes it.

Chronic cough — cause → clue → diagnostic move
CauseCluesDiagnostic move
UACSupper airway cough syndrome / postnasal dripThroat clearing, drainage, cobblestoningEmpiric antihistamine/decongestant — response is the diagnosis
Cough-variant asthmaNocturnal + triggers (cold, exercise), ± wheezeSpirometry → methacholine challenge; empiric ICS
GERDWorse supine/after meals; often silent — no heartburn in 40–75%Empiric PPI × 8 weeks; pH monitoring if refractory
ACE inhibitorCheck the med list — onset days to months after startingStop the drug (resolves in 1–4 weeks)
PostinfectiousRecent URI, self-limited<8 weeks by definition
Lung cancer / TB Can't missWeight loss, hemoptysis, risk factorsCXR first in all chronic cough
Scenario bank
  1. 45 yo F, 3 months of cough, normal chest X-ray, post-nasal drip and throat clearing → upper airway cough syndrome → first-generation antihistamine trial
  2. 45 yo F on lisinopril with 3 months of dry cough → ACE-inhibitor cough → stop the drug
  3. 45 yo F whose cough is worse at night and with cold air, spirometry normal → cough-variant asthma → methacholine challenge
  4. 45 yo F with cough and heartburn after failed antihistamine and inhaled steroid trials → gastroesophageal reflux → proton pump inhibitor trial
  5. 45 yo F, smoker, cough with hemoptysis and 6 kg weight loss → malignancy → chest CT
  6. 45 yo F with cough for 5 weeks after a viral illness, normal chest X-ray → postinfectious cough → observation
Transferable rule When a stem says "did not respond to X," it is not giving history — it is crossing an answer off for you. Read treatment failures as eliminations. Nocturnal dry cough + normal exam + normal everything = GERD until proven otherwise.

Occupational Lung Disease

A lookup question wearing a clinical costume

The decision point

The occupation names the dust; the lobe distribution and pleural involvement confirm it. Asbestosis is the odd one out — it goes to the lower lobes and involves the pleura. Everything else with a mining/quarry history goes upper.

Occupational lung diseases
DiseaseExposureLobesThe tellAssociation
AsbestosisBrake linings, shipyard, insulation, plumbing, roofingLOWERPleural plaques; ferruginous bodiesBronchogenic CA > mesothelioma; smoking multiplies bronchogenic only
SilicosisSandblasting, mining, foundry, stone countertopsUPPEREggshell calcification of hilar nodes↑ TB risk — annual PPD
Coal workers'Coal miningUPPERCoal macules → progressive massive fibrosisCaplan syndrome (+ RA nodules)
BerylliosisAerospace, nuclearDiffuseNoncaseating granulomas — sarcoid mimicResponds to steroids
ByssinosisCotton / textile mills—"Monday fever" — worse at the start of the work weekObstructive
Hypersensitivity pneumonitisMoldy hay, birds—Episodic fever/cough hours after exposureAvoidance cures
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo M shipyard insulator with lower-lobe fibrosis and pleural plaques → asbestosis
  2. 55 yo M sandblaster with upper-lobe nodules and eggshell-calcified hilar nodes → silicosis
  3. 58 yo M coal miner with upper-lobe nodules and black sputum → coal workers' pneumoconiosis
  4. 50 yo M aerospace machinist with noncaseating granulomas on biopsy → berylliosis
  5. 45 yo F cotton mill worker with chest tightness worst on the first day back at work → byssinosis
  6. 40 yo M pigeon breeder with fever and dyspnea 6 hours after exposure → hypersensitivity pneumonitis
  7. 62 yo M with asbestos exposure, a pleural mass and an effusion → mesothelioma
Mnemonic and timing Asbestos comes from the roof but affects the base; silica and coal come from the ground but affect the top. Latency is typically 20–30 years, so exposure that ended decades ago still counts. Pleural plaques alone are a marker of exposure, benign, and need no treatment.
Transferable rule A long stem answered in under 40 seconds means one cue was pattern-matched and the verification pass was skipped. Occupational stems reward it least — the lobe distribution is usually the deciding line, and it sits at the end.

Allergic Rhinitis

Step-up therapy in the right order

The decision point

Moderate-to-severe seasonal rhinitis that has failed antihistamines → step up to an intranasal corticosteroid, the single most effective drug class for allergic rhinitis. "Late winter" is the prophylaxis clue: start it ~2 weeks before pollen season, because ICS suppresses the mucosal inflammatory response and needs lead time.

Option analysis — why each fails
ChoiceWhy it fails
Minimize outdoor activitiesImpractical for pollen (unlike dust mites or pets); inadequate once disease is complicated
Continue OTC antihistaminesAlready failing — and first-generation agents bring sedation and anticholinergic effects
Desensitization (immunotherapy)The real bait — the only disease-modifying option, but reserved for failure of maximal pharmacotherapy. He has never tried a nasal steroid
MontelukastLess effective than intranasal steroids; carries an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects
Oral prednisoneSystemic steroids for a benign chronic condition — never the answer
Scenario bank
  1. 28 yo F with moderate seasonal rhinitis failing OTC antihistamines → intranasal corticosteroid
  2. 28 yo F seeking durable control after several drug classes have failed → allergen immunotherapy
  3. 28 yo F advised to minimize outdoor activity for her pollen allergy → impractical for pollen, unlike dust-mite control
  4. 28 yo F with rhinitis and asthma who wants a single oral agent → montelukast, with neuropsychiatric counselling
  5. 28 yo F using oxymetazoline for 10 days with worsening congestion → rhinitis medicamentosa → stop the spray
  6. 28 yo F with clear rhinorrhea, no itch or sneezing, triggered by temperature change → vasomotor rhinitis
The ladder Allergen avoidance (when practical) → intranasal corticosteroid → add second-generation oral or intranasal antihistamine → immunotherapy only after pharmacotherapy fails. Any first-generation antihistamine in a stem is usually there to be replaced, not continued.
Sequencing trap

Recurrent Sinopulmonary Infection

the exam finding picks the test · board question · Which single structural clue in the stem is incompatible with every cause but one?

The decision point

The infection history is deliberately non-discriminating: eight antibiotic courses for sinusitis and pneumonia is compatible with every option on the list except "normal." The fork is settled by one line of the physical exam — the PMI is in the right chest, i.e. dextrocardia, i.e. situs inversus. Antibody deficiencies do not move the heart; retained secretions do not move the heart; only a disorder of ciliary motility does, because the same dynein-arm defect that leaves airway cilia dysmotile also leaves embryonic nodal cilia unable to establish left–right asymmetry, so laterality is randomized. That converts "recurrent sinopulmonary infection" into Kartagener syndrome — the situs inversus / recurrent sinusitis / bronchiectasis subgroup of primary ciliary dyskinesia. The secondary confirmation is the tonsils: lymphoid tissue is present, which is inconsistent with X-linked agammaglobulinemia.

Defining criteria Kartagener syndrome — situs inversus + recurrent sinusitis + bronchiectasis, occurring as a subgroup of primary ciliary dyskinesia · Pathologic infection frequency — healthy young children in daycare or with older siblings may have up to 12 respiratory infections per year, but these are predominantly viral and do not require antibiotics; recurrent antibiotic-requiring bacterial sinusitis and pneumonia is what crosses the gate
Pertinent positives & negatives PMI in the right chest — dextrocardia/situs inversus; rules in ciliary dysmotility and rules out every other option on the list, none of which relocates the heart · Mildly enlarged tonsils — mature B cells have populated lymphoid tissue; excludes X-linked agammaglobulinemia, in which tonsillar and adenoidal tissue is absent · Age 18 months — excludes CVID, which presents in adolescence or adulthood · Eight episodes, all antibiotic-requiring — excludes "normal childhood infections," which are viral and self-limited · Bilateral rales and rhonchi, SpO₂ 99% — diffuse secretion retention, not focal endobronchial obstruction; argues against retained foreign body · Affected older brother — consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance (PCD, CF); by itself it does not separate them, and it does not exclude X-linked disease — the tonsils do
Recurrent sinopulmonary infection — the differential
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Primary ciliary dyskinesia / KartagenerAutosomal recessive dynein-arm defect → dysmotile cilia, poor mucociliary clearance; chronic wet cough, chronic otitis and sinusitis from infancy, bronchiectasis; term neonate with unexplained respiratory distress ⚠︎Dextrocardia / situs inversus (present in about half ⚠︎); adult male with normal sperm count but absent motility ⚠︎— (the answer)
Cystic fibrosisAutosomal recessive CFTR defect → inspissated secretions, repeated respiratory infection, bronchiectasisPancreatic insufficiency — failure to thrive, greasy stools; meconium ileus; nasal polyps; no dextrocardiaNormal growth described, no steatorrhea, and the heart is on the right
Retained foreign bodyToddler, abrupt choking episode, then endobronchial obstruction with retained secretions and eventually focal bronchiectasisUnilateral/focal wheeze, unilateral hyperinflation on expiratory or decubitus film; no dextrocardiaBilateral findings, 1-year multifocal course, affected sibling
Antibody deficiency (XLA, CVID) — companion brief's axisRecurrent encapsulated sinopulmonary infection with normal airway anatomy; the immunoglobulin panel names the defectXLA: absent tonsils and adenoids; CVID: adolescent/adult onset with low IgGTonsils present; age 18 months; neither shifts the heart
Normal childhood infectionsDaycare or older siblings; up to 12 viral respiratory illnesses per year, self-limited, normal growth and normal interval examNo antibiotics required, well between episodesEight antibiotic-treated bacterial infections plus dextrocardia
Management, in one line The confirmatory ladder is not what this stem tests, so it collapses to one sentence: a suggestive phenotype is worked up with low nasal nitric oxide, then bronchoscopic biopsy with electron microscopy showing ciliary/dynein-arm abnormality, then genetic testing (all in-context) — with sweat chloride obtained first whenever growth or stools raise cystic fibrosis ⚠︎, because there is no single gold standard for PCD.
Decision spine Are the infections actually pathologic? — Antibiotic-requiring bacterial sinusitis + pneumonia → yes, past the normal gate · Where is the heart / where are the organs? — PMI on the right → situs inversus → ciliary axis, and stop · If situs is normal: — is growth or stool abnormal? → cystic fibrosis axis (sweat chloride) · If growth is normal: — is the disease focal and abrupt in onset? → foreign body (bronchoscopy) · If the airway anatomy is normal and lymphoid tissue is absent or the patient is an adolescent/adult: — antibody axis (quantitative immunoglobulins), the companion brief
Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo F, chronic wet cough and recurrent otitis media since infancy, normal growth; chest film shows a right-sided cardiac silhouette and right-sided stomach bubble → Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) → Nasal nitric oxide, then ciliary electron microscopy
  2. 2 yo M, third pneumonia this year, chronic loose greasy stools, weight below the 3rd percentile, PMI in the left chest → Sweat chloride testing → Cystic fibrosis
  3. 14 mo M, choking episode while eating nuts 3 weeks ago, now focal right-sided wheeze and a second right lower lobe pneumonia; film shows right-sided hyperinflation → Rigid bronchoscopy → Retained foreign body
  4. 5 yo M, recurrent sinusitis and pneumonia since 9 months of age; no palpable tonsils and no cervical lymphadenopathy → Quantitative serum immunoglobulins with B-cell flow cytometry → X-linked agammaglobulinemia
  5. 8 yo M, unexplained respiratory distress as a term newborn, year-round wet cough, chronic otitis, normal growth, heart on the left → Nasal nitric oxide measurement → PCD without situs inversus
  6. 9 yo M with confirmed PCD, daily purulent sputum, HRCT with lower-lobe bronchiectasis, on no maintenance therapy → Begin daily airway clearance therapy → Bronchiectasis from failed mucociliary clearance
  7. 17 yo M, lifelong sinusitis and chronic productive cough, now infertile; semen analysis shows a normal sperm count with absent motility → Electron microscopy of respiratory cilia for dynein-arm defects → Primary ciliary dyskinesia
  8. 4 yo M, chronic wet cough, recurrent otitis, situs inversus totalis on chest film - the defective structure → Dynein arms of the ciliary axoneme → Impaired mucociliary clearance
  9. 3 yo F in daycare, 9 upper respiratory illnesses in the past year, each self-limited without antibiotics, growth at the 50th percentile, normal exam between illnesses → Normal frequency of childhood viral infection → Reassurance, no immune workup
  10. 10 yo F with heterotaxy - midline liver, complex congenital heart disease, no spleen on abdominal imaging - and two prior pneumococcal bacteremias → Pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccination plus daily antibiotic prophylaxis → Functional asplenia of heterotaxy
Decoy note "Delivered vaginally without complications" is planted to close off perinatal explanations and quietly withholds the neonatal respiratory distress that many PCD infants have ⚠︎ — its absence does not weaken the diagnosis. The SpO₂ of 99% is inert for the diagnosis but does work against focal obstruction, and the affected older brother is compatible with autosomal recessive PCD, autosomal recessive CF, and X-linked disease simultaneously, so it decides nothing on its own.
Pearls Dextrocardia is incompatible with every other cause here, because only dysmotile cilia also fail to set the embryonic left–right axis. · Anything that moves an organ in a recurrent-infection stem — dextrocardia, right-sided stomach bubble, midline liver — takes you off the immunoglobulin axis immediately; antibody defects never alter anatomy. · Situs inversus appears in only about half of primary ciliary dyskinesia ⚠︎, so a normal PMI does not exclude it; the substitute clues are chronic otitis from infancy, year-round wet cough, and unexplained respiratory distress in a term newborn ⚠︎. · Male infertility separates the two clearance diseases at the mechanism: PCD gives normal sperm counts with absent motility, CF gives obstructive azoospermia from congenital absence of the vas deferens ⚠︎. · Situs inversus totalis points at cilia; situs ambiguus (heterotaxy) points at asplenia or polysplenia with congenital heart disease, and the management question becomes encapsulated-organism prophylaxis ⚠︎. · Any cause of persistently retained secretions — dysmotile cilia, thick mucus, or an obstructing foreign body — converges on the same endpoint of bronchiectasis, so bronchiectasis names the endpoint, never the etiology.
Pairs with Candidate twin — confirm: Part I The Immunoglobulin Panel (shared complaint: recurrent sinopulmonary infection; discriminator stored as a question: does the physical exam show an anatomic or clearance abnormality, or is the airway structurally normal? — if normal, the immunoglobulin levels and B-cell count take over). Part I When Antibiotics Fail in a Structural Lung owns what happens once the structural diagnosis is established and an exacerbation stops responding.
Transferable rule When a recurrent-infection stem hands you a physical finding that no immune defect could produce, that finding is the entire question — infection frequency establishes only that something is wrong, while anatomy establishes what. Store the clue as a question about structure, not as a reflex to the loudest buzzword.
Salient decoyX-linked agammaglobulinemia — Tonsils are present; XLA patients have no tonsillar or adenoidal tissue, and no antibody defect displaces the PMI
Class-vs-memberCystic fibrosis — No pancreatic insufficiency described and no mechanism by which CFTR relocates the heart
True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency — Presents in adolescence or adulthood, not at 18 months, and does not produce dextrocardia
True-fact-wrong-slotForeign body — Bilateral disease over a year with a normal SpO₂, no aspiration event, and no explanation for the heart position
Uniform-answer doubtNormal childhood infections — Those infections are viral and do not require antibiotics; eight antibiotic courses plus dextrocardia is a phenotype, not a base rate

Mechanisms of Hypoxemia

sort by A-a gradient and the oxygen response · board question · Is the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia correct when you raise inspired oxygen?

The decision point

The five options are one mechanism each, so the stem is asking you to classify physiology, not to name a disease — and two findings close it. Grunting with bilaterally decreased breath sounds at one hour of life in a 28-weeker is diffuse alveolar collapse: surfactant deficiency raises alveolar surface tension, alveoli close, and those units stay perfused while ventilation falls to zero. Blood traversing them reaches the left heart unoxygenated. That is intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt, and it is the only listed mechanism that produces cyanosis with increased work of breathing and bilaterally reduced air entry.

Defining criteria A-a gradient — alveolar minus arterial PO2. Widened in shunt, V/Q mismatch, and diffusion limitation; normal in hypoventilation and in low inspired PO2. Normal value approximately (age/4) + 4 ⚠︎ · Shunt vs V/Q mismatch — shunt is the limiting case of mismatch (V/Q = 0). The gate is the oxygen response: mismatch corrects with modest supplemental oxygen; true shunt barely moves, because blood bypassing ventilated alveoli never sees the higher FiO2 ⚠︎ · Saturation gap — pulse oximetry far below what the measured PaO2 predicts → the hemoglobin is the problem (methemoglobin pins the reading near 85% ⚠︎; carboxyhemoglobin is read as oxygenated, so the pulse oximeter is falsely reassuring ⚠︎)
Pertinent positives & negatives Grunting with bilaterally decreased breath sounds — auto-PEEP against closed alveoli; locates the lesion in the parenchyma and excludes both cardiac shunt and central hypoventilation · Increased work of breathing at 1 hour — excludes apnea of prematurity, which appears days later with apnea and bradycardia and no respiratory effort · No murmur, regular rhythm — does not by itself exclude cyanotic heart disease, but with loud parenchymal findings it makes an intracardiac cause the second explanation, not the first · Normal CBC — no anemia to lower content, no leukocytosis; the sepsis workup already running is not the answer (in-context: CBC is typically normal in RDS) · Still hypoxemic on 30% oxygen by CPAP — the shunt fraction is large enough that a modest FiO2 cannot overcome it; the fix is recruitment, not concentration
Hypoxemia — sorting by A&ndash;a gradient and oxygen response
MechanismIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt (V/Q = 0)Alveoli perfused but unventilated — RDS, lobar atelectasis/mucus plug, pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary edemaWidened A-a, hypoxemia refractory to raising FiO2, corrected by recruitment (CPAP, PEEP, surfactant)— (the answer)
V/Q mismatch (low but non-zero)Asthma, COPD, early pneumonia, atelectasis in evolutionWidened A-a that corrects on a few liters of oxygen — the commonest mechanism in adult medicineThe vendor keys the extreme: collapsed alveoli with zero ventilation
Right-to-left shunt outside the lungCyanotic CHD; hepatopulmonary syndrome; PFO opened by high right-sided pressuresNo rise in PaO2 on 100% oxygen; lungs clear, work of breathing normal or minimalGrunting and bilaterally decreased breath sounds — the lungs are abnormal
Dead space (ventilated, not perfused)Pulmonary embolism, low cardiac outputSudden dyspnea with a clear chest; hypercapnia is the primary consequenceBilateral decreased breath sounds; PE is vanishingly rare in young children
Normal-A-a hypoxemia: hypoventilation or low inspired PO2Opioids, neuromuscular disease, obesity hypoventilation, apnea of prematurity · altitude, hypoxic gas mixtureNormal A-a gradient; hypoventilation adds a high PaCO2, altitude does not; both fully correct with a little oxygenTachypnea and grunting — effort is increased, not depressed; he is already receiving 30% oxygen
Abnormal hemoglobin affinity or carryingCO poisoning, methemoglobinemia, fetal hemoglobinNormal PaO2 with cyanosis or a saturation gap; cyanosis unmoved by oxygenNormal Hb, no exposure; fetal hemoglobin's left shift is physiologic and does not cause distress
Management, in one line Diffusion limitation is the seventh category and does not earn a row here: it is a chronic, exertional finding (interstitial disease, emphysema) with a low DLCO and a resting saturation that is often normal — it is tested by a stem where the patient desaturates only on the walk down the hall. Sequencing is not the fork in this stem, and the whole ladder it contains is one line: shunt from collapsed alveoli is treated by reopening them — surfactant plus CPAP — not by turning the oxygen up.
Decision spine Is the PaO2 low, or only the saturation? — Saturation-only → hemoglobin problem (CO, metHb) · Is the A-a gradient normal? — Normal → hypoventilation (high PaCO2) or low inspired PO2 (normal PaCO2). Done · Widened — what happens on oxygen? — Corrects → V/Q mismatch. Refractory → shunt · Shunt: are the lungs abnormal? — Grunting, decreased breath sounds, infiltrate → intrapulmonary. Clear lungs, no distress → intracardiac or intravascular · Any reason to think dead space? — Sudden onset, clear chest, risk factors — otherwise the exam is not asking about embolus
Scenario bank
  1. 27 wk preterm M, 3 h old, grunting, ground-glass film with air bronchograms, SpO2 85% on CPAP FiO2 0.6 and rising → Intubate and give intratracheal surfactant → Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
  2. 24 yo M, POD 1, RR 6, pinpoint pupils, PaO2 55, PaCO2 68, normal A-a gradient → Naloxone → Opioid-induced hypoventilation
  3. 4 mo F, cyanosis after topical teething gel, chocolate-brown blood, SpO2 fixed at 85% on 100% oxygen, PaO2 96 → Methylene blue IV → Methemoglobinemia
  4. 34 yo F and two housemates with headache and nausea after a furnace failure, COHb 18%, no syncope, normal neurologic exam → High-flow 100% oxygen by nonrebreather → Carbon monoxide poisoning
  5. 58 yo M with ARDS, PaO2 58 on FiO2 0.8 with PEEP 8, diffuse bilateral opacities → Increase PEEP → Refractory intrapulmonary shunt
  6. 68 yo M, COPD exacerbation, baseline PaCO2 62, now receiving oxygen → Titrating oxygen to a saturation of 100% → Oxygen-induced hypercapnia
  7. 62 yo F, 8 months of exertional dyspnea, resting SpO2 96% falling to 86% with ambulation, clear lungs, normal chest film → Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide → Diffusion limitation
  8. 44 yo F, POD 5 from knee arthroplasty, sudden dyspnea, clear lungs, normal film, widened A-a gradient → CT pulmonary angiography → Pulmonary embolism
  9. 29 yo M trekker at 4,500 m, dyspnea with SpO2 84%, clear lungs, PaCO2 30, normal A-a gradient → Reduced inspired oxygen tension → Descent; acetazolamide
  10. 72 yo F, POD 2 laparotomy, febrile, SpO2 88%, absent breath sounds at the left base, film shows left lower lobe collapse → Intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt → Incentive spirometry and mobilization
Decoy note The umbilical line and the started antibiotics are the sepsis frame, and they are inert here: the CBC is normal and no fever or instability is reported. Apgar 7 at both marks argues against perinatal depression, which would present as hypoventilation. The absent murmur does not exclude cyanotic heart disease on its own — the parenchymal findings do.
Pearls Normal A-a means hypoventilation or thin air; widened and oxygen-responsive means V/Q mismatch; widened and oxygen-refractory means shunt. · Shunt is the hypoxemia that oxygen will not fix. When the FiO2 goes up and the saturation does not follow, stop titrating and start recruiting — PEEP, CPAP, surfactant, drainage, or a diuretic for the edema behind it. · The vendor calls the RDS hypoxemia "responsive to oxygen administration" and it is, clinically — but the reason is that partially collapsed alveoli are recruitable by the CPAP delivering that oxygen, not that shunted blood responds to FiO2. Keep the answer; correct the mechanism. · Hypoventilation is the one hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient and a high PaCO2; low inspired PO2 is the one with a normal gradient and a low PaCO2 from the compensatory hyperventilation. · A normal or high PaO2 in a cyanotic patient means the hemoglobin cannot carry or release oxygen — methemoglobin, carbon monoxide, cyanide (where the tissue, not the blood, is the problem). · Boundary: refractory hypoxemia with clear lungs and no cardiac history can still be an embolus — if it raises right-sided pressures enough to open a PFO, a dead-space disease presents as a right-to-left shunt. Look for the cause of the raised pressure, not just the shunt.
Pairs with Neonatal Respiratory Distress owns the parenchymal differential by chest film (ground glass and air bronchograms versus retained fluid, meconium, or air leak) and Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease owns the lesions themselves; the newborn-cyanosis brief authored this week owns sorting at-rest physiology in the delivery room. This brief owns the layer above all three — the mechanism categories, stored as a question: is the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia answer oxygen?
Transferable rule Hypoxemia is a physiology question wearing a disease costume: compute the A-a gradient, then ask what happens on supplemental oxygen — those two answers name the mechanism before you have named the illness, and the mechanism is what the option list is made of.
True-fact-wrong-slotUnderdeveloped medullary respiratory center — Apnea of prematurity appears days later as apnea with bradycardia and no respiratory effort; this infant is grunting and tachypneic at one hour
Salient decoyObstructed pulmonary arterial blood flow — Obstruction creates dead space, not bilaterally reduced breath sounds; embolus is nearly nonexistent in neonates
True-fact-wrong-slotGreater red blood cell oxygen affinity — It is the normal neonatal state — physiologic, and it does not cause respiratory distress
Class-vs-memberIncreased intracardiac left-to-right shunting — Left-to-right recirculates already-oxygenated blood; systemic saturation is unaffected, so it cannot desaturate a newborn

When Antibiotics Fail in a Structural Lung

eosinophils and IgE reclassify the exacerbation · board question · Did an adequate antibiotic course fail, and are the eosinophils and IgE up?

The decision point

The stem's structure is a two-step gate, and the second step is the one being scored. First, a week of appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotics with no improvement — the explicit trigger for suspecting allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in cystic fibrosis, because the presentation is otherwise indistinguishable from a cystic fibrosis bronchopneumonia. Second, the two laboratory values that assign a category: eosinophilia and an IgE of 3,225, which is a Th2 allergic response rather than a bacterial one. The mechanism follows from the host — Aspergillus spores are inhaled by everyone and cleared by the mucociliary escalator, but a structurally damaged airway traps them, colonisation becomes chronic, and chronic exposure becomes hypersensitisation. The disease is the immune response, which is why the treatment is a steroid and the antifungal is adjunctive.

Defining criteria Aspergillus sensitisation — elevated total serum IgE, usually above 1,000 IU/mL, plus a positive Aspergillus skin test or Aspergillus-specific IgE · Supportive but not diagnostic — peripheral eosinophilia and a positive Aspergillus IgG · Imaging — bronchiectasis with bronchial mucoid impaction, fleeting infiltrates, and intrabronchial exudates as tubular finger-in-glove radiodensities · The clinical trigger to suspect it — unexplained lung-function decline, or persistent lower-respiratory symptoms despite an adequate antibiotic course of more than one week · Screening — in cystic fibrosis, annual total serum IgE
Pertinent positives & negatives Cystic fibrosis — structural airway disease is the required host; this disease essentially does not occur in a normal airway · Failure to improve after a week of broad-spectrum antibiotics — the gate; a bacterial exacerbation would have moved · IgE 3,225 IU/mL — more than triple the usual threshold, and the single most specific finding among the options · Peripheral eosinophilia — narrows to the eosinophilic causes and eliminates the vasculitis, the pneumonitis and the mycobacterium at a stroke · Fever and malaise present — does not argue against the answer, since fever, malaise and thick blood-streaked sputum are common in it · No travel, no rash, no gastrointestinal symptoms — removes strongyloidiasis, which travels with skin and gut findings · Symptoms persisted throughout admission — removes hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which improves in hospital once the exposure is removed · Age 11 with no upper-airway destruction or renal findings — removes granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a disease of older adults without eosinophilia
Antibiotic-refractory symptoms in structural lung disease — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosisStructural airway disease traps A. fumigatus spores, producing chronic colonisation then Th2 hypersensitisationAntibiotic-refractory symptoms with eosinophilia and IgE above 1,000; mucoid impaction and finger-in-glove opacities— (the answer)
Cystic fibrosis exacerbation with a resistant organismThe same host, the same picture, a bacterial causeImproves once the coverage is right; sputum culture grows the organismA week of broad-spectrum therapy without improvement, and the eosinophilia
Hypersensitivity pneumonitisInhaled organic antigen causing fever, malaise and airspace infiltrates unresponsive to antibioticsImproves spontaneously in hospital once removed from the exposure; no eosinophilia and a normal IgEPersisted through a week of admission; eosinophils and IgE both high
StrongyloidiasisHelminth of rural tropics and subtropics; larvae penetrate skin and are swallowedEosinophilia and high IgE, but with roaming urticaria and gastrointestinal symptoms; exposure geographyNo travel, rash or gastrointestinal findings
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis Can't missANCA vasculitis producing necrotising bronchiectasis that mimics refractory pneumoniaOlder men, sinus destruction, hemoptysis, glomerulonephritis; not eosinophilic and IgE normalAge 11, eosinophilia and high IgE, no renal or sinus destruction
Nontuberculous mycobacteriaMycobacterium avium complex colonises cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis — not M. tuberculosisChronic over months to years, nodular then cavitary then fibrotic disease; no eosinophilia or IgE riseOne week of symptoms, and the eosinophilia
Management, in one line Management is not this question's fork, so in two sentences: systemic glucocorticoids are first-line because the pathology is allergic inflammation, and an antifungal such as voriconazole is added to reduce spore burden alongside treatment of the underlying airway disease. The corollary worth storing is that an antifungal alone does not treat this disease, because it addresses the antigen and not the response.
Decision spine What is the host? — Structural airway disease — cystic fibrosis or asthma, which is the entry condition · Was the antibiotic course adequate? — A week of broad-spectrum therapy without improvement → this is not the bacteria · Are the eosinophils up? — Yes → the vasculitis, the pneumonitis and the mycobacterium are gone · Is the IgE above 1,000? — 3,225 → allergic sensitisation, and only two options carry it · Is there exposure geography or extrapulmonary disease? — No travel, no rash, no gut findings → not the helminth
Scenario bank
  1. 11 yo boy with cystic fibrosis, a week of fever and productive cough with no improvement after a week of broad-spectrum antibiotics, peripheral eosinophilia and IgE 3,225 IU/mL → Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis → Antibiotic failure plus Th2 markers
  2. Adolescent with cystic fibrosis, antibiotic-refractory symptoms and a total IgE above 1,000 IU/mL; establishing Aspergillus sensitization → Aspergillus-specific IgE or Aspergillus skin testing → Total IgE suggests, specific testing confirms
  3. Adolescent with cystic fibrosis and confirmed allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis → Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent → The pathology is allergic inflammation
  4. Well 14-year-old with cystic fibrosis at routine annual review; surveillance for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis → Total serum IgE → Recommended annually in cystic fibrosis
  5. Adult with difficult-to-control asthma, recurrent brown mucus plugs, central bronchiectasis and IgE 2,400 IU/mL → Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent → Same disease, different structural host
  6. Rural tropical resident with refractory pulmonary infiltrates, eosinophilia, high IgE, migratory urticaria and abdominal pain → Treat for strongyloidiasis before giving systemic glucocorticoids → Steroids risk disseminated hyperinfection
  7. 45-year-old with cystic fibrosis, several months of cough and weight loss, nodular and cavitary opacities on CT, and a normal eosinophil count and IgE → Nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease → Mycobacterium avium complex rather than tuberculosis
  8. Farmer with fever, malaise and airspace infiltrates unresponsive to antibiotics whose symptoms improve over 3 days in hospital, with a normal IgE → Identify and eliminate the inciting antigen exposure → Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
  9. Why Aspergillus causes disease in cystic fibrosis but is cleared harmlessly in a normal lung → Mucus trapping defeats mucociliary clearance, allowing colonization and Th2 sensitization → The disease is the immune response
  10. Adolescent with cystic fibrosis whose exacerbation fails initial therapy; sputum grows a resistant Pseudomonas and the eosinophil count and IgE are normal → Adjust antibiotics according to culture sensitivities → Still a bacterial exacerbation
Decoy note The stem is engineered so the infectious framing survives as long as possible: an admission, broad-spectrum antibiotics, fever and crackles all point one way, and the two findings that overturn it arrive last and quietly as a laboratory line. The fever is not evidence against the answer — fever, malaise and thick blood-streaked sputum are explicitly common in it — so a reader who uses fever as an infection marker never reaches the reclassification. The real discriminator sentence is a week later, there is no improvement, and it is doing the work of an entire negative workup.
Pearls Eosinophilia with an IgE above 1,000 in cystic fibrosis or asthma is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, treated with glucocorticoids plus an antifungal. · Antibiotic failure is a finding rather than a dosing problem. In structural lung disease it should prompt a change of category — allergic, mycobacterial, vasculitic — before a change of spectrum. · This disease needs a damaged airway: asthma or cystic fibrosis. The spores are inhaled by everyone, and only a trapped airway sensitises. · Total IgE above 1,000 IU/mL is the screening threshold; specific Aspergillus IgE or skin testing confirms sensitisation, and eosinophilia only supports. · Treatment is a glucocorticoid first and an antifungal second — the disease is the immune response, so treating only the fungus treats only the trigger. · Cystic fibrosis earns an annual total IgE, one of the few purely serologic screening intervals on the paediatric pulmonary syllabus. · Before starting systemic steroids in anyone with eosinophilia and plausible tropical exposure, exclude or empirically treat strongyloidiasis, because steroids convert it to hyperinfection ⚠︎.
Pairs with Verified: Part I Recurrent Sinopulmonary Infection owns the upstream question of why a child keeps getting infections and lands on cystic fibrosis and the mucociliary axis; this brief owns what happens once that diagnosis is established and an exacerbation stops responding. Part I Asthma vs. COPD carries this disease as one line of its adult test-selection block, with the brown-mucus-plug presentation. Store the discriminator as a question: did an adequate antibiotic course fail, and are the eosinophils and IgE up?
Transferable rule When a treatment that should work does not, the failure itself is diagnostic information, and the next move is to ask which category of disease you are in rather than to intensify within the category you assumed. In a host with structural organ damage the commonest reclassification is from infection to hypersensitivity, and the laboratory tests that make it are cheap. --- Batch 5, brief 02 · 2026-09-10.
Class-vs-memberHypersensitivity pneumonitis — It improves spontaneously in hospital once the exposure is removed, and neither eosinophilia nor a high IgE is expected
True-fact-wrong-slotStrongyloidiasis — Requires rural tropical or subtropical exposure and travels with roaming urticaria and gastrointestinal symptoms, none of which is present
Salient decoyGranulomatosis with polyangiitis — Typically older men, and it is not associated with eosinophilia or elevated IgE
Class-vs-memberTuberculosis — Cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis is colonised by nontuberculous mycobacteria, whose disease is chronic and cavitary and carries no eosinophilia

Chronic Dyspnea in Sickle Cell Disease

the timing pattern picks the test · board question · Are the symptoms nocturnal and intermittent, or exertional and progressive?

The decision point

The sickle cell disease is real, relevant, and not the discriminator. What decides this is a two-word symptom pattern — nocturnal and intermittent — and everything else in the examination exists to remove the alternatives that would have been exertional. Normal vital signs and a normal chest film remove pulmonary embolism, which arrives acute and persistent with tachycardia and hypoxia. No peripheral edema with the apex beat in the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line removes pulmonary hypertension and heart failure, both of which announce themselves with right-sided signs or a displaced point of maximal impulse. A normal film with no reticular markings removes fibrosis, which is progressive and exertional. No hilar adenopathy removes sarcoidosis, and the family history of sarcoid is there precisely to make you forget that sarcoid is not associated with sickle cell disease at all. What remains is obstructive airway disease, and asthma is a common comorbidity in children and adolescents with sickle cell disease — so the first test is spirometry, looking for obstruction that reverses with a bronchodilator.

Defining criteria Asthma in sickle cell disease — intermittent or chronic wheezing, chest tightness or cough, often worse at night, with exercise, or with upper respiratory infection, and wheezing need not be present on examination · The confirmatory finding — pulmonary function testing showing reversible airway obstruction · Pulmonary hypertension — exertional dyspnea with signs of right-sided failure such as jugular venous distension and edema, tricuspid regurgitation on echocardiography, and raised pulmonary arterial pressure at catheterisation · Pulmonary fibrosis — exertional and progressive dyspnea, honeycombing on chest CT, and a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing
Pertinent positives & negatives Worse in the middle of the night — the single discriminating attribute, because nocturnal symptoms are airway rather than vascular or interstitial · Four weeks, intermittent, chest tightness and dry cough — chronic and episodic, which excludes the acute vascular events · Clear lungs on examination — wheezing is often absent in mild or intermittent disease and does not argue against the answer · Normal chest x-ray — expected in asthma, and it simultaneously removes fibrosis, sarcoid and acute chest syndrome · Vital signs within normal limits — no hypoxia or tachycardia, which is what a pulmonary embolism would supply · No peripheral edema — no right-sided heart failure, so pulmonary hypertension is unsupported · Apex in the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line — undisplaced, whereas congestive heart failure would displace it · Family history of sarcoidosis — sarcoid is not associated with sickle cell disease and the film shows no adenopathy, so the history is bait · Prior acute chest syndrome — raises the prior for asthma rather than lowering it, because the two are bidirectionally linked
Chronic respiratory symptoms in sickle cell disease — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
AsthmaAirway hyperreactivity, a common comorbidity in paediatric sickle cell disease, with recurrent acute chest syndrome contributing to itIntermittent or chronic wheeze, tightness or cough worse at night, on exertion or with a URI, with a normal film— (the answer)
Pulmonary hypertensionChronic hemolysis and vasculopathy raise pulmonary pressuresExertional dyspnea with jugular venous distension and edema, tricuspid regurgitation on echo, enlarged pulmonary arteriesNo edema, normal apex, symptoms nocturnal rather than exertional
Pulmonary fibrosisRepeated vasoocclusive lung injury scars the parenchymaProgressive exertional dyspnea, increased reticular markings, honeycombing on CT, restrictive functionNormal film, with intermittent nocturnal symptoms
Pulmonary embolism Can't missSickle cell disease raises thrombotic riskAcute and persistent pleuritic pain and cough with tachycardia and hypoxia, raised D-dimer, filling defect on CT angiographyFour weeks, intermittent, normal vitals
Acute chest syndrome Can't missPulmonary vasoocclusion, often with infectionFever, hypoxia, chest pain and a new infiltrateAfebrile, normal saturations, normal film
SarcoidosisNoncaseating granulomas, and not associated with sickle cell diseaseBilateral hilar adenopathy on film, with serum ACE having poor sensitivity and specificityNo adenopathy, and family history is not a risk transfer
Management, in one line Management follows the test and is one sentence: asthma in sickle cell disease is treated as asthma is treated in anyone else, with inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids, with the added stake that controlling it lowers the risk of the next acute chest syndrome.
Decision spine Acute or chronic? — Four weeks, intermittent → the acute vascular events are out · Nocturnal or exertional? — Nocturnal → airway rather than vascular or interstitial · Any right-sided signs? — No edema and an undisplaced apex → pulmonary hypertension and heart failure are out · What does the film show? — Nothing — no infiltrate, no reticular markings, no hilar nodes → acute chest, fibrosis and sarcoid are out · What confirms reversible obstruction? — Spirometry before and after a bronchodilator
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo girl with homozygous sickle cell disease and 4 weeks of chest tightness and dry cough worse in the middle of the night, with clear lungs and a normal chest x-ray → Spirometry with bronchodilator testing → Asthma
  2. Same patient whose spirometry shows airway obstruction improving after albuterol → Inhaled corticosteroid with a short-acting bronchodilator → Managed as asthma is in anyone else
  3. 19 yo man with sickle cell disease, exertional dyspnea, jugular venous distension, pedal edema and a loud pulmonic component of S2 → Echocardiography → Pulmonary hypertension
  4. 24 yo woman with sickle cell disease and a year of progressive exertional dyspnea, with increased reticular markings on chest x-ray → CT scan of the chest → Pulmonary fibrosis
  5. 16 yo boy with sickle cell disease, 1 day of pleuritic chest pain, temperature 38.9 C, oxygen saturation 88%, and a new left lower lobe infiltrate → Transfusion with antibiotic therapy → Acute chest syndrome
  6. 20 yo woman with sickle cell disease, sudden pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia and hypoxia, with a clear chest x-ray → CT pulmonary angiogram → Pulmonary embolism
  7. Adolescent with sickle cell disease and suspected asthma; the pulmonary function finding that confirms the diagnosis → Airway obstruction that reverses after bronchodilator administration → Not a restrictive pattern
  8. 22 yo with cough, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest x-ray, anterior uveitis and hypercalcemia → Sarcoidosis → The chest film makes the diagnosis
  9. Why asthma and acute chest syndrome each increase the risk of the other in sickle cell disease → Parenchymal hypoxia promotes inflammation and sickling within the pulmonary vasculature → And acute chest syndrome worsens airway hyperreactivity
  10. Adolescent with sickle cell disease and nocturnal cough with a normal chest x-ray; which test should not be ordered first → Serum ACE activity → Poor sensitivity and specificity, and sarcoidosis is unsupported
Decoy note Almost every sentence of the history is doing decoy work, and none of it is doing discrimination. Acute chest syndrome six months ago, prior vasoocclusive episodes requiring transfusion, hydroxyurea and a family history of sarcoidosis together create the impression that a sickle cell patient must have a sickle cell answer. The counterintuitive fact is stated outright: asthma is a common comorbidity, and the prior acute chest syndrome makes it more likely rather than less. Note also that clear lungs on examination is not evidence against asthma, since wheezing is often absent when symptoms are mild or intermittent, and that the deliberately normal point of maximal impulse and absence of edema are two findings whose only job is to kill the echocardiogram.
Pearls Nocturnal chest tightness and dry cough with a normal chest film is asthma, and spirometry with bronchodilator response is the first test. · Nocturnal and intermittent means airway; exertional and progressive means vascular or interstitial — that single axis sorts the whole chronic-dyspnea differential in sickle cell disease. · Asthma is a common comorbidity of sickle cell disease and the relationship is bidirectional — acute chest syndrome drives airway hyperreactivity, and asthma raises the risk of the next acute chest syndrome. · A normal chest x-ray is expected in asthma and simultaneously excludes fibrosis, sarcoid and acute chest syndrome, making it one of the most informative normal tests in the differential. · Absent wheeze does not exclude asthma; spirometry with reversibility is the test rather than auscultation. · Sarcoidosis has no association with sickle cell disease, and serum ACE has poor sensitivity and specificity even when sarcoid is genuinely suspected — the chest film leads. · Treating the asthma is not just symptom control, it is acute chest syndrome prevention, which is why the exam wants it found.
Pairs with Verified: Part II Sickle Cell Trait versus Disease owns the trait–disease boundary and carries acute chest syndrome as the acute event; this brief owns the chronic pulmonary sequelae that follow it. Part I Asthma: Severity Classification owns what happens after spirometry confirms the diagnosis, and Part I Asthma vs. COPD owns the adult version of the which-test question. Store the discriminator as a question: are the symptoms nocturnal and intermittent, or exertional and progressive?
Transferable rule A dramatic chronic disease in the history sets the prior for its own complications, but it does not suspend the base rate of common disease — so when a patient with a rare condition develops common symptoms, the symptom pattern still selects the test. Ask what the timing of the complaint means before asking what the diagnosis in the first line predisposes to. --- Batch 5, brief 06 · 2026-09-10.
Unchecked attributeCT pulmonary angiogram — Embolism is acute and persistent with tachycardia and hypoxia, while this is 4 weeks, intermittent and nocturnal with normal vitals
Unchecked attributeCT scan of the chest — Fibrosis is progressive and exertional with increased reticular markings, while the film is normal and the symptoms are nocturnal
Class-vs-memberEchocardiogram — It presents with exertional dyspnea and right-sided failure signs, and there is no edema with an undisplaced apex
Salient decoySerum ACE activity — Sarcoid is not associated with sickle cell disease, there is no hilar adenopathy, and the test has poor sensitivity and specificity anyway
Sequencing trapD-dimer — The same failure as the angiogram, because the clinical picture is not an embolism picture, so no rung of that pathway applies
Salient decoyBronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy — Invasive, and it answers fibrosis, which the normal film and the symptom pattern have already excluded

Stridor vs. wheeze · toxic vs. well

Decision spine 1. Stridor (upper) or wheeze (lower)? 2. Sudden + afebrile → foreign body — absence of fever does heavy lifting. 3. Toxic + drooling + tripod → epiglottitis, airway first in the OR; throat exam or X-ray first is the trap. 4. Barky + nontoxic → croup. 5. Croup not behaving → bacterial tracheitis. 6. Vaccination status is never decoration.
Paired pearls Croup improves with racemic epi, tracheitis doesn't · laryngomalacia better prone, croup worse at night · bronchiolitis gets nothing · expiratory film for foreign body because the trapped lung stays inflated.

Pediatric Community-Acquired Pneumonia

Typical vs. atypical · the assassin scan in action

The decision point

2 weeks of gradually worsening dry cough + low-grade fever + "tired but not ill" + bilateral diffuse findings + normal saturation = atypical pneumonia in a school-aged child = Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Every distractor in these stems is killed by an explicit sentence — read it as a list of assassinations, not a puzzle.

Typical vs atypical pneumonia
Typical (S. pneumo, H. flu)Atypical (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila)
OnsetAbruptGradual, over 1–2 weeks
Fever / coughHigh with rigors; productiveLow-grade; dry, persistent
AppearanceIll, chest pain, ↑ work of breathingWalking around, functional
Exam / CXRFocal consolidation; lobarBilateral crackles ± wheeze; diffuse interstitial
TreatmentAmoxicillinMacrolide; doxycycline if >8 yr
Age-based organisms Neonate = GBS / E. coli / Listeria · <5 = viruses (RSV, parainfluenza, adenovirus, hMPV) · ≥5 = Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, S. pneumoniae · 1–3 months = Chlamydia trachomatis — staccato cough, afebrile, conjunctivitis, eosinophilia.
The adult version — a second discriminator

Upper AND lower respiratory tract involvement together. Pharyngitis plus an interstitial pneumonia is distinctive — typical bacterial pneumonia does not cause pharyngitis. A small serous pleural effusion occurs in ~25% of Mycoplasma, so an effusion is not evidence for pneumococcus; what separates them is everything around it (abrupt onset, rigors, rusty sputum, lobar consolidation, ill appearance).

Atypical organisms — settings & features
Atypical organismSettingDistinguishing features
MycoplasmaYoung, dorms/barracks, fall–winterIndolent, dry cough, nonexudative pharyngitis, macular rash, cold agglutinins, normal WBC, bullous myringitis
Chlamydophila pneumoniaeYoung adultsSimilar; hoarseness prominent, often biphasic
LegionellaOlder, smokers, immunosuppressed; water systems, AC, cruise ships, hotelsHigh fever + diarrhea/vomiting + confusion, hyponatremia, ↑LFTs, relative bradycardia → urine antigen
Chlamydophila psittaciBird exposureSevere headache, splenomegaly
Coxiella burnetii (Q fever)Farm animals, sheep, parturient catsNo rash; hepatitis; culture-negative endocarditis later
Mycoplasma micro & extrapulmonary disease No cell wall → beta-lactams useless; smallest free-living organism; sterols in its membrane; grows on Eaton agar; invisible on Gram stain. Extrapulmonary: cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia (IgM vs the I antigen, Coombs-positive, ± Raynaud) · erythema multiforme / MIRM — the leading infectious cause of EM after HSV · bullous myringitis · Guillain-Barré, encephalitis, transverse myelitis.
Scenario bank
  1. Same picture plus jaundice, anemia, positive Coombs → cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia
  2. Same plus target lesions and oral mucositis → erythema multiforme / MIRM
  3. Older smoker with diarrhea, confusion, hyponatremia, high fever → Legionella → urine antigen
  4. Bird exposure + severe headache → Chlamydophila psittaci
  5. Farm animal or parturient cat exposure → Coxiella burnetii
  6. Abrupt onset, rigors, rusty sputum, lobar consolidation → S. pneumoniae
  7. Ascending weakness weeks after a respiratory illness → Guillain-Barré post-Mycoplasma
  8. Started on amoxicillin with no improvement → no cell wall → switch to a macrolide
  9. Child <5 with wheeze and an interstitial pattern → viral, not Mycoplasma

Transferable rule When a stem gives symptoms in two anatomic compartments at once (upper + lower airway), ask which organisms actually span both. Compartment-spanning is a discriminator most people never check, and it collapses the atypical-vs-typical fork instantly.

Pediatric Upper Respiratory Infection

Green mucus is not a bacterial sign

The decision point

Purulent or colored discharge does not mean bacterial. Green comes from myeloperoxidase in neutrophils recruited by any inflammation, viral included. Afebrile + well-appearing + 2 days + clear mobile TMs + no exudate + clear lungs → viral URI → supportive care.

When a "cold" earns antibiotics — three doors
  • Acute bacterial sinusitis: symptoms ≥10 days without improvement, OR high fever + purulence ≥3–4 consecutive days, OR "double worsening." Clinical diagnosis — no imaging.
  • Strep pharyngitis: Centor (fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough) → test before treating. Treatment prevents rheumatic fever, not PSGN.
  • Acute otitis media: bulging, immobile, erythematous TM. Mobility on pneumatic otoscopy is the discriminator.
Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo M, 2 days of green nasal discharge, afebrile, well, clear mobile tympanic membranes → viral upper respiratory infection → supportive care
  2. 3 yo M with 12 days of nasal discharge and no improvement → acute bacterial rhinosinusitis → amoxicillin-clavulanate
  3. 3 yo M with a bulging, immobile, erythematous tympanic membrane and fever → acute otitis media
  4. 3 yo M who improved then developed new fever and worsening discharge on day 7 → double worsening — bacterial sinusitis
  5. 3 yo M with clear rhinorrhea, sneezing, itchy eyes and seasonal recurrence → allergic rhinitis → intranasal corticosteroid
  6. A parent asks whether green discharge proves bacterial infection → no — colour reflects neutrophil myeloperoxidase in any inflammation
Transferable rule Loud detail → ask "what job is this doing?" If the answer is "making me nervous," it's bait. Those seconds belong to the two-step genetics problem later in the block.

Asthma: Severity Classification

Exam answer vs. current guideline

The decision point

NBME tests the NAEPP/EPR-3 severity ladder. Intermittent (≤2 days/wk symptoms, ≤2 nights/mo, normal FEV₁, no activity limits) → SABA PRN alone. Mild persistent → add low-dose ICS. Moderate → low-dose ICS+LABA or medium ICS. Severe → high-dose ICS+LABA.

Defining criteria Intermittent — ≤2 days/wk symptoms, ≤2 nights/mo, normal FEV₁, no activity limits → SABA PRN alone · Mild persistent — add low-dose ICS · Moderate persistent — low-dose ICS+LABA or medium-dose ICS · Severe persistent — high-dose ICS+LABA
Scenario bank
  1. 9 yo M, symptoms 1 day per week, night waking once a month, normal FEV₁ → intermittent → SABA as needed
  2. 9 yo M, symptoms 4 days per week, 3 nights a month, FEV₁ 85% → mild persistent → low-dose inhaled corticosteroid
  3. 9 yo M with daily symptoms, weekly night waking, FEV₁ 70% → moderate persistent → low-dose ICS plus LABA
  4. 9 yo M with symptoms throughout the day, nightly waking, FEV₁ 55% → severe persistent
  5. 9 yo M using his rescue inhaler four times a week → not intermittent — step up to a controller
  6. 9 yo M with symptoms only on exertion, otherwise well → SABA before exercise
Guideline currency GINA now states SABA monotherapy is not supported at any step, any severity, any age — even intermittent asthma gets ICS-containing therapy (as-needed ICS-formoterol, or ICS-SABA combination reliever). Rationale: intermittent symptoms do not mean intermittent inflammation. On the exam, play NAEPP; in clinic, GINA. The tell that a question wants NAEPP is an answer ladder running "nothing extra / montelukast / low-dose ICS / ICS+LABA."
Numbers that key the answer 2 per week · 2 nights per month · daily · nightly. The stem's frequency counts are the question.

Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia

Chronic lung disease of prematurity · the 28-day clock

The decision point

The stem states the diagnosis verbatim: preterm infant + supplemental O₂ requirement at ≥28 days of life = BPD. The remaining step is translation — modern "new" BPD is arrested alveolar development (reduced alveolar number and septation, disrupted vasculogenesis), not the old fibrotic ventilator injury, not air leak. Every preemie lung complication owns a window on the clock, and the clock is read before the findings.

Defining criteria Diagnosis — preterm infant with supplemental O₂ requirement ≥28 days of life · Severity — graded by support required at 36 weeks postmenstrual age · Histology — reduced alveolar number and septation, impaired vasculogenesis

  2. Term infant born by elective C-section, tachypnea at 2 hours, fluid in the fissures, well by 48 hours → transient tachypnea of the newborn → supportive care only
  3. 27 wk preemie, day 3 on high-pressure ventilation, abrupt hypoxia with unilateral perivascular cystic lucencies → pulmonary interstitial emphysema → reduce ventilator pressures

Pearls Caffeine (for apnea of prematurity) and vitamin A each reduce BPD incidence · antenatal steroids + surfactant converted BPD from fibrotic injury to developmental arrest · management is supportive — oxygen, nutrition, fluid restriction; alveoli continue to form over months · complications: pulmonary HTN, systemic HTN, recurrent respiratory infections, neurodevelopmental delay · RSV prophylaxis update (AAP): palivizumab discontinued end of 2025; nirsevimab is standard, and BPD earns a second-season dose.

Transferable rule Prematurity complication stems are clock questions — birth = RDS, ventilator days = air leak, ≥28 days = BPD, months = pulmonary HTN. Match the timeline before the findings, and when a stem states a diagnostic criterion verbatim, convert it directly to the answer.
