Gastroenterology & Hepatology

The Sick Jaundiced Neonate with a Positive Screen

The screen names the panel, the presentation names the disease · handoff · conjugated, big liver, reducing sugar

The decision point

The phone call is the decoy and the urine is the decider. Every option is on the newborn screen, so a positive screen eliminates nothing. What separates them is that this infant has conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, a large liver, and a non-glucose reducing sugar in the urine after ten days of milk feeds. That triad is galactose-1-phosphate accumulating in a GALT-deficient liver: classic galactosemia.

The fever is not incidental. Galactosemia predisposes to Escherichia coli sepsis, and a febrile 10-day-old is septic until cultured — the sepsis workup runs in parallel with the metabolic answer, never after it.

Defining criteria Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia — direct bilirubin above 1.0 mg/dL ⚠, or above 20% of total; never physiologic and never breast-milk jaundice · Urine reducing substances — positive with dipstick glucose negative means a non-glucose reducing sugar, so galactose or fructose; requires recent intake of that sugar to be positive ⚠ · Classic galactosemia — galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency, confirmed by red cell GALT enzyme activity ⚠, which reads falsely normal after transfusion
The screen-positive neonate - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Classic galactosemiaAutosomal recessive GALT deficiency, symptoms within days of milk feedsConjugated jaundice with hepatomegaly and urine reducing substances in a milk-fed neonate
Hereditary fructose intoleranceAldolase B deficiency, identical hepatic picture with hypoglycemiaOnset with fruit, juice or sucrose at weaning, months old rather than days
Biliary atresia Can't missObstructive cholestasis, Kasai before about 60 days ⚠Direct hyperbilirubinemia in a well infant with acholic stools, reducing substances negative
Maple syrup urine diseaseBranched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, day 4 to 7 ⚠Encephalopathy without hepatomegaly or cholestasis, sweet-smelling urine, ketosis
Cystic fibrosisScreened by immunoreactive trypsinogenMeconium ileus or quiet cholestasis, not fever with vomiting and urinary sugar
Sickle cell or neonatal hyperthyroidismScreen-positive with no hepatic pictureNo cholestasis, no hepatomegaly, no urinary sugar; sickle is silent at 10 days because of HbF
Scenario bank
  1. 3-day-old, asymptomatic, breastfeeding well, newborn screen positive for galactosemia → stop breastfeeding and start soy-based formula pending confirmation → presumptive galactosemia
  2. 8-day-old with jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting after breastfeeds and positive urine reducing substances → stop breast milk and start soy-based formula → classic galactosemia
  3. 12-day-old with galactosemia on soy formula, temperature 38.8 C, lethargic → blood and urine cultures with empiric intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin ⚠ → Escherichia coli sepsis
  4. 10-day-old with jaundice, hepatomegaly, positive urine reducing substances and a newborn screen positive for galactosemia → red cell GALT enzyme activity → classic galactosemia
  5. 3-week-old with galactosemia and bilateral cataracts on examination → galactitol accumulation via aldose reductase → osmotic lens injury
  6. 6-week-old, well and growing, bilateral cataracts only, no hepatomegaly, positive urine reducing substances → galactokinase deficiency → lactose-free diet
  7. 9-month-old with vomiting, hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly and jaundice since juice and fruit were introduced, positive urine reducing substances → hereditary fructose intolerance → remove fructose, sucrose and sorbitol
  8. 4-week-old, well and feeding well, direct bilirubin 5, acholic stools, urine reducing substances negative → abdominal ultrasound and HIDA scan → biliary atresia, with Kasai before about 60 days ⚠
  9. 5-day-old with poor feeding, lethargy, seizures and urine that smells like maple syrup, newborn screen positive → protein-free feeds with intravenous dextrose → maple syrup urine disease
  10. 2-week-old with confirmed galactosemia whose parents ask what to feed → breast milk → soy-based formula is the substitute
Two things happen at once Stop all lactose and galactose immediately — breast milk and standard formula give way to soy-based formula — without waiting for confirmation, because the injury is ongoing. In parallel, send blood and urine cultures and start empiric neonatal antibiotics ⚠ for Escherichia coli. Confirm afterwards with red cell GALT activity. A negative urine reducing substance test in an infant who has stopped feeding excludes nothing ⚠, because the test needs recent galactose intake.
Pearls Classic galactosemia is GALT deficiency affecting liver, kidney, brain and lens with a predisposition to Escherichia coli sepsis; galactokinase deficiency gives cataracts alone · Reducing substances positive with dipstick glucose negative means galactose or fructose, because glucose is itself a reducing sugar, so read both tests · Cataracts in both galactose disorders come from galactitol via aldose reductase, the same enzyme that makes sorbitol in the diabetic lens · Hereditary fructose intolerance is the diet-shifted twin with the same hepatic picture plus hypoglycemia, appearing at weaning · Direct hyperbilirubinemia in a well infant with acholic stools is biliary atresia, and the Kasai clock runs to about 60 days ⚠ · Girls with treated galactosemia still develop premature ovarian insufficiency ⚠, because the diet does not prevent it
Pairs with Part I Cholestasis & the LFT Patterns owns the adult conjugated-versus-unconjugated framework; this brief owns its neonatal form. Candidate twins — confirm: hereditary fructose intolerance, with the discriminator stored as a question: when did symptoms start relative to fruit or sucrose? And biliary atresia — is the infant sick or well, and are reducing substances present? Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism is the other positive newborn screen that turns on a direction: there the TSH direction and the neck locate the defect, here the enzyme and the organism do.
Transferable rule A positive newborn screen never names the disease because every option is on the panel, so the bilirubin fraction, the liver and the urine do the naming, and a febrile neonate is cultured and treated for sepsis in parallel with the metabolic answer rather than after it.
Class-vs-memberMaple syrup urine disease is the right class of screen-flagged inborn error but has no hepatomegaly and carries ketoacids rather than a reducing sugar.
Salient decoyThe positive screen sells cystic fibrosis, whose neonatal face is meconium ileus rather than fever with urinary sugar.
True-fact-wrong-slotSickle cell causes jaundice, but unconjugated and not at 10 days, because fetal hemoglobin protects the neonate.

Fecal Impaction & Overflow Diarrhea

The rectal exam is the diagnosis

The decision point

"Rectal examination shows firm stool in the rectal vault." That finding is the diagnosis — and it is incompatible with the usual competing answer: adhesive small bowel obstruction gives an empty rectum, a distended abdomen, and high-pitched or absent bowel sounds.

The detail that invites over-reading: last bowel movement 5 days ago, "characterized by loose stool." Constipation with loose stool feels contradictory — it's overflow diarrhea, liquid tracking around a hard impaction, and it's near-pathognomonic.

Stem findings → options ruled out
OptionThe sentence that kills it
AdhesionsFirm stool in the rectal vault (SBO empties the rectum); soft, undistended abdomen
Colon cancer"Colonoscopy 3 years ago showed no abnormalities"
DiverticulitisNo fever; diffuse, not focal LLQ, tenderness
Ischemic bowelNo hematochezia; no AF or atherosclerotic risk factors
VolvulusSoft abdomen without distension; no coffee-bean film
Two details most people skip Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic — it slows colonic transit and is the cause here, which is why the objective says "treatment of underlying causes." And "warm, dry skin" is the anticholinergic sign planted alongside the drug. Constipating culprits: anticholinergics (oxybutynin, TCAs, antihistamines, antipsychotics), opioids, verapamil, iron, calcium, aluminum antacids, ondansetron.
Management ladder — fecal impaction
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Enema (in-context: first-line)Fails to clear
2Manual disimpactionEnema unsuccessful
3Treat the cause — stop or reduce the oxybutynin; then maintenance PEG, fluids, mobilityAlways, after clearing
Scenario bank
  1. 77 yo F, 5 days without a BM, empty rectal vault, distended abdomen, high-pitched bowel sounds, prior laparotomy → adhesive SBO → NG decompression + imaging
  2. 77 yo F, sudden severe pain, distended tympanitic abdomen, coffee-bean sign → sigmoid volvulus → endoscopic decompression
  3. 68 yo M, LLQ pain with fever 38.5 and focal tenderness → diverticulitis → CT
  4. 72 yo F with atrial fibrillation, crampy pain and hematochezia → ischemic colitis
  5. 60 yo M, progressive constipation with iron deficiency anemia and weight loss, no recent colonoscopy → colon cancer → colonoscopy
  6. 77 yo F, impaction cleared by enema, still constipated → stop the oxybutynin, start PEG
  7. 80 yo M on chronic opioids, 6 days without a BM, hard stool in the vault → disimpaction + methylnaltrexone or naloxegol
Where the rule breaks Impaction can sit distal to a second pathology — a slow-growing tumor or partial obstruction. What licenses stopping at impaction here is the normal colonoscopy 3 years ago plus absent weight loss and anemia. Change any of those and you relieve the impaction and investigate.
Pairs with Part I Constipation in a Child is the paediatric mirror — there the rectal vault is empty and an anal fissure closes the rectal route that is first-line here.
Transferable rule A switch requires new incompatibility, not new plausibility. Before changing an answer, ask whether the detail makes your current choice impossible — and check whether the stem contains an assassin for the option you're moving toward. Here it did, one sentence away from the finding already in hand.
Salient decoy

Tracheoesophageal Fistula with Esophageal Atresia

Choking on the first feed · UWorld · pass a tube before you order a picture

The decision point

Formula mixed with saliva is the diagnosis. Milk that returns mixed with pooled secretions never reached a stomach — it filled a blind proximal pouch and overflowed. Add choking on the very first feed and coarse lungs from aspiration, and this is esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula.

The question is then not what but what first, and the answer is the cheapest thing at the bedside: pass an orogastric tube. It meets resistance at the pouch, and the film shows it coiled. The murmur, the maternal drug history and the absent prenatal care are all planted to sell an imaging or pharmacologic answer instead.

Defining criteria Type C — proximal pouch with a distal fistula, about 85% of cases · Gas in the abdomen — a distal fistula is present · Gasless abdomen — pure atresia with no distal fistula · H-type — no atresia, presenting months later with recurrent pneumonia
Neonatal choking and vomiting — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
EA with distal TEFChoking on the first feed, copious frothy secretions, polyhydramnios in uteroFormula mixed with saliva; tube will not pass
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaSevere distress at deliveryScaphoid abdomen, bowel gas in the chest, shifted heart sounds
Congenital heart diseaseFeeding difficulty with cyanosisCyanosis and diaphoresis with feeds, no excess secretions
EpiglottitisFebrile stridor with droolingSchool-aged child, never a newborn
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosisNonbilious projectile vomitingAge 3 to 6 weeks, hungry after vomiting, olive mass
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiencyGround-glass with air bronchograms, low lung volumes
Neonatal abstinence syndromeMaternal opioid useOnset at or beyond 24 hours, hypertonia and irritability
Scenario bank
  1. 3 h old term newborn, coughing and vomiting with the first feed, frothy oral secretions, coarse breath sounds → esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula → attempt nasogastric tube placement
  2. Newborn with a coiled nasogastric tube in the proximal esophagus and gas throughout the abdomen → esophageal atresia with a distal fistula → surgical repair
  3. Newborn with a coiled nasogastric tube and a gasless abdomen → pure esophageal atresia without a fistula
  4. 8 mo infant with recurrent pneumonia and coughing with every feed since birth, feeds otherwise pass normally → H-type tracheoesophageal fistula → esophagram or bronchoscopy
  5. Newborn with confirmed esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula, what to screen for → VACTERL association → echocardiogram and renal ultrasound
  6. 4 wk old with nonbilious projectile vomiting, hungry after vomiting, and an olive-like epigastric mass → hypertrophic pyloric stenosis → abdominal ultrasound
  7. Newborn with bilious vomiting, a double bubble on x-ray, and maternal polyhydramnios → duodenal atresia
  8. 28 wk preemie, grunting and retracting at 2 h, diffuse ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms → respiratory distress syndrome → surfactant administration
  9. 36 h old, irritable, hypertonic, sneezing and feeding poorly, mother maintained on methadone → neonatal abstinence syndrome
  10. Newborn with esophageal atresia awaiting surgery, immediate management → NPO with continuous suction of the proximal pouch, head elevated
The newborn clock Age at presentation is a diagnostic instrument. Minutes to hours: TEF/EA, choanal atresia, diaphragmatic hernia, respiratory distress syndrome, Potter sequence. Beyond 24 hours: neonatal abstinence, sepsis, ductal-dependent lesions as the PDA closes, bilious vomiting and malrotation. 3 to 6 weeks: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Months: H-type fistula, laryngomalacia. Every wrong option in this stem is a real disease placed at the wrong point on that clock.
Pearls Polyhydramnios in utero, because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid · Diagnosis is made by the tube, not the scanner — resistance at roughly 10 cm, confirmed on film · The abdominal gas pattern names the anatomic type before any endoscopy · VACTERL screening after diagnosis: echocardiogram and renal ultrasound at minimum · A soft systolic murmur on day one is usually a closing ductus, not structural disease
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves is the mechanistic twin: amniotic fluid volume reads out fetal function in opposite directions. Cannot make urine gives oligohydramnios and Potter sequence; cannot swallow gives polyhydramnios and foregut or duodenal atresia. Store it as a question: which way did the fluid go? Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn owns the trigger axis — cyanosis worse with feeding and better with crying is choanal atresia, not a fistula.
Transferable rule Board next-step questions in neonates reward the cheapest bedside maneuver that confirms the diagnosis, so when every option but one is an imaging study, the odd one out is usually the answer.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpiglottitis is a febrile school-age disease; a 3-hour-old cannot have it.
Sequencing trapEchocardiography is indicated — for VACTERL, after the diagnosis, not before it.
Class-vs-memberPyloric stenosis is the right entity family at the wrong age by six weeks.

Renal & Genitourinary 10 topics + 4 board-style

Two recurring lessons: normal values are eliminations, and a single discordant test component never overturns a convergent picture.

Pyelonephritis: Route & Disposition

The diagnosis is given; the question is where and how

The decision point

Fever + chills + dysuria + CVA tenderness hands you pyelonephritis. The real question is route and setting, and one line usually decides it: "only clear fluids for 2 days" means the patient cannot tolerate oral therapy.

Criteria for admission / IV therapy
  • Unable to tolerate oral intake
  • Hemodynamic instability or sepsis
  • Complicated anatomy: male sex, obstruction, stones, catheter, pregnancy
  • Failure of outpatient therapy, immunocompromise, extremes of age
Scenario bank
  1. 28 yo F with fever and CVA tenderness, tolerating oral intake, no comorbidity → outpatient oral therapy
  2. 28 yo F with pyelonephritis who is vomiting and cannot keep fluids down → admit for IV antibiotics
  3. 28 yo F at 24 weeks of pregnancy with pyelonephritis → admit — pregnancy alone warrants admission
  4. 28 yo F with dysuria and frequency, no fever and no CVA tenderness → cystitis — nitrofurantoin → it does not treat pyelonephritis
  5. 28 yo F on appropriate antibiotics still febrile at 72 hours → CT for abscess or obstruction
  6. 28 yo F with pyelonephritis and a known resistant organism → admit for IV therapy
Two reading skills this stem teaches "Long-standing hypertension + BP 104/68" is NBME writing hypotensive without saying it — vitals must be read against the patient's baseline · a benign abdominal exam means no CT: imaging in pyelonephritis is reserved for failure to improve at 48–72 hours, suspected obstruction or stone, recurrence, or concern for emphysematous pyelonephritis in a diabetic.
Pairs with Part I Vesicoureteral Reflux owns what happens after the febrile UTI is treated and the imaging comes back. Part I Recurrent Urinary Infection in a Child owns the afebrile recurrences that never reach the kidney.
Transferable rule When the clinical diagnosis is sufficient and the patient is infected, treat — don't image. Uncomplicated version (healthy young woman tolerating PO, stable) → outpatient oral therapy.

BPH & Acute Urinary Retention

Reading a three-act chronology

The decision point

"Underlying cause" questions want the trunk of the causal tree, not a branch. Six months of hesitancy and dribbling → five days of frequency and incomplete emptying → one day of anuria with suprapubic pain. The retention, the UTI, and the creatinine of 3.4 all flow from prostatic obstruction.

Why 1+ blood means nothing Trace-to-1+ hematuria is expected with UTI, with bladder distension, and with BPH itself. Nephrolithiasis needs the pain syndrome — colicky flank pain radiating to the groin — and doesn't explain six months of hesitancy. A single nonspecific dipstick finding cannot outvote a six-month narrative.
Scenario bank
  1. 72 yo M with 6 months of hesitancy, now anuric for a day with suprapubic fullness → acute urinary retention from BPH → catheterize
  2. 72 yo M in retention; the question asks the underlying cause → benign prostatic hyperplasia
  3. 72 yo M after catheter relief; first-line medical therapy → alpha-blocker
  4. 72 yo M with a very large prostate seeking long-term volume reduction → add a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor
  5. 72 yo M with BPH started on oxybutynin for urgency, now in retention → anticholinergic-induced retention → stop the drug
  6. 72 yo M in retention with a hard nodular prostate and PSA 40 → prostate cancer → biopsy
The management sequel Acute retention → bladder catheterization first (suprapubic if the urethra is impassable) → treat the UTI → watch for post-obstructive diuresis → expect the creatinine to fall, proving the AKI was post-renal. Renal ultrasound shows hydronephrosis if confirmation is needed. Long-term: tamsulosin ± finasteride; TURP if refractory.
Transferable rule A single lab value should flip your answer only if it is incompatible with your diagnosis — not merely compatible with another one.
Treat-the-number

Diabetic Nephropathy Screening

Detection threshold, not accuracy

The decision point

"Most sensitive" asks for the lowest detection threshold. UACR detects 30–300 mg/g — the reversible window. Dipstick needs ~≥300 mg/day and is concentration-dependent. And early nephropathy causes hyperfiltration, so creatinine can be normal or low while glomeruli are being destroyed.

Defining criteria UACR window — detects 30–300 mg/g, the reversible stage · Dipstick threshold — ~≥300 mg/day, concentration-dependent · Early disease — hyperfiltration; creatinine normal or low while glomeruli are lost
Albuminuria screening schedule
PopulationStartFrequency
Type 2 diabetesAt diagnosis — silent hyperglycemia predates diagnosis by yearsAnnually
Type 1 diabetes5 years after diagnosisAnnually
Hypertension, CKD, SLE, sickle cell, HIV, nephrotoxic drugsAt diagnosisAnnually or by risk
Healthy asymptomatic adultDo not screen — USPSTF insufficient evidence—
Question verb → answer selected
Question asks…Answer
Most sensitive / screeningSpot urine albumin/creatinine ratio
Confirm an abnormal screen2 of 3 abnormal over 3–6 months — excludes transient albuminuria from exercise, fever, infection, CHF, hyperglycemia
Quantify total protein (non-albumin suspected)UPCR or 24-hour protein — dipstick and UACR miss light chains (myeloma: dipstick negative, SSA positive, UPEP shows M-spike)
Most accurate GFRMeasured clearance; cystatin C when creatinine is unreliable (amputees, cachexia, bodybuilders, cirrhosis)
Definitive / most accurate for causeRenal biopsy — but only when features are atypical
Most likely to slow progressionACE-I or ARB + SGLT2 inhibitor (never ACE-I with ARB)
Scenario bank
  1. 56 yo M with type 2 diabetes diagnosed today; when does nephropathy screening start → at diagnosis
  2. 24 yo F with type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 16; when does screening start → 5 years after diagnosis
  3. 56 yo M with type 2 diabetes; the most sensitive screening test → spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
  4. 56 yo M with a single abnormal albumin-to-creatinine ratio → repeat the albumin-to-creatinine ratio → confirmation requires 2 of 3 abnormal over 3–6 months
  5. 56 yo M with confirmed albuminuria; what slows progression most → ACE inhibitor or ARB plus an SGLT2 inhibitor
  6. 56 yo M; the most accurate measurement of GFR → inulin or iothalamate clearance
Biopsy triggers — "this isn't ordinary diabetic nephropathy" Absence of retinopathy · active sediment (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts) · rapid GFR decline · nephrotic-range proteinuria too early · diabetes duration too short.
Buzzword → Step 2 phrasing "Microalbuminuria" → "UACR 85 mg/g" · "hyperfiltration" → "creatinine 0.7" in a diabetic · "Kimmelstiel-Wilson" → "nodular glomerulosclerosis on biopsy" · "transient albuminuria" → "he ran a 10K yesterday."
Transferable rule "Most sensitive" = lowest detection threshold. "Most specific / confirmatory" = hardest to fool. Normal creatinine never excludes early diabetic kidney disease.
Test-overrides-findings

Hematuria

Glomerular vs. non-glomerular

The decision point

When the urinalysis contains dysuria + leukocyte esterase + pyuria, hematuria is a feature of cystitis, not a separate finding requiring parallel workup. Treat the infection, then repeat the UA after antibiotics. If the blood doesn't clear, that's when imaging enters.

Nitrite is only ~50% sensitive It requires a nitrate-reducing organism (Enterococcus, S. saprophyticus, and Pseudomonas don't) and adequate bladder dwell time. A negative nitrite never excludes UTI when LE, pyuria, and symptoms agree.
Glomerular vs non-glomerular hematuria
GlomerularNon-glomerular
ColorBrown / tea / colaBright red, clots
SedimentRBC casts, dysmorphic RBCsNormal RBC morphology
ProteinPresentAbsent
CausesIgA nephropathy, PSGN, Alport, thin basement membrane, lupusUTI, stones, trauma, tumor, hypercalciuria, sickle trait, exercise
Scenario bank
  1. Hematuria 1–2 days after a URI, recurrent → IgA nephropathy (synpharyngitic)
  2. Tea-colored urine + RBC casts + proteinuria + HTN, 2 weeks after sore throat → PSGN → low C3, positive ASO
  3. Painless gross hematuria in an older smoker → cystoscopy + CT urography
  4. Hematuria + sensorineural hearing loss + family history of renal failure → Alport (type IV collagen)
  5. Isolated microscopic hematuria in a well child, normal BP, no protein → urine calcium/creatinine ratio (hypercalciuria is the most common cause)
  6. Sterile pyuria with dysuria in a sexually active teen → chlamydia/gonorrhea NAAT (also: renal TB, interstitial nephritis, partially treated UTI, appendicitis)
  7. On cyclophosphamide → hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein → mesna + hydration; post-transplant → BK or adenovirus
Transferable rule When a stem gives a full lab panel, the diagnosis is in the pattern of the panel, not the most alarming single value. A discordant component is a sensitivity problem, not a veto.
Test-overrides-findings

Acute Scrotum & Scrotal Mass

Two separate trees, split by pain

The decision point

Timeline + location + infection signs. Torsion is sudden and maximal within minutes-to-hours; a 3-day escalating course with fever and dysuria and posterior tenderness is epididymitis — a clinical diagnosis. Ultrasound and urology are torsion answers transplanted onto an epididymitis stem.

The acute scrotum — the differential
ConditionOnsetThe tellCremastericNext step
Testicular torsion EmergencySudden, minutesHigh-riding transverse testis, N/V, no feverAbsentEmergent urology — salvage window ~6 h
EpididymitisGradual, daysPosterior tenderness, dysuria, fever; Prehn sign +IntactAntibiotics (clinical dx) + NAAT + UA
OrchitisDaysMumps history, unvaccinatedIntactSupportive
Torsion of appendix testisGradual, prepubertalBlue dot sign, superior poleIntactSupportive
Fournier gangrene EmergencyHoursToxic, crepitus, necrosis; diabetic—Emergent debridement
Scrotal mass (painless tree)
FindingDiagnosis
Bag of worms, ↑ standing/Valsalva, ↓ supineVaricocele — ~90% left-sided (left spermatic vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle)
Right-sided, sudden onset, or fails to decompress supineRetroperitoneal mass or RCC invading the renal vein → abdominal imaging
Transilluminates, uniform, testis palpable withinHydrocele
Enlarges with Valsalva, reducible, doesn't transilluminateInguinal hernia
Firm, fixed, painless, on the testis, no transilluminationTumor → ultrasound + AFP/β-hCG/LDH → inguinal orchiectomy, never transscrotal biopsy
Testicular mass with gynecomastia, ↓ libido, or precocious puberty in a boy; markers normalLeydig cell tumor — a sex cord–stromal tumor secreting testosterone or estrogen. Reinke crystals on histology. Mostly benign; the hormonal syndrome is the tell, and AFP/β-hCG are negative
Testicular mass, heterogeneous with calcification and cystic areas on ultrasound; AFP and/or β-hCG elevatedTeratoma (nonseminomatous). In adults, malignant regardless of maturity; in prepubertal boys, benign — the one tumor whose behavior flips with age. Chemoresistant → resect residual masses after chemotherapy
Marker logic ties the mass table together AFP elevated → never a seminoma (yolk sac or embryonal/teratoma component) · β-hCG can rise in seminoma and nonseminoma — only AFP is exclusionary · both markers normal with a solid mass → pure seminoma or a sex cord–stromal tumor (Leydig, Sertoli), and the presence of a hormonal syndrome separates them · LDH tracks tumor burden, not histology · Sertoli cell tumor is the mirror twin of Leydig — also stromal, also usually benign, but typically hormonally silent.
Pearls Epididymitis treatment splits by age: <35 / sexually active → ceftriaxone + doxycycline; >35 / low STI risk → levofloxacin or TMP-SMX · varicocele is the most common correctable cause of male infertility; testicular size discrepancy in an adolescent is the surgical indication · seminoma never makes AFP.
The two hard pairs
  • Varicocele vs. indirect inguinal hernia — both non-transilluminating, both enlarge with Valsalva. Separators: a hernia is reducible, feels like soft tissue or bowel, and you cannot palpate above it (it descends through the canal). A varicocele feels like worms, isn't reducible, and is confined to the scrotum.
  • Varicocele vs. spermatocele — both sit above and separate from the testis. Separators: the spermatocele transilluminates and does not change with position or Valsalva.
  • Femoral hernia presents below the inguinal ligament in the upper thigh, in older women, and anatomically cannot reach the scrotum — high incarceration risk.
Varicocele mechanism ~90% left-sided: the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle (± "nutcracker" compression between aorta and SMA), while the right drains obliquely into the IVC · subfertility comes from increased scrotal temperature impairing spermatogenesis; may cause ipsilateral atrophy · treatment: observation if asymptomatic → gonadal vein ligation or embolization for pain, >20% testicular volume discrepancy in adolescents, or abnormal semen analysis; scrotal support and NSAIDs for older men not seeking fertility.
Scenario bank
  1. Right-sided varicocele, sudden onset, or one that fails to decompress supine → retroperitoneal mass or RCC invading the renal vein → abdominal CT
  2. Mass transilluminates with the testis palpable within → hydrocele → observe (infantile hydroceles usually close by age 1)
  3. Reducible mass extending from the inguinal canal, can't get above it → indirect inguinal hernia → repair
  4. Firm, fixed, on the testis, no positional change → ultrasound + AFP, β-hCG, LDH → radical inguinal orchiectomy (never transscrotal — it seeds lymphatics). Cryptorchidism is the biggest risk factor, for both testes
  5. Small transilluminating cyst at the superior pole, unchanging → spermatocele → reassurance
  6. Adolescent with a varicocele and >20% testicular volume discrepancy → refer for ligation
  7. Groin bulge below the inguinal ligament in an older woman → femoral hernia → prompt repair
  8. Sudden severe pain, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex → torsion → emergent surgery
Transferable rules A 3-day timeline in a scrotal pain stem is not laziness — that number is the torsion exclusion; confirmed-enough clinical infection → treat, don't image. And read the grammatical form of the answer choices before the stem: all anatomic processes → the question wants mechanism; all tests → next step in diagnosis; all drugs → treatment. The choice format tells you what kind of thinking is being graded.

Hypercalcemia Workup

PTH first, always

The decision point

Calcium high + phosphorus low = PTH-driven until proven otherwise. The first step in any confirmed hypercalcemia is PTH, because it splits the entire differential before anything else gets ordered.

  • PTH high or inappropriately normal → primary hyperparathyroidism (most likely) or familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (separate with urine calcium)
  • PTH suppressed → then hunt: malignancy (PTHrP, bone mets), vitamin D excess or granulomatous disease, milk-alkali, thiazides, hyperthyroidism, immobilization
The Ca–Phos decoder ring Ca↑ / Phos↓ = PTH or PTHrP · Ca↑ / Phos↑ = vitamin D–mediated · Ca↓ / Phos↑ = renal failure or hypoparathyroidism · Ca↓ / Phos↓ = vitamin D deficiency. Symptoms: "stones, bones, groans, thrones, psychiatric overtones" — and polyuria with a dilute urine is hypercalcemia-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo F with calcium 11.6 and phosphorus 2.1, found incidentally → check PTH first
  2. 58 yo F with calcium 11.6 and an elevated PTH → primary hyperparathyroidism
  3. 58 yo F with calcium 13.4, suppressed PTH and weight loss → malignancy → PTHrP and imaging
  4. 24 yo M with lifelong mild hypercalcemia, normal PTH and a urine calcium-creatinine clearance ratio under 0.01 → familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia → no surgery
  5. 58 yo F with hypercalcemia, suppressed PTH, high 1,25-OH vitamin D and hilar adenopathy → granulomatous disease
  6. 58 yo F with calcium 14.5, confusion and dehydration → isotonic saline first, then calcitonin and a bisphosphonate
Normal labs that assassinate distractors A normal albumin means the calcium is truly elevated (no correction needed) · a specific gravity of 1.005 kills diabetes mellitus, because glucosuria drags SG up · low phosphorus argues against vitamin D excess, which raises both · enalapril rather than a thiazide removes the drug confounder deliberately.

Vesicoureteral Reflux

the grade decides both the treatment and the ending · board question · Did the VCUG show ureteral filling only, or dilation with blunted calices?

The decision point

The whole question is one phrase on the VCUG: dilation and blunting of the renal calices. Reflux that reaches only the ureter is mild and usually disappears on its own as the intravesical ureter lengthens with growth; reflux that has already deformed the calices is severe, and severe reflux untreated means recurrent febrile UTIs, bacteria in the parenchyma, an inflammatory response, ischemia, and focal wedges of interstitial fibrosis — renal scarring. Enough of it becomes chronic kidney disease, which in a child announces itself as secondary hypertension, proteinuria, and failure to thrive.

Defining criteria Vesicoureteral reflux — retrograde urine flow through a congenitally short intravesical ureter · Mild (grade I–II) — reflux into the ureter, with or without the kidney, and no renal damage · Severe (grade III–IV) — reflux into ureter and kidney with renal damage: dilated ureter, blunting of the calices, papillary damage · How each study contributes — ultrasound shows the hydronephrosis; the VCUG shows ureteral filling with or without a dilated collecting system, and is what assigns the grade
Pertinent positives & negatives Blunting of the renal calices — renal damage is already present; this single finding moves him from the resolving group to the scarring group · Dilation of the ureter and collecting system — grade III–IV territory, not I–II · First febrile UTI at 6 months — the presentation that earns imaging in the first place · Normal vital signs and examination — no hypertension, proteinuria or growth failure yet; the question asks about a trajectory, not today · "Mild" hydronephrosis — that adjective belongs to the ultrasound's degree of dilation, not to the reflux grade, which only the VCUG assigns
Classify first — vesicoureteral reflux
AxisThe stem sentence that settles itConsequence
Grade"dilation and blunting of the renal calices"Severe → prophylaxis ± surgery; observation alone is not an option
Primary vs. secondaryNo outlet obstruction, weak stream or neurogenic bladder describedPrimary reflux through a short intravesical ureter
Bladder and bowel functionNot yet applicable at 6 months ⚠︎In a toilet-trained child, screening and treating bladder–bowel dysfunction is part of management at every grade
