Endocrine & Bone

DEXA: When Screening Starts Early

Run the risk-factor list before applying the default

The decision point

Four screening risk factors — prior fragility fracture (wrist), family history of hip fracture, 30 pack-years, and low body weight (50 kg). Any one overrides the age-65 default → DEXA now.

This is a mirror twin, and the wrong answer is the twin's right answer. "DEXA at 65" is correct for the no-risk-factor version: 55 yo F, timely menopause, BMI 31, never smoked, no fractures.

⚠︎ Two ledgers on the early-screening trigger Exam ledger (bank, verbatim): DEXA "at age 65 years or earlier in those who have at least one risk factor — family history of hip fracture, prior fragility fracture, smoking history, low BMI, or use of corticosteroids."
Clinic ledger (USPSTF): under 65, screen when FRAX 10-year major osteoporotic risk ≥9.3%. The bank's version is the operational shorthand; the exam scores the shorthand.
Classification axes — DEXA timing
AxisThe settling sentenceConsequence
Risk-stratified?"sister… hip fracture" · "fracture of her right wrist in a fall" · "one pack daily for 30 years" · "50 kg"Age-65 default does not apply
Diagnosed?No DEXA performedAll pharmacotherapy is premature
Which bone fractured?Wrist, not hip or vertebraDoes not auto-diagnose osteoporosis → still needs DEXA
Lifestyle addressed?Physician already advised cessation, calcium, exerciseTier 1 is spent
Management ladder — osteoporosis screening & treatment
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Smoking cessation, calcium + vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, fall preventionAlways concurrent — never sufficient alone once a risk factor exists
2DEXAAge 65, or now with ≥1 risk factor
3BisphosphonateT ≤ −2.5 · or hip/vertebral fragility fracture · or T −1.0 to −2.5 with FRAX ≥20% major / ≥3% hip ⚠︎
Exit ramps Hip or vertebral fragility fracture → osteoporosis is diagnosed clinically → treat, don't just screen · chronic glucocorticoids → DEXA regardless of age · premenopausal or male <50 → Z-score and hunt secondary causes · aromatase inhibitor or ADT → screen · height loss or kyphosis → vertebral imaging.
Scenario bank
  1. 55 yo F, menopause at 50, BMI 31, never smoked, no fractures → DEXA at 65 — obesity is protective for bone
  2. 57 yo F with a vertebral compression fracture from standing height → diagnosed clinically → bisphosphonate now
  3. 48 yo F on prednisone 10 mg × 4 months → DEXA now, regardless of age
  4. 68 yo F, never screened → DEXA now
  5. 60 yo F, T-score −1.8 → run FRAX → treat if ≥20% major or ≥3% hip
  6. 32 yo F with a fragility fracture → Z-score; work up celiac, hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, eating disorder
  7. 57 yo F starting alendronate → check vitamin D and calcium first
  8. 72 yo M on androgen deprivation therapy → screen
  9. 57 yo F, smoker, requesting HRT for bone protection → avoid estrogen — smoking raises VTE risk, and HRT isn't first-line
Adversarial pass — one real hole The bank's list says "family history of hip fracture." FRAX asks specifically about a parental hip fracture, not a sibling's. It doesn't change this answer — three other factors qualify — but a stem whose only risk factor is a sibling fracture splits the ledgers. Parent counts everywhere; sibling counts on the exam.
Pairs with Part I Osteoporosis Screening. Store the discriminator as a question: "Does she have ≥1 risk factor — and did I actually count them?"
Transferable rule An age-based screening default is the answer only after the risk-factor list comes back empty. Run the list before applying the default.
Mirror twinSkipped tier

Diabetes: the Annual Care Bundle

Morbidity is not mortality

The decision point

Morbidity ≠ death. Morbidity is disease burden — complications, disability. Mortality is death. They're paired precisely because they differ. "Prevent disease-related morbidity" in a diabetic means prevent the complications of diabetes, and the annual dilated eye exam catches the most common preventable one: retinopathy is asymptomatic until advanced and the leading cause of new blindness in working-age adults.

Defining criteria A1c interval — every 3 months if not at goal or after a therapy change; every 6 months when stable at goal · Pneumococcal vaccination — diabetes is itself an ACIP indication in adults 19–64
Outcome word → intervention selected
The stem asksIt meansIt selects
"prevent morbidity"Complications, disabilityScreening for the complication
"reduce mortality"DeathInterventions with survival data (COPD → LTOT)
"reduce hospitalization"AdmissionsThe driver of decompensation (CHF → BP control)
"most beneficial"Magnitude, any outcomeUsually smoking cessation
The annual bundle Dilated eye exam annually · foot exam with monofilament annually · UACR + serum creatinine annually · blood pressure at every visit · lipids at least q5y · depression screening · weight and tobacco counseling.
⚠︎ Two problems with the vendor explanation 1. The pneumococcal rationale is wrong. It says vaccination "is recommended for patients over the age of 65 or for patients who are asplenic" — but diabetes is itself an ACIP indication in adults 19–64. She is a candidate. E loses because vaccination addresses infection risk downstream of diabetes while the eye exam targets a diabetes-specific complication — not because she doesn't qualify.
2. The attribution is off. The annual bundle and A1c intervals are ADA Standards of Care, not USPSTF.
Why monthly A1c is wrong A1c reflects glycation across the 90–120 day RBC lifespan, so consecutive monthly values measure heavily overlapping windows. Intervals: q3 months if not at goal or after a therapy change; q6 months if stable and at goal. At A1c 6.1% she's at goal → 6-month schedule, making monthly wrong by a factor of six.
Scenario bank
  1. 28 yo F, T2DM ×1 month, A1c 6.1%, asymptomatic → annual dilated eye exam (plus foot exam, UACR)
  2. 28 yo F, T2DM at goal, asks about A1c frequency → every 6 months
  3. 28 yo F, T2DM, A1c 9.4% after adding a second agent → every 3 months
  4. 32 yo F, type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 8 → eye screening begins 5 years after diagnosis; T2DM screens at diagnosis
  5. 55 yo M, T2DM, question asks what reduces mortality → smoking cessation, then BP and statin — not the eye exam
  6. 60 yo F, T2DM, UACR 85 mg/g → ACE inhibitor or ARB + SGLT2 inhibitor
  7. 45 yo M, T2DM, painless plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head → neuropathic ulcer → off-loading + glycemic control
  8. 28 yo F with T2DM, due for vaccines; in addition to influenza → pneumococcal vaccination → diabetes is itself an ACIP indication at 19–64
Pairs with Part I Diabetic Nephropathy Screening — the renal limb of the same bundle. Store the discriminator: "Which outcome word is in the stem?"
Transferable rule Read the outcome noun before the options. Morbidity, mortality, hospitalization, and benefit are four different targets, and a question can place the right intervention for the wrong target among the distractors.

Hematology 2 topics + 3 board-style

Anemia is sorted by the smear and the reticulocyte count before any name is reached; the drug, the platelet count and the direct antiglobulin test decide the rest.

Anemia with Thrombocytopenia

the smear, the Coombs and the coags name the process · board question · Are two cell lines down, is the smear sheared, and are the coagulation studies normal?

The decision point

The stem hands you two legs of a three-legged syndrome and asks for the third. Scleral icterus with fatigue is hemolytic anemia; anuria for 24 hours with pedal edema is acute kidney injury; and the missing leg of hemolytic uremic syndrome is thrombocytopenia. The mechanism supplies it: Shiga toxin damages endothelium, platelets are consumed into microthrombi, and red cells are sheared as they pass — so the platelet count falls because of the same process that produces the schistocytes and the bilirubin. The bloody diarrhea a week ago, in a cluster of people who ate together and recovered, is the exposure that starts the clock.

Defining criteria HUS triad — microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury (rising BUN and creatinine) · Microangiopathic hemolysis — red cells sheared by platelet microthrombi, giving schistocytes, increased indirect bilirubin, and decreased haptoglobin · The preceding illness — Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O157:H7 or Shigella dysenteriae; bloody diarrhea first, with HUS appearing about a week later · Coombs in HUS — negative, because the red cells are destroyed mechanically rather than coated by antibody
Pertinent positives & negatives Bloody diarrhea one week ago — Shiga toxin colitis; the one-week latency between the diarrhea and the syndrome is the concept's signature · Shared meal with relatives who recovered — a point-source exposure that confirms the organism and explains nothing about the labs; most infected people never develop HUS ⚠︎ · Anuria for 24 hours with normal intake, plus 2+ pedal edema — acute kidney injury with volume overload, the third leg · Scleral icterus — indirect hyperbilirubinemia from hemolysis, the first leg · Fatigue and refusing to get out of bed — symptomatic anemia rather than ongoing volume loss; the diarrhea has resolved · No bruising or petechiae described — consumptive thrombocytopenia in HUS is often not severe enough to bleed; its absence never argues against the diagnosis · No fever or neurologic change — argues away from the TTP end of the family and from sepsis-driven DIC ⚠︎
Anemia with thrombocytopenia — the differential
ProcessIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Hemolytic uremic syndromeChild, Shiga toxin colitis, then endothelial injury with platelet microthrombi ~1 week laterBloody diarrhea → anemia + low platelets + AKI, normal coags, negative Coombs— (the answer)
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpuraAdult; ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves ultralarge von Willebrand multimers ⚠︎Fever and neurologic changes without diarrhea; plasma exchange, not supportive care ⚠︎Age 7, preceding bloody diarrhea, no fever or neurologic findings
Disseminated intravascular coagulationA severely ill patient — sepsis, trauma, malignancy; consumption of factors as well as plateletsProlonged PT and aPTT with low fibrinogen ⚠︎ alongside the schistocytesPT is normal in HUS; no critical illness described
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemiaIgG coats red cells; lupus, lymphoproliferative disease, or a drugDirect Coombs positive; spherocytes, not schistocytes; platelets and kidneys sparedRenal failure and edema, which antibody-mediated hemolysis does not cause
Isolated thrombocytopenia (immune)Low platelets alone after a viral illness; bruising and petechiae in a well childNormal hemoglobin and a normal smear — one cytopenia, not twoAnemia, jaundice and anuria are all present
Management, in one line Management is not this question's fork, so in one sentence: HUS is treated supportively — fluid and electrolyte management, transfusion, and dialysis when needed — with antibiotics and antimotility agents withheld in suspected Shiga toxin infection ⚠︎.
Decision spine How many cell lines are down? — Anemia plus a consumed platelet count → the microangiopathy family, not a single-lineage problem · Is the hemolysis mechanical or immune? — Schistocytes with a negative Coombs → mechanical shearing · Are the coagulation studies normal? — Yes → HUS or TTP, not DIC · Which organ, and what came first? — Kidney, after bloody diarrhea in a child → HUS · Now read each marker off the mechanism — haptoglobin consumed and falling, reticulocytes rising, indirect bilirubin rising, Coombs negative
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo with bloody diarrhea a week ago, now anuric and icteric; which laboratory value is expected → A decreased platelet count → The third leg of the HUS triad
  2. 5 yo on day 3 of bloody diarrhea, stool culture pending, well hydrated and making urine → Supportive care with fluids, withholding antibiotics → Antibiotics may increase Shiga toxin release
  3. 7 yo with hemolytic uremic syndrome, hemoglobin 6.2, urine output 10 mL/h, potassium 6.8 → Hemodialysis → Supportive care includes dialysis
  4. 42 yo F with fever, confusion, schistocytes, platelets 15,000, normal PT and normal creatinine → Plasma exchange → Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
  5. 42 yo F with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, platelets 12,000, no active bleeding → Platelet transfusion → It feeds the microthrombi
  6. 60 yo M with gram-negative sepsis, schistocytes, platelets 40,000, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen → Treat the underlying sepsis → Disseminated intravascular coagulation is secondary
  7. 9 yo F with 2 weeks of jaundice and fatigue, spherocytes on smear, direct Coombs positive, normal platelets and creatinine → Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia → Antibody-coated cells rather than sheared ones
  8. Child with brisk hemolysis; why the serum haptoglobin falls rather than rises → It binds free hemoglobin and the complex is cleared → Consumed, unlike the acute-phase reactants
  9. 6 yo with bloody diarrhea 6 days ago, now pale with hemoglobin 8 and platelets 60,000; confirming the mechanism → Peripheral blood smear for schistocytes → Mechanical hemolysis
  10. 5 yo, well appearing, petechiae 2 weeks after a viral illness, platelets 20,000, hemoglobin 12.8, otherwise normal smear → Immune thrombocytopenia → One cytopenia with no hemolysis
Decoy note The cookout and the recovered relatives are epidemiology, not pathophysiology — they confirm a point-source Shiga toxin exposure and settle no laboratory value. "Significant blood in his stool, which has since resolved" is the sharpest bait: it invites an iron-deficiency answer for bleeding that stopped days ago and was never chronic. And the absence of bruising or petechiae quietly tempts you away from the platelet answer, when consumptive thrombocytopenia in HUS frequently produces no bleeding at all.
Pearls Bloody diarrhea a week ago plus anuria and jaundice is HUS: schistocytes, low platelets, rising creatinine, and a negative Coombs. · Two cytopenias with schistocytes means mechanical destruction, and mechanical destruction means the Coombs is negative by definition — nothing is antibody-coated. · Haptoglobin is consumed in hemolysis while ferritin and other acute-phase reactants rise; a marker's direction follows from whether the process uses it up or the liver makes more of it. · Reticulocytes rise in hemolysis and fall in marrow failure — a falling reticulocyte count in a known hemolytic patient is aplastic crisis until proven otherwise ⚠︎. · Normal coagulation studies separate HUS and TTP from DIC; the kidney after bloody diarrhea in a child is HUS, the brain without diarrhea in an adult is TTP ⚠︎. · The two transfusions to withhold: platelets in TTP, which feed the microthrombi ⚠︎, and antibiotics in suspected Shiga toxin colitis, which may increase toxin release ⚠︎.
Pairs with Verified: Part II NSAID Prerenal AKI in a Child owns the acute-kidney-injury compartments and carries the HUS row from the renal side, and Part II Hereditary Spherocytosis owns the Coombs-negative hemolysis fork when the platelets and kidneys are normal. This brief owns the case where both cell lines fall together. Store the discriminator as a question: is a second cell line down, and is the smear sheared or spherocytic? Part I Drug-Induced Immune Hemolysis owns the other side of the platelet count, where hemolysis arrives with a normal platelet count and an antibody rather than a clot.
Transferable rule When a question asks which laboratory abnormality is "associated," it is testing the direction each marker moves under a stated mechanism, not whether you can name the marker — so derive direction from the mechanism (consumed or produced, mechanical or immune), and when the findings assemble a named syndrome, enumerate its triad rather than re-deriving each leg.
Unchecked attributeIncreased serum haptoglobin — The direction is inverted — haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin and is consumed, so it falls in hemolysis
True-fact-wrong-slotPositive direct Coombs test — Coombs detects antibody-coated cells; HUS destroys red cells mechanically, so it is negative — and antibody hemolysis would not cause anuria and edema
Salient decoyDecreased ferritin level — The bleeding was acute and has resolved; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and rises with inflammation
Class-vs-memberIncreased PT — DIC also consumes clotting factors and needs a critically ill patient; in HUS the PT is normal
Unchecked attributeDecreased reticulocyte count — Reticulocytes rise in hemolysis; a falling count means the marrow has stopped, which is a different disease

Drug-Induced Immune Hemolysis

exposure and latency name the mechanism · board question · Which drug was given, how long ago, and are the platelets and liver enzymes normal?

The decision point

Three numbers close this, and none of them is the hemoglobin. Platelets 285,000 is normal, which kills disseminated intravascular coagulation and makes the fibrinogen pointless, because that is a consumptive process and cannot spare the platelet count. Alkaline phosphatase 66 with AST 42 and ALT 28 are all normal, which kills biliary obstruction and makes both abdominal images pointless; the bilirubin of 2.3 is therefore unconjugated, from red-cell breakdown rather than from a blocked duct. What is left is hemolysis, and the discrimination is between its two drug mechanisms — and here the stem is unusually generous, because it gives both discriminating attributes. The drug is a cephalosporin, which hemolyses by coating the erythrocyte as a hapten so IgG attaches and splenic macrophages destroy it. The latency is one hour, while oxidative hemolysis from G6PD deficiency arrives 2 to 4 days after exposure, and neither ceftriaxone nor azithromycin is a typical oxidant in the first place. Immune hemolysis is diagnosed by detecting IgG or C3 on the red cell — the direct antiglobulin test.

Defining criteria Hapten mechanism — the drug binds the erythrocyte surface, IgG attaches to the drug-cell complex, and splenic macrophages destroy the coated cell, which is extravascular hemolysis; penicillins and cephalosporins do this · Immune-complex mechanism — the drug triggers immune complexes that fix complement for intravascular destruction · Onset — within hours to a few days of exposure for drug-induced immune hemolysis, and 2 to 4 days for G6PD oxidative hemolysis · The confirmatory test — the direct antiglobulin test, which detects IgG or C3 on the erythrocyte surface · Supporting laboratory pattern — raised indirect bilirubin, LDH and reticulocytes, low haptoglobin, and spherocytes on the smear · The commonest triggers — NSAIDs such as diclofenac, penicillins such as piperacillin, and cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone
Pertinent positives & negatives Symptoms one hour after the first dose — the latency itself is diagnostic, because it is too fast for oxidative injury · Ceftriaxone — a named hapten-type trigger, and the single most important word in the stem · Platelets 285,000 — excludes disseminated intravascular coagulation and every consumptive microangiopathy, so the fibrinogen would be normal too · ALP 66, AST 42, ALT 28 — excludes biliary obstruction, and both imaging options die here rather than on clinical judgment · Total bilirubin 2.3 with normal liver enzymes — an unconjugated rise, which is a hemolysis pattern rather than a hepatobiliary one · Dark urine — hemoglobinuria or urobilinogen from hemolysis; in a child with normal liver tests this is red cells rather than bile · Mild upper abdominal tenderness — severe hemolysis causes abdominal or back pain, while biliary obstruction would hurt considerably more · Creatinine 0.9 — no renal failure, which argues against a microangiopathy and against massive intravascular hemolysis
Acute hemolysis in a hospitalized patient — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Drug-induced immune hemolytic anemiaA cephalosporin, penicillin or NSAID coats the red cell as a hapten, IgG binds, and the spleen clears itHemolysis within hours of the drug, normal platelets, positive direct antiglobulin test— (the answer)
G6PD deficiencyOxidant stress depletes glutathione; sulfonamides, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, fava beans ⚠︎Hemolysis 2 to 4 days after an oxidant, bite cells and Heinz bodies, with a negative direct antiglobulin testOne hour, and neither drug is a typical oxidant
Mycoplasma cold agglutinin hemolysisAtypical pneumonia drives IgM against the I antigen, which fixes complement ⚠︎Direct antiglobulin test positive for C3 only, cold agglutinins, following the pneumonia by 1 to 2 weeks ⚠︎Onset one hour after the drug rather than weeks into the illness
Disseminated intravascular coagulation Can't missConsumptive coagulopathy from sepsis or shockSchistocytes, severe thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen, prolonged coagulation timesPlatelets 285,000, which is normal
Biliary obstructionA stone or sludge blocks the ductSevere pain with raised alkaline phosphatase and transaminases, and conjugated hyperbilirubinemiaALP 66, AST 42 and ALT 28 all normal, with mild pain
Acute hemolytic transfusion reactionABO incompatibility drives complement-mediated intravascular lysis ⚠︎Fever, back pain and dark urine minutes into a transfusionNo transfusion was given
Management, in one line Management is two sentences, because this stem asked only for the test: discontinue the offending drug, which usually resolves the hemolysis within hours to days, and transfuse if the anemia is severe, with glucocorticoids and IVIG reserved for severe cases.
Decision spine Is this hemolysis? — Anemia, unconjugated bilirubin, dark urine, normal liver enzymes → yes · Are the platelets normal? — 285,000 → the consumptive causes are gone, and so is the fibrinogen option · Are the liver enzymes normal? — Alkaline phosphatase and transaminases normal → both abdominal images are gone · Which drug, and how long ago? — Ceftriaxone, one hour → hapten rather than oxidant · What detects a hapten-driven process? — IgG on the red cell → the direct antiglobulin test
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo girl with pneumonia who develops dark urine, abdominal pain and hemoglobin 6.3 one hour after intravenous ceftriaxone, with normal platelets and normal liver enzymes → Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test → Immune-mediated hemolysis
  2. 5 yo girl with hemolysis after ceftriaxone whose direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG → Discontinue the ceftriaxone → Withdrawal resolves the hemolysis
  3. Same child whose hemoglobin falls to 4.5 g/dL with tachycardia, lethargy and continued dark urine → Transfuse and discontinue the offending drug → Severity gates transfusion
  4. 7 yo boy on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 3 days with dark urine, bite cells and Heinz bodies on smear and a negative direct antiglobulin test → Stop the drug and measure glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase after recovery → Oxidative rather than immune hemolysis
  5. Child with known glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency who needs antibiotic coverage for pneumonia; which agent to avoid → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole → Oxidant exposure precipitates hemolysis
  6. Adolescent 10 days into an atypical pneumonia who develops anemia and jaundice, with cold agglutinins and a direct antiglobulin test positive for C3 but not IgG → Mycoplasma-associated cold agglutinin hemolysis → IgM fixes complement on the red cell
  7. Child with drug-induced immune hemolysis whose drug was stopped 2 days ago, with a stable and rising hemoglobin and residual mild jaundice → Observation without glucocorticoids → Drug withdrawal is the treatment
  8. Hospitalized septic child with hemolysis, platelets 18,000, schistocytes on smear and a low fibrinogen → Treat the underlying sepsis with coagulation support → Consumptive coagulopathy
  9. Child 15 minutes into a packed red cell transfusion who develops fever, back pain and dark urine → Stop the transfusion immediately → Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
  10. How cephalosporins and penicillins produce hemolytic anemia → The drug binds the erythrocyte surface as a hapten, IgG attaches, and splenic macrophages destroy the cell → Extravascular hemolysis
Decoy note The stem's abdominal findings do almost all of the misdirection. Upper abdominal discomfort, mild upper abdominal tenderness and a bilirubin of 2.3 assemble into a biliary picture for anyone who reads symptoms before chemistry, and two of the five options are abdominal imaging, which validates the impulse. But the actual reason for the pain is not the gallbladder: severe hemolysis causes abdominal or back pain from red-cell destruction in the vertebral bodies, liver and spleen. The other quiet detail is azithromycin, present to make you think of Mycoplasma and its cold agglutinins — a real cause of hemolysis in a child with pneumonia, and one that would give a C3-positive test rather than a negative one, so it still routes to the same answer.
Pearls Hemolysis within hours of a cephalosporin or penicillin is hapten-mediated and IgG-coated, so the direct antiglobulin test is what reveals it. · Latency is a diagnostic variable. Immune drug hemolysis arrives in hours, oxidative hemolysis in 2 to 4 days, and cold agglutinin hemolysis a week or two into the pneumonia that caused it ⚠︎. · Penicillins and cephalosporins hemolyse by hapten adsorption with IgG and splenic clearance — extravascular, spherocytes, positive direct antiglobulin test. · A normal platelet count excludes the consumptive causes. Disseminated intravascular coagulation, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and hemolytic uremic syndrome all destroy platelets, and drug-induced immune hemolysis does not touch them. · Normal alkaline phosphatase and transaminases with a raised bilirubin means hemolysis rather than obstruction — the enzymes separate the two, not the pain. · The direct antiglobulin test distinguishes what is stuck to the cell: IgG for warm and hapten-mediated disease, C3 for complement-fixing IgM such as cold agglutinins ⚠︎. · The treatment is stopping the drug; steroids and IVIG are for severe cases, and continuing the drug while treating the hemolysis is the error the bank tests.
Pairs with Verified: Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia owns the seam on the other side of the platelet count, where hemolysis arriving with thrombocytopenia means the smear and the coagulation studies name a different process. Part II Hereditary Spherocytosis owns the Coombs-negative spherocytic anemia that mirrors this brief's Coombs-positive one, and Part I Pediatric Community-Acquired Pneumonia carries the Mycoplasma cold-agglutinin association. Store the discriminator as a question: which drug, how many hours, and is the platelet count normal?
Transferable rule When two options are two mechanisms of the same syndrome, the stem has almost always supplied the attribute that separates them, usually an exposure and an interval, and the test you choose is downstream of the mechanism rather than of the syndrome. Spherocytes with a normal platelet count means an antibody; schistocytes with a low platelet count means a clot. --- Batch 5, brief 05 · 2026-09-10.
Unchecked attributeGlucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level — Neither ceftriaxone nor azithromycin is a typical oxidant, and that hemolysis arrives 2 to 4 days after exposure rather than in one hour
True-fact-wrong-slotCT scan of the abdomen — Obstruction produces severe pain with raised alkaline phosphatase and transaminases, and all three are normal here
Sequencing trapLiver ultrasonography — The same failure as the CT, and it cannot explain a hemoglobin of 6.3
Unchecked attributeSerum fibrinogen level — That disease is consumptive and requires severe thrombocytopenia with prolonged coagulation times; platelets are 285,000
3 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Hematology

Pediatric Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia

Pancytopenia with bone pain · UWorld and Aquifer · screen versus confirm

The decision point

Three findings together permit one disease: tri-lineage cytopenia, diaphyseal bone pain and diffuse nontender adenopathy with splenomegaly. That is marrow replacement, and marrow replacement is confirmed in the marrow.

But read the verb, because the same disease has two right answers. Most useful in making the diagnosis, or initial selects the complete blood count — cheap, fast, and enough to convert a vague illness into an oncologic emergency. Confirms, or diagnostic selects the bone marrow aspirate. The CBC makes you suspect leukemia; the marrow proves it.

Defining criteria Pancytopenia — reduction in all three lineages, the word that eliminates every single-lineage disease · ALL diagnostic gate — at least 20% lymphoblasts of marrow nucleated cells · M1, M2, M3 marrow — under 5%, 5 to 25%, over 25% blasts, a burden and response category rather than the diagnostic gate · Leukemic bone pain — diaphyseal or metaphyseal tenderness from marrow expansion, distinct from joint-line pain · Petechiae — a platelet problem, so PT and PTT are normal
The pale child with bone pain — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Acute lymphoblastic leukemiaPeak 2 to 5 yr; marrow replaced by lymphoblastsPancytopenia with diaphyseal pain and nontender adenopathy; counts go down
Sickle cell aplastic crisisParvovirus B19 arrests erythropoiesisIsolated anemia with reticulocytopenia; platelets and WBC normal
Infectious mononucleosisAdolescent, prolonged fever and fatigueTender posterior cervical nodes, atypical lymphocytosis, transaminitis
Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritisQuotidian fever, evanescent rashCounts go up — leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, ferritin high
Aplastic anemiaMarrow failure without infiltrationPancytopenia with an empty exam: no adenopathy, no organomegaly, no bone pain
Neuroblastoma Can't missUnder 5 yr; marrow metastases give identical cytopenia and bone painPeriorbital ecchymoses, proptosis, midline-crossing abdominal mass
Immune thrombocytopeniaPost-viral, well-appearing childIsolated thrombocytopenia with normal PT and PTT
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M with 2 wk of fatigue, 1 wk of leg pain and 1 day of fever with petechiae, pale, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, cervical and axillary adenopathy, most useful test → complete blood count with differential and peripheral smear → bone marrow confirms afterwards
  2. 5 yo M whose complete blood count shows hemoglobin 7, platelets 22,000 and WBC 3,100, confirmatory test → bone marrow aspirate and biopsy → greater than 20% lymphoblasts
  3. 4 yo M, 3 wk fever, pallor, petechiae, nontender diffuse adenopathy, splenomegaly, midshaft femoral tenderness, WBC 2,800 and platelets 18,000 → acute lymphoblastic leukemia → bone marrow aspirate and biopsy
  4. 4 yo M with fever, limp and pancytopenia in whom a colleague proposes empiric prednisone for presumed systemic JIA → obtain bone marrow before any corticosteroid → steroids partially treat ALL and destroy the specimen
  5. 5 yo M with 4 wk of fatigue and pallor, pancytopenia, no adenopathy, no organomegaly and no bone pain → aplastic anemia → bone marrow biopsy showing a hypocellular marrow
  6. 6 yo F, 5 wk of daily spiking fever, evanescent salmon rash, WBC 24,000 and platelets 700,000 → systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
  7. 4 yo M with petechiae and bruising 2 wk after a viral illness, well-appearing and afebrile, platelets 12,000 with normal hemoglobin and WBC → immune thrombocytopenia → observation
  8. 8 yo M with sickle cell disease, hemoglobin 4.2, reticulocytes 0.2%, normal platelets and WBC → parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis → transfuse and supportive care
  9. 3 yo M with fever, refusal to walk, pancytopenia, periorbital ecchymoses and proptosis, and an abdominal mass crossing the midline → neuroblastoma → urine HVA and VMA
  10. 16 yo M, 3 wk fever, sore throat, tender posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes → infectious mononucleosis → avoid contact sports for 3 to 4 weeks
  11. 6 yo F with petechiae and gum bleeding, platelets 9,000, PT and PTT normal, otherwise well → no further coagulation testing is needed → petechiae are a platelet problem
  12. 5 yo M with pancytopenia and adenopathy in whom a normal white count on an earlier CBC is offered as reassurance → accepting a normal white count as excluding leukemia → some ALL presents with under 1% circulating blasts
  13. 7 yo M, day 3 of ALL induction, potassium 6.8, phosphate 8.1, uric acid 14, calcium 6.8 and creatinine 2.1 → tumor lysis syndrome → intravenous hydration and urate-lowering therapy
Never steroids before the marrow Corticosteroids partially treat ALL, transiently improving the child while destroying the diagnostic specimen and degrading risk stratification. Systemic JIA and ALL must be separated before treatment, not after. And a normal white count does not exclude ALL — the cytopenias carry the signal, not the blasts.
Pearls Leukemia lowers counts, systemic JIA raises them — ferritin, platelets and WBC all rise in sJIA · Neuroblastoma and ALL are confirmed by the same test; periorbital ecchymoses and a midline-crossing mass separate them · A mediastinal mass points to T-cell ALL, and a normal chest film does not exclude B-cell ALL · Inflammatory markers monitor disease, they do not select between diagnoses that all raise them · Tumor lysis — potassium up, phosphate up, uric acid up, calcium down, with acute kidney injury
Pairs with Part I Systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis is the mirror twin, and Part I The Limping Child shares the presenting complaint. Store the discriminator as a question: are the counts up or down?
Transferable rule Sort laboratory options by what a result could change rather than by sophistication, because a test abnormal in every diagnosis on the differential discriminates nothing and a test measuring an uninvolved compartment answers a question nobody asked.
Salient decoyEthnicity and travel are epidemiologic priors, not findings, and cannot outrank the blood count.
True-fact-wrong-slotSplenomegaly and generalised adenopathy are not features of Kawasaki or of leukemia's mimics in the way offered.
Class-vs-memberPTT is the right class of haematologic test on the wrong compartment.

Hereditary Spherocytosis

Spherocytes with a negative Coombs · handoff · map the disease to its assay

The decision point

The word doing the work is spherocytes: on a board smear they have exactly two owners, hereditary spherocytosis and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The negative Coombs settles that fork — antibody-coated cells are excluded, so the spherocytes are a membrane defect. MCHC 38% and the affected father corroborate; neither is the decider.

The last move is a mapping rather than a diagnosis. The options are tests, so name the disease and then name its assay: eosin-5-maleimide binding, with osmotic fragility as the older equivalent. Choosing CD55/CD59 is a stored-outcome error — Coombs-negative hemolysis retrieved as a conclusion rather than as a question, so the three findings that fail PNH here (normal white cells and platelets, spherocytes, an affected father) were never asked.

Defining criteria MCHC in HS — above 36%, because membrane loss dehydrates the cell and concentrates hemoglobin; the one common anemia in which MCHC is high · Confirmatory test — eosin-5-maleimide binding by flow cytometry showing reduced fluorescence, or increased osmotic fragility · The HS triad — Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with jaundice and splenomegaly
Coombs-negative hemolysis in a child - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Hereditary spherocytosisAutosomal dominant ankyrin, spectrin or band 3 defect; extravascular splenic hemolysis, pigment stonesSpherocytes with a negative Coombs and MCHC above 36%
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemiaIgG against red cells; lupus, CLL, methyldopa or penicillins; subacuteDirect Coombs positive — the only line separating it from HS
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuriaAcquired PIGA clone, complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis, adultsHemolysis with cytopenias and thrombosis at odd sites, bland smear
G6PD deficiencyX-linked, episodic 2 to 3 days after an oxidantBite cells and Heinz bodies after a named trigger, MCHC normal
HemoglobinopathySickle or thalassemia, chronic inherited hemolysis with splenomegalyTarget cells or sickled forms with a low MCV
Production failureIron, B12 or folate deficiency, or marrow disease; pallor without jaundiceLow reticulocytes, with the MCV pointing the way
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo M, months of jaundice, splenomegaly, spherocytes, MCHC 38%, Coombs negative, father affected → eosin-5-maleimide binding test → hereditary spherocytosis
  2. 24 yo F with lupus, 2 wk of fatigue and jaundice, spherocytes, direct Coombs positive → prednisone → warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia
  3. 5 yo M with dark urine 3 days after TMP-SMX, bite cells and Heinz bodies, still actively hemolysing → measuring G6PD activity during the acute episode → young surviving cells read falsely normal
  4. 30 yo M, dark morning urine, pancytopenia, new hepatic vein thrombosis, Coombs negative, bland smear → flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 → paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
  5. 10 yo F with known hereditary spherocytosis, hemoglobin 12 falling to 5 over a week, reticulocytes 0.1%, slapped-cheek rash at school → transfusion → parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis
  6. 14 yo M with hereditary spherocytosis and colicky right upper quadrant pain after meals → right upper quadrant ultrasound → pigment gallstones
  7. 8 yo M, splenectomy a year ago for hereditary spherocytosis, temperature 39.5 C, ill-appearing → blood cultures and intravenous ceftriaxone now → overwhelming post-splenectomy infection
  8. 18-hour-old newborn with jaundice, mother blood group O positive, infant A positive, spherocytes on smear, direct antiglobulin weakly positive → phototherapy → ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn
  9. 7 yo M with jaundice, splenomegaly, spherocytes, Coombs negative and MCHC 37%, with no family history → hereditary spherocytosis → a meaningful fraction are de novo or recessive
  10. 16 yo F with hereditary spherocytosis, hemoglobin 8, fatigue limiting sport, gallstones on ultrasound, planned for splenectomy → pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination before surgery → moderate disease, splenectomy deferred to age 6 or older
Management, and what splenectomy does not fix Folic acid for chronic reticulocytosis, transfusion for aplastic or hemolytic crisis, and splenectomy for moderate to severe disease deferred until age 6 or older ⚠ and preceded by pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination, with cholecystectomy if pigment stones are present. Splenectomy stops the hemolysis but not the defect — spherocytes persist and Howell-Jolly bodies appear, and every post-splenectomy fever is treated as sepsis until proven otherwise.
Pearls Spherocytes have two owners, hereditary spherocytosis and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and the Coombs test is the entire discrimination; in a newborn add ABO incompatibility as a third · MCHC is the only red-cell index that rises in a common anemia, and RDW rises with it · HS is extravascular with indirect bilirubin, splenomegaly and pigment stones; PNH and severe G6PD hemolysis are intravascular with hemoglobinuria, low haptoglobin and high LDH · A falling hemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count in any chronic hemolytic patient is parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis until proven otherwise · Do not assay G6PD during acute hemolysis, because the surviving young cells carry near-normal enzyme and read falsely normal; repeat weeks later · A normal MCV does not exclude hemolysis, because a 10% reticulocytosis inflates it
Pairs with Candidate twin — confirm: warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, sharing jaundice, anemia and spherocytes, with the discriminator stored as a question: is the direct Coombs positive? Second candidate: paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria — are the white cells and platelets normal? Neither partner brief exists yet, so no reverse links are owed. Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia is the seam: an isolated hemolytic anemia is one process, and a hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia is another. Part I Drug-Induced Immune Hemolysis is the Coombs-positive mirror of this brief's Coombs-negative spherocytic anemia.
Transferable rule When the options are tests the question is still which disease, so name it from the smear plus one separating test and then map disease to assay, because when two diagnoses share a morphologic finding the answer is the test that separates them rather than the finding they share.
True-fact-wrong-slotPNH is the other famous Coombs-negative hemolysis, but it means cytopenias, a bland smear and acquired disease.
Salient decoyBoy with jaundice and hemolysis sells G6PD, which needs an oxidant trigger and is not passed father to son.
Class-vs-memberHemoglobinopathy is the right class of inherited red-cell disorder but gives targets or sickles, never spherocytes.

Sickle Cell Trait versus Disease

HbA exceeds HbS · UWorld · read the electrophoresis before the options

The decision point

HbA 60% with HbS 40% and a stone-normal CBC is trait, not disease. Every wrong option — acute chest, dactylitis, stroke, osteomyelitis — is a genuine complication of sickle cell anemia, and none belongs to a carrier. Five of seven options die to one line of the lab panel.

Then a second layer catches those who did read it: the stem asks for the most common complication, not one that can occur. Splenic infarction is real in trait, at altitude, uncommonly. Painless hematuria is the common one, because the renal medulla is hypoxic, acidic and hypertonic — the one microenvironment that polymerises HbS at the 40% a carrier has.

Defining criteria Trait — HbA about 60% exceeding HbS about 40%, with a completely normal CBC · Disease — HbA absent; any HbA at all excludes HbSS · Sickle-beta-plus thalassemia — HbA present but S exceeds A, with a low MCV · Newborn screen — FAS is trait, FS is disease; F leads because fetal hemoglobin predominates at birth
Hemoglobin electrophoresis — reading the pattern
ConditionElectrophoresis and CBCThe NBME tell
NormalHbA about 97%, A2 about 2.5%, F under 1%; normal CBC—
Sickle cell traitHbA about 60% over HbS about 40%; completely normal CBCA exceeds S, and there is no anemia
Sickle cell anemiaHbA 0%, HbS about 90%; anemia with reticulocytes 10 to 20%Absence of HbA is the finding
Hemoglobin SCHbA 0%, HbS about equal to HbC; milder anemiaRetinopathy and avascular necrosis out of proportion to the anemia
Sickle-beta-zero thalassemiaHbA 0%, HbS high, A2 elevated; low MCVLooks like SS but microcytic
Sickle-beta-plus thalassemiaHbA present but low, S exceeds A; low MCVHbA present yet S exceeds A, the sharpest mimic of trait
Scenario bank
  1. 1 yo F, HbA 60% and HbS 40%, normal CBC → sickle cell trait → most common complication is painless hematuria
  2. 1 yo F with HbA 0% and HbS 90%, hemoglobin 7.5, reticulocytes 14% → sickle cell anemia → penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal vaccination
  3. 20 yo M with sickle cell trait, nocturia and polyuria → hyposthenuria → impaired urinary concentrating ability
  4. 22 yo M with sickle cell trait who collapses during military basic training → exertional rhabdomyolysis
  5. 28 yo M with sickle cell trait and a renal mass → renal medullary carcinoma
  6. 19 yo F with sickle cell trait and left upper quadrant pain after a high-altitude flight → splenic infarction
  7. 26 yo F with sickle cell trait, pregnant, with dysuria → urinary tract infection
  8. 9 mo M with painful swelling of the hands and feet and hemoglobin 7 → dactylitis → often the first presentation of sickle cell disease
  9. 14 yo M with sickle cell disease, chest pain, hypoxia and a new infiltrate → acute chest syndrome → transfusion and antibiotics
  10. 7 yo M with sickle cell disease and sudden hemiparesis → ischemic stroke → exchange transfusion
  11. 6 yo M with sickle cell disease, sudden pallor and a reticulocyte count of 0.2% → parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis
  12. 2 yo M with HbA 15%, HbS 70% and an MCV of 68 → sickle-beta-plus thalassemia → HbA is present but S exceeds A
  13. Newborn screen reported as FAS → sickle cell trait → counsel the parents, no treatment
  14. 26 yo F with trait whose partner also carries trait, asking about future children → 25% disease, 50% trait, 25% unaffected
Why the kidney is the one organ trait touches The renal medulla is hypoxic, acidic and hypertonic — exactly the conditions that polymerise HbS at the 40% concentration a carrier has. Nowhere else in the body reproduces that microenvironment, which is why a carrier's spleen, lungs and bones are spared and the vasa recta are not.
Pearls In trait HbA always exceeds HbS, because alpha chains bind normal beta with higher affinity — memorise the inequality, not the numbers · HbF is 0% by 12 months, so a raised HbF later means hydroxyurea or a thalassemia · Renal medullary carcinoma is rare but nearly pathognomonic for trait · Trait carries a real risk of exertional rhabdomyolysis and sudden death under extreme exertion, which is why it matters in athletes and recruits
Pairs with Part I Hematuria in Renal and GU should gain a sickle trait row; painless hematuria in a carrier is the commonest trait complication. Part I Chronic Dyspnea in Sickle Cell Disease owns the chronic pulmonary sequelae that follow the acute chest syndrome named here.
Transferable rule When a stem supplies a diagnostic lab panel that panel is the assassin, usually eliminating most options in one line, and family history is placed to make you skip it.
True-fact-wrong-slotSplenic infarction is real in trait but uncommon, and the stem asks for the most common.
Mirror twinDactylitis is the disease version of the carrier stem.
Salient decoyThe affected sister sells the whole disease-complication list at once.

Infectious Disease 6 topics + 3 board-style

Screening thresholds, drug toxicities, and sequencing. Isolation precedes medication; aspiration precedes antibiotics.

Tuberculosis

Screen → sort → treat

The decision point

A positive test plus a normal CXR and no symptoms = latent TB → monotherapy. Positive test plus symptoms or an abnormal CXR = active TB → isolate first, then four drugs. No test distinguishes latent from active — the CXR and symptoms do.

PPD positivity thresholds by risk group
PPD is positive at…Group
≥5 mmHIV+ · recent TB contact · fibrotic changes on CXR · transplant, TNF-α inhibitor, prednisone ≥15 mg/day
≥10 mmHealthcare workers · immigrants <5 yrs from endemic areas · prisoners · homeless · IVDU · diabetes · CKD · children <4
≥15 mmNo risk factors
Test mechanics BCG-vaccinated → IGRA (unaffected by BCG) · anergy = false-negative PPD in HIV, steroids, sarcoid · PPD is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction.
RIPE drug toxicities
RIPE drugToxicity
RifampinOrange secretions (benign — counsel, don't stop) · potent CYP inducer → OCP failure, warfarin; use rifabutin with HIV protease inhibitors
IsoniazidPeripheral neuropathy → give B6 · hepatitis · drug-induced lupus · sideroblastic anemia
PyrazinamideHyperuricemia / gout · hepatitis
EthambutolOptic neuritis — red-green vision lost first. "Eye-thambutol"
The costumes — how the same question keeps showing up
  1. Booster / two-step: HCW with a negative first PPD, positive on repeat 1–3 weeks later = old memory, not conversion → treat as latent
  2. Window period: contact of an active case → PPD now and at 8–10 weeks — the only time "repeat later" is correct
  3. Before biologics: starting a TNF-α inhibitor (RA or IBD stem) → screen for latent TB first
  4. HIV co-infection: PPD ≥5 mm = treat · TB drugs first, ART at 2–8 weeks (immediate risks IRIS) · rifabutin with protease inhibitors
  5. Extrapulmonary: Pott (spine) · scrofula (cervical node) · meningitis (↑protein, ↓glucose, basilar) · sterile pyuria · miliary CXR · adrenal insufficiency
  6. Location logic: primary = lower/mid lobe (Ghon complex); reactivation = apices (highest pO₂)
  7. Sequencing trap: coughing + cavitary CXR → the answer is airborne isolation, not medication
Treatment Latent: rifampin ×4 mo (preferred) · INH ×9 mo + B6 · INH + rifapentine weekly ×3 mo. Active: RIPE ×2 mo → INH + rifampin ×4 mo; reportable; DOT if nonadherent.
Sequencing trap

Bacterial Meningitis

The CSF 2×2

The decision point

The whole CSF grid collapses to a 2×2: cell type on one axis, glucose on the other.

CSF interpretation — the 2×2
Glucose LOWGlucose NORMAL
NeutrophilsBacterialEarly viral · parameningeal focus
LymphocytesTB · fungal (± partially treated bacterial)Viral
Organism by host
  • Neonate: GBS · E. coli (K1 capsule) · Listeria  |  Unvaccinated toddler: Hib
  • Teen / dorm / military: N. meningitidis  |  Adult (most common): S. pneumoniae
  • >50, pregnant, immunosuppressed: + Listeria → add ampicillin
  • VP shunt: S. epidermidis  |  Basilar skull fracture / CSF rhinorrhea: S. pneumoniae  |  HIV CD4 <100: Cryptococcus
Mechanism pearls Encapsulated organisms need opsonization — hit hardest in asplenia/sickle cell (lost filter), complement deficiency (lost MAC → recurrent Neisseria; screen with CH50), and cirrhosis (lost complement synthesis) · lipid A of LOS → TNF/IL-1 → shock, DIC, Waterhouse-Friderichsen · Listeria escapes the phagosome with listeriolysin O and spreads via ActA-driven host actin polymerization; intrinsic cephalosporin resistance · conjugate vaccines convert T-independent polysaccharide into a T-dependent response, which is why they work under age 2.
Scenario bank
  1. 22 yo M with fever and neck stiffness; CSF 3,000 neutrophils, glucose 25, protein 180 → bacterial meningitis → dexamethasone with ceftriaxone and vancomycin
  2. 22 yo M with CSF 200 lymphocytes, normal glucose and mildly raised protein → viral meningitis
  3. 35 yo M with HIV; CSF lymphocytes, very low glucose, high protein, basilar involvement → tuberculous meningitis
  4. 22 yo M with suspected meningitis and papilledema on fundoscopy → CT head before lumbar puncture
  5. 22 yo M with suspected bacterial meningitis and a delayed CT scanner → blood cultures and antibiotics before imaging
  6. 68 yo M with bacterial meningitis; what coverage must be added → ampicillin for Listeria
Sequencing CT before LP only if: papilledema, focal deficit, seizure, immunocompromise, depressed consciousness, age >60 — an open fontanelle in an infant generally removes the requirement, since it acts as a pop-off valve. Never delay antibiotics — draw cultures and treat. Empiric: vancomycin + ceftriaxone (+ ampicillin for Listeria); neonates get cefotaxime, not ceftriaxone (biliary sludging, bilirubin displacement). Dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose — it blunts the cytokine burst from bacterial lysis.
Follow-up facts Classic triad present in only 44% (van de Beek, NEJM 2004; n=696) · most common sequela is sensorineural hearing loss — check hearing in every survivor · prophylaxis: meningococcus → rifampin, cipro, or ceftriaxone; Hib → rifampin · eculizumab blocks C5 → mandatory meningococcal vaccination first.
Pairs with Part I Seizure with Fever in a Child owns the decision to obtain the fluid that this brief interprets.

Vaccines in HIV

Live vaccines are CD4-gated, not banned

The decision point

The stored rule should be "HIV → check the CD4 count," not "HIV → no live vaccines." CD4 ≥200 permits varicella, MMR, and yellow fever (with caution). CD4 <200 contraindicates them. Never at any CD4: LAIV (use inactivated influenza), BCG, oral polio.

Defining criteria CD4 ≥200 — varicella, MMR, and yellow fever permitted (with caution) · CD4 <200 — live vaccines contraindicated · Never at any CD4 — LAIV, BCG, oral polio
Hepatitis B serology interpretation
HBsAganti-HBcanti-HBsInterpretation
−−−Susceptible → vaccinate
−−+Immune from vaccination
−++Immune from natural infection
++ (IgM)−Acute infection
++ (IgG)−Chronic infection
Scenario bank
  1. 30 yo M with HIV, CD4 320, not immune to varicella → varicella vaccine is permitted
  2. 30 yo M with HIV, CD4 120, not immune to measles → MMR is contraindicated until CD4 is 200 or above
  3. 30 yo M with HIV at any CD4 count, in influenza season → inactivated influenza vaccine
  4. 30 yo M with HIV, CD4 400, travelling to a yellow fever zone → yellow fever may be given with caution
  5. 30 yo M with HIV asking about pneumococcal vaccination → indicated regardless of CD4 count
  6. 30 yo M with HIV, CD4 90, asking about shingles vaccination → recombinant zoster vaccine — non-live and permitted
HIV-specific additions to the adult schedule Meningococcal ACWY with boosters every 5 years (unique to HIV, asplenia, and complement deficiency — the opsonization club) · pneumococcal regardless of age · hepatitis A and B unless immune · HPV through 26 (consider to 45) · recombinant zoster from age 19 rather than waiting until 50 · influenza annually, inactivated.
Transferable rule Before rejecting a uniform option ("yes to all four"), you need a specific disqualifying criterion you can name — not a general sense that it's too easy.
Uniform-answer doubtMirror twin

DTaP: Contraindication vs. Precaution

Three false contraindications in one stem

The decision point

Separate contraindication (never give) from precaution (weigh risk vs. benefit) from neither. A brief self-limited seizure hours after a prior dose is technically a precaution — and precautions are overcome when benefit is high, as in an outbreak. Family history of epilepsy is in the "neither" bucket entirely.

DTaP — contraindications vs precautions
CategoryItems
Contraindication
(all pertussis-containing)		Anaphylaxis to the vaccine or a component · Encephalopathy (coma, decreased consciousness, prolonged seizures) within 7 days of a prior dose → give DT instead
Precaution
(defer or weigh)		Progressive/unstable neurologic disorder — infantile spasms, uncontrolled epilepsy · seizure ≤3 days after a prior dose · temp ≥40.5 °C within 48 h · hypotonic-hyporesponsive episode within 48 h · inconsolable crying ≥3 h · Guillain-Barré within 6 weeks of prior tetanus toxoid · Arthus reaction · moderate-severe acute illness
Not a contraindicationFamily history of seizures or epilepsy · personal febrile seizure · mild illness · recent exposure
Scenario bank
  1. 2 mo M whose sibling had encephalopathy within 7 days of a pertussis dose; the patient himself had it → contraindication — use DT
  2. 2 mo M with a brief self-limited seizure hours after a previous dose → precaution — weigh risk against benefit
  3. 2 mo M with a family history of seizures → not a contraindication
  4. 2 mo M with a mild febrile upper respiratory infection on the day of the visit → not a contraindication — vaccinate
  5. 2 mo M with anaphylaxis after a previous dose → contraindication
  6. 2 mo M with a temperature of 41 °C within 48 hours of a previous dose → precaution
Standard pediatric immunizations by classwhich ones are live is the load-bearing fact
ClassVaccines

The universal false-contraindication list Mild illness or low-grade fever · current antibiotic therapy · prematurity (vaccinate by chronologic age, full dose) · breastfeeding · family history of anything · recent exposure to an infectious disease · egg allergy (no longer a barrier to influenza vaccine) · penicillin allergy · pregnancy or immunosuppression in a household contact (exception: smallpox; avoid LAIV if a severely immunocompromised contact) · mild local reaction to a prior dose.
Schedule & timing DTaP at 2, 4, 6 months; 15–18 months; 4–6 years · Tdap at 11–12 and every pregnancy at 27–36 weeks · pertussis post-exposure prophylaxis only useful within 21 days · live vaccines same day or ≥28 days apart · after IVIG or blood products, defer MMR/varicella 3–11 months.
Transferable rule Vaccine questions are eligibility questions, and the stem's job is to make an ineligible-sounding history feel disqualifying. If you can't name the criterion, the answer is vaccinate.

Acute Cervicitis

Chlamydia & gonorrhea · treat before the test returns

The decision point

Mucopurulent cervical discharge + a friable cervix that bleeds on contact is a clinical diagnosis of cervicitis, most prevalent in women under 25. NAAT for both organisms is sent — and empiric ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is given before results return, to interrupt transmission and prevent PID, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility. The absence of cervical motion tenderness does not reassure: CMT marks ascent, and early or low-burden infection lacks it.

Defining criteria Clinical diagnosis — mucopurulent cervical discharge + friable cervix · Empiric regimen — ceftriaxone (covers N gonorrhoeae) + doxycycline (covers C trachomatis); azithromycin replaces doxycycline in pregnancy · Testing — NAAT for both organisms; treatment does not wait for it
Chlamydia & gonorrhea in women
AxisFindings
Risk factorsAge <25, high-risk sexual behavior
ManifestationsAsymptomatic most commonly; cervicitis, urethritis, perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh–Curtis)
DiagnosisNucleic acid amplification testing
TreatmentEmpiric ceftriaxone + doxycycline; confirmed chlamydia alone → doxycycline (azithromycin in pregnancy)
ComplicationsPID, ectopic pregnancy, infertility
Scenario bank
  1. 22 yo F, mucopurulent discharge, cervix bleeds on swab contact → ceftriaxone + doxycycline now → empiric dual therapy precedes the NAAT result
  2. 24 yo G1 at 12 weeks with NAAT-confirmed chlamydia → azithromycin → doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy
  3. 23 yo F with mucopurulent discharge, now uterine and adnexal tenderness with cervical motion tenderness → pelvic inflammatory disease → the infection has ascended
  4. 25 yo F, fever and uterine tenderness 3 days after vaginal delivery → clindamycin plus gentamicin → polymicrobial ascent of vaginal flora, not an STI regimen
  5. 21 yo F, dysuria, leukocyte esterase positive but nitrite negative, mucopurulent cervical discharge on exam → chlamydial urethritis with cervicitis → NAAT; the pelvic exam reframes the "UTI"
Pearls Azithromycin + doxycycline doubles atypical coverage and leaves N gonorrhoeae untreated — the classic wrong pairing · gonococcus is multidrug-resistant, including to sulfonamides — TMP-SMX never treats an STI syndrome · sterile pyuria in a sexually active woman (LE-positive, nitrite-negative) is chlamydia until the pelvic exam says otherwise · treat partners.
Transferable rule When a clinical diagnosis is sufficient and the sequelae are irreversible, the exam rewards treating at the visit — testing runs in parallel, never as a gate.
Class-vs-memberAzithromycin + doxycycline looks like dual therapy but both cover the same organism.
Test-overrides-findingsA negative nitrite cannot rule out infection that nitrite was never sensitive for — atypicals don't reduce nitrate.

The Immunoglobulin Panel

which antibody defect, and what it predicts · board question · Are B cells present, and which isotype is preserved or elevated?

The decision point

The infection history only establishes that this is a primary immunodeficiency rather than ordinary toddler illness — ICU-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic perforation with otorrhea, and weight below the 3rd percentile clear that bar. The actual fork is decided by one line of the panel: IgM 450 against IgG 250 and IgA 24. Every other option on the list requires IgM to be low (XLA, CVID), normal (selective IgA deficiency, Job), or accompanied by a non-immunologic finding this child does not have (Wiskott-Aldrich's microthrombocytopenia, HIV's inverted CD4/CD8). An isolated elevation of IgM with everything downstream absent is class-switch failure — CD40 ligand on the T cell cannot engage CD40 on the B cell, so the B cell stays locked on its native isotype. The neutropenia (15% of 9,000) is the free confirmatory detail: it accompanies CD40L deficiency and does not belong to XLA or CVID.

Defining criteria Class switching (isotype switch recombination) — the CD40L(T cell)–CD40(B cell) interaction that lets an IgM-committed B cell rearrange to IgG, IgA, or IgE; when it fails, IgM is preserved or elevated and every other isotype falls · The CD40L signature — B cells normal · IgM ↑ · IgG ↓ · IgA ↓ · IgE ↓. B and T cell counts are normal; they are dysfunctional, not absent · The B-cell count is the first gate — low or absent CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia; normal B cells → the block is downstream of B-cell development, and the isotype pattern names it
Pertinent positives & negatives IgM 450 with IgG 250 and IgA 24 — class-switch failure; simultaneously excludes XLA and CVID (both require all isotypes low) and selective IgA deficiency (requires normal IgG and IgM) · Neutropenia (ANC ≈1,350) — common in CD40L deficiency; not a feature of XLA or CVID · Lymphocytes 75%, CD4/CD8 2.2 — normal lymphocyte compartment; excludes HIV, where leukopenia and an inverted ratio are expected · Platelets 260,000 — excludes Wiskott-Aldrich, which requires small, low platelets · Age 14 months with disease since early infancy — argues against CVID, which surfaces in adolescents and young adults · Vaccinations up to date, yet invasive pneumococcal disease — vaccine failure from absent opsonizing IgG, not from missed doses; it also makes live vaccines a live safety question ⚠︎
Antibody deficiencies — reading the isotype panel
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficiency)X-linked recessive boy, infancy; recurrent AOM/sinusitis/pneumonia from encapsulated bacteria, plus opportunistic infection (Pneumocystis) because the T-cell–APC limb is also brokenIgM high, IgG/IgA/IgE low, B cells normal — plus neutropenia— (the answer)
X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemiaBoy, infections begin ~6 months as maternal IgG wanes ⚠︎; recurrent sinopulmonary and enteroviral diseaseB cells absent/low with ALL isotypes low; scant tonsils and lymph nodes ⚠︎IgM 450 (high) with a normal lymphocyte compartment
Common variable immunodeficiencyAdolescent/young adult; sinopulmonary infections → bronchiectasis, plus autoimmunity, granulomas, and lymphoma risk ⚠︎All isotypes low with a NORMAL B-cell count; late onsetIgM 450 (high); age 14 months
Selective IgA deficiencyOften asymptomatic; otherwise recurrent respiratory/GI (giardiasis) or urogenital infection; anaphylaxis to IgA-containing blood products ⚠︎IgA alone low; IgG and IgM normalIgG 250 — the deficiency is not isolated
Syndromic defects with an Ig signature (Wiskott-Aldrich · Job/hyper-IgE)WAS: eczema + microthrombocytopenia + infection, X-linked. Job: cold staphylococcal abscesses, retained primary teeth, pneumatoceles ⚠︎The non-immunologic finding makes the diagnosis, not the panel — small platelets; IgE markedly highPlatelets 260,000 and normal-sized; no eczema or abscess history
Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia (HIV; protein-losing states ⚠︎)Opportunistic infection, diarrhea, failure to thriveInverted CD4/CD8 with leukopenia; IgG/IgA may be elevated from chronic stimulation while IgM is lowCD4/CD8 2.2, WBC 9,000
Management, in one line Management is not the fork this question tests, so in one sentence: replace what is missing and cover what the defect exposes — immunoglobulin replacement for any low-IgG defect plus antibiotic prophylaxis (in-context; TMP-SMX as the agent is memory-sourced ⚠︎), no live vaccines ⚠︎, washed/IgA-depleted products instead of IVIG in selective IgA deficiency ⚠︎, and allogeneic HSCT as the only cure for CD40L deficiency ⚠︎.
Decision spine Is this beyond normal childhood illness? — ICU pneumonia, perforated TMs, weight <3rd percentile → yes, work it up as primary immunodeficiency · Are B cells / lymphocytes present? — Normal → XLA is out before you read another line · Is IgM high, normal, or low? — High with everything else low → class-switch failure → CD40L deficiency · Is any isotype normal or high? — IgG normal with IgA alone low → selective IgA deficiency; IgE very high → Job · Any finding off the panel? — Small low platelets → Wiskott-Aldrich; inverted CD4/CD8 → HIV · Now use the pattern: — which organisms and which treatment does this specific block predict?
Scenario bank
  1. 11 mo M with newly diagnosed CD40 ligand deficiency, started on monthly immunoglobulin replacement → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis → Hyper-IgM syndrome
  2. 12 mo M with X-linked agammaglobulinemia on immunoglobulin replacement, presenting for the 12-month visit → Measles-mumps-rubella vaccine → X-linked agammaglobulinemia
  3. 23 yo F, sinopulmonary infections since age 16, bronchiectasis on CT, IgG/IgA/IgM all low, normal CD19+ B cells → Immunoglobulin replacement therapy → Common variable immunodeficiency
  4. 24 yo M with known selective IgA deficiency, upper GI bleed, hemoglobin 6.5, requires transfusion → Transfuse washed red blood cells → Selective IgA deficiency
  5. 9 yo M, recurrent nontender staphylococcal skin abscesses, chronic eczema, retained primary teeth, lung cyst after pneumonia, IgE 4,200 → Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome → Antistaphylococcal prophylaxis and skin care
  6. 3 yo M, eczema, recurrent otitis media, bloody diarrhea, platelets 38,000 and small on smear → Refer for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation → Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
  7. 18 mo M with hyper-IgM syndrome, 2 weeks of dry cough, hypoxemia, diffuse interstitial infiltrates, elevated LDH → Pneumocystis jirovecii → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treatment
  8. 10 mo M, recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections, IgG, IgA and IgM all markedly low → Flow cytometry for CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia if B cells are absent
  9. 4 yo M with CD40 ligand deficiency on immunoglobulin replacement, family asks how to reduce infection risk at home → Boiled or filtered drinking water → Cryptosporidium and sclerosing cholangitis
  10. 7 mo M, third otitis media, thriving, IgG mildly low with normal IgA and IgM, normal B cells, protective tetanus titers → Reassurance and repeat immunoglobulin levels → Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
  11. 7 mo M with two otitis media episodes and prior bronchiolitis, growing at the 65th percentile, facial eczema, IgG low for age with normal IgA and IgM, normal leukocytes, and elevated tetanus- and diphtheria-specific IgG → transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy → a normal vaccine response is the discriminator
  12. 7 mo M with transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy, thriving, with two otitis media episodes → observation with repeat immunoglobulin levels → it self-resolves by early childhood
Decoy note Lymphocytes at 75% look alarming but are in-context expected — lymphocytosis accompanies active infection and, more usefully, confirms that lymphocyte numbers are intact, which is what kills XLA. The three bronchiolitis episodes read as ordinary infant viral illness but actually support the answer: CD40L deficiency impairs viral defense as well as opsonization. "Vaccinations up to date" is not filler — it converts the pneumococcal ICU admission into vaccine failure, which is an immunodeficiency finding rather than a gap in care.
Pearls High IgM with low IgG/IgA is class-switch failure; absent B cells is XLA; all isotypes low with B cells present is CVID. · Read the panel in fixed order — B cells, then IgM, then IgG/IgA/IgE — and the disease names itself. Naming the disease first is how the wrong panel gets forced to fit. · The missing isotype predicts the organism: no opsonizing IgG → encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, H. influenzae); a broken CD40L–CD40 axis also breaks T-cell licensing of macrophages → Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium ⚠︎. · Neutropenia alongside hypogammaglobulinemia points at CD40L deficiency rather than XLA. · Selective IgA deficiency is the defect whose management is what you withhold: no IVIG, and washed or IgA-deficient blood products for transfusion ⚠︎. · Any patient on immunoglobulin replacement or with a defective T-cell limb gets no live vaccines ⚠︎; and replacement IgG makes serologic testing uninterpretable afterward. · A mildly low IgG at 6–9 months in a thriving infant with normal IgM, normal B cells, and protective vaccine titers is transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy — recheck, don't treat ⚠︎.
The physiologic IgG nadir The nadir — maternally derived IgG wanes after birth and troughs at 3 to 6 months, when the infant's own synthesis takes over · Transient hypogammaglobulinemia — that synthesis is delayed and the nadir is prolonged beyond 6 months, with recurrent respiratory infection and atopy · Vaccine response is the most discriminating line on the panel — a normal response excludes common variable immunodeficiency and X-linked agammaglobulinemia at once, whatever the isotype levels say
Pairs with Verified: Part I Recurrent Sinopulmonary Infection (shared complaint: recurrent otitis media and pneumonia in a child; discriminator as a question: does the immunoglobulin panel explain it, or does the anatomy?). When the panel is normal, that brief owns the structural and mucociliary axis; when an isotype is out of step, this one does.
Transferable rule When recurrent sinopulmonary infection arrives with an immunoglobulin panel, the question is a pattern read, not a disease recalled: count the B cells, then ask which isotype is preserved — the preserved isotype names the block, and the missing ones name the organisms you must cover.
Unchecked attributeEczema plus recurrent infection is the Wiskott-Aldrich shape, but that syndrome requires small, low platelets — a normal count retires it, and atopy is itself a feature of transient hypogammaglobulinemia.
Class-vs-memberBruton agammaglobulinemia — That member of the class requires absent B cells and low IgM; IgM is 450 and the lymphocyte compartment is intact
True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency — CVID needs IgM low as well, and presents in adolescence or later, not at 14 months
Salient decoyHIV infection — Would show leukopenia and a low CD4/CD8; ratio is 2.2 and WBC 9,000. Chronic HIV raises IgG/IgA and lowers IgM — the mirror image of this panel
True-fact-wrong-slotIgA deficiency — Isolated IgA deficiency requires normal IgG and IgM; IgG 250 makes the deficiency global-with-a-block, not selective
Class-vs-memberWiskott-Aldrich syndrome — The syndromic member is defined by microthrombocytopenia; platelets are 260,000 and normal-sized, and there is no eczema
