Grade the reflexes first · UWorld · a number outranks a story

The decision point

1+ reflexes is the entire question. Hyporeflexia is a lower motor neuron sign, which localises at or below the anterior horn cell and eliminates spastic diplegia outright, since cerebral palsy is by definition an upper motor neuron disorder. Three findings then pick the lesion: bladder involvement, because muscle and peripheral nerve diseases spare the bladder; back pain, which points at a structural spinal lesion; and pes cavus, which is chronic denervation of the intrinsic foot muscles.

One lesion sits upstream of all four systems: a tethered cord from closed spinal dysraphism, stretched by two months of growth.

Defining criteria Reflex grading — 0 absent, 1+ diminished, 2+ normal, 3+ brisk, 4+ clonus · Lower motor neuron signs — weakness with hypotonia, hyporeflexia and atrophy, localising at or below the anterior horn cell · Upper motor neuron signs — weakness with spasticity, hyperreflexia and Babinski, localising above the anterior horn cell · Secondary incontinence — continence achieved and held, then lost; always pathologic · Low-lying conus — the conus reaches L1 to L2 by about 3 months, so below mid-L2 is low; a filum over 2 mm is thickened
The child with progressive leg weakness - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Tethered cordCord anchored caudally and stretched by growthLMN signs with bladder dysfunction, pes cavus and back pain together
Duchenne muscular dystrophy3 to 5 yo boy, progressive degenerationProximal weakness, Gower sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, pes planus; no bladder involvement
Spastic diplegiaStatic perinatal insult, often prematurityHypertonia and hyperreflexia, scissoring gait, nonprogressive
Transverse myelitisPost-infectious cord demyelinationAcute over hours to days with a sensory level
Charcot-Marie-ToothHereditary neuropathy, autosomal dominantPes cavus with foot drop and family history; no bladder involvement
Friedreich ataxiaAutosomal recessive, teensPes cavus with ataxia and areflexia with upgoing toes, cardiomyopathy
Spinal cord tumor Can't missAstrocytoma or ependymomaNight-waking back pain with progressive deficits; same MRI answers both
Scenario bank
  1. 6 yo M, 2 mo of progressive gait difficulty and back pain, new incontinence, pes cavus and hammer toes, 1+ lower extremity reflexes → tethered cord → MRI of the spine
  2. 5 yo M, difficulty climbing stairs, Gower sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, CK 18,000, continent → Duchenne muscular dystrophy → genetic testing
  3. 3 yo, former 27-week preemie, toe-walking with a scissoring gait, hypertonia, 3+ reflexes, nonprogressive → spastic diplegic cerebral palsy
  4. 12 yo F, 3 days of leg weakness, a sensory level at T8, urinary retention, 2 wk after a viral illness → transverse myelitis → MRI and high-dose intravenous steroids
  5. 14 yo M, distal weakness, foot drop with steppage gait, pes cavus, absent ankle reflexes, father has the same feet → Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
  6. 13 yo M, progressive ataxia and dysarthria, pes cavus, areflexia with upgoing toes, scoliosis, cardiomyopathy → Friedreich ataxia → echocardiogram
  7. Newborn with a lumbosacral hair tuft and a dimple above the gluteal cleft, normal neurologic exam → closed spinal dysraphism → ultrasound of the spine
  8. 8 yo F, back pain that wakes her at night, progressive leg weakness, bladder dysfunction, normal feet → spinal cord tumor → MRI of the spine
  9. 7 yo M, bedwetting at night only, never been dry, normal exam and urinalysis → primary nocturnal enuresis → reassurance
  10. 6 yo M with tethered cord on MRI and progressive symptoms → surgical detethering
Occulta means hidden A normal-looking back does not exclude dysraphism. Cutaneous stigmata are common but not universal, and their absence is the intended trap. Look for a hair tuft, lipoma, hemangioma, sacral appendage, or a dimple above the gluteal cleft; a simple dimple within the cleft with a visible base is benign. Image with ultrasound before about 3 months, while the posterior elements are cartilaginous, and MRI after.
Pearls Pes cavus is a neurologic sign, not an orthopedic one — Charcot-Marie-Tooth, Friedreich ataxia, and tethered cord · Secondary enuresis is never assumed functional; consider infection, diabetes, constipation, neurologic disease, stress and sleep apnea · Back pain in a child under 10 is pathologic until proven otherwise · Occulta — skin intact, no herniation · Meningocele — meninges herniate, cord normal · Myelomeningocele — meninges and neural tissue, with Chiari II and hydrocephalus · Folate prevents neural tube defects: 0.4 mg periconceptionally, 4 mg with a prior affected pregnancy
Pairs with Part I Nocturnal Enuresis is the mirror twin: shared complaint of a school-age child wetting, and the classification flips from functional to neurologic. Store the discriminator as a question: was the child ever dry, and is anything else abnormal? Part I Constipation in a Child screens for this brief on every perineal examination — a sacral dimple or hair tuft is what converts constipation into imaging.
Transferable rule Grade the reflexes before you name the disease, because hyperreflexia and hyporeflexia split the weakness differential into halves that share no members, and that split survives every compelling history the stem can offer.
Class-vs-memberDuchenne is the right age and sex with proximal weakness, flat feet and no bladder involvement.
Mirror twinSpastic diplegia is the upper motor neuron version of the same complaint.
True-fact-wrong-slotTransverse myelitis is a real cord syndrome on the wrong timeline.

Posterior Fossa Localization

Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral · Aquifer · side first, then structure

The decision point

Every abnormal finding is on the left and every one is cerebellar: dysmetria reaching with the left hand, slow rapid alternating movements on the left, and a gait that lists to the left. Cerebellar output decussates twice, so the crossings cancel and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral — which eliminates the right middle cerebellar peduncle in one step.

The pattern also names the part. Limb dysmetria is hemispheric, while a midline vermian lesion gives truncal and gait ataxia with spared limbs. He has both, so the mass is hemispheric and large enough to disturb midline structures — which fits the left facial numbness, since the trigeminal system serves the face ipsilaterally, and the papilledema from fourth-ventricular compression.

Defining criteria Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral — and the patient falls and lists toward the side of the lesion · Hemisphere — limb ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor · Vermis or midline — truncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and titubation · Central nystagmus — direction-changing and gaze-evoked, versus peripheral which is unidirectional and suppresses with fixation · Raised-pressure headache — daily or progressive, worse on waking or lying flat, poorly analgesia-responsive, with papilledema
Where is the mass - localizing the pediatric brain tumor
LocationIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Cerebellar hemispherePilocytic astrocytoma most classically, cystic with a mural noduleIpsilateral limb dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, falls toward the lesion
Cerebellar vermisMedulloblastoma, early fourth-ventricular obstructionTruncal and gait ataxia with a wide base, relatively spared limbs
Middle cerebellar peduncleCarries pontocerebellar inputAtaxia is still ipsilateral, so a right peduncle gives right-sided signs
Brainstem, ponsDiffuse intrinsic pontine gliomaCrossed findings — cranial nerve palsy one side, long-tract weakness the other
Pineal regionGerminoma, adolescent boysParinaud syndrome — upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation
Frontal lobeSupratentorial gliomaContralateral weakness, personality change, expressive aphasia
Occipital lobeSupratentorial massContralateral homonymous hemianopia
Scenario bank
  1. 9 yo M with left-hand dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, listing to the left, bilateral papilledema and left facial numbness → left cerebellar hemisphere → cerebellar signs are ipsilateral
  2. Why a lesion in one cerebellar hemisphere produces signs on the same side of the body → cerebellar output decussates twice → the two crossings cancel
  3. 6 yo M with truncal and gait ataxia, a wide-based stance, minimal limb dysmetria and a midline fourth-ventricular mass → medulloblastoma of the vermis → seeds drop metastases through the CSF
  4. 5 yo F with progressive left sixth and seventh nerve palsies, right hemiparesis and diffuse expansion of the pons → diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma → crossed findings localise to the pons
  5. 12 yo M with an upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and light-near dissociation → MRI of the brain with serum and CSF tumor markers → pineal germinoma
  6. 9 yo M with papilledema and cerebellar signs in whom a lumbar puncture is proposed → obtain MRI of the brain instead → lumbar puncture risks herniation
  7. 9 yo M whose MRI shows a posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus and who has become drowsy → dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation → CSF diversion then resection
  8. 7 yo F with newly confirmed medulloblastoma, staging evaluation → MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology → medulloblastoma seeds the cerebrospinal fluid
  9. 4 yo M with 3 weeks of headache waking him from sleep and morning vomiting, with a normal neurologic examination → MRI of the brain → a normal examination does not exclude a posterior fossa tumor
Papilledema forbids the tap With a posterior fossa mass, lumbar puncture risks herniation. Image first. Posterior fossa tumours are 54 to 70% of childhood brain tumours against only 15 to 20% in adults, so in a child ataxia with raised pressure is infratentorial until imaged.
Pearls Cerebellum — ipsilateral · Face — ipsilateral · Body long tracts — contralateral, so crossed findings mean brainstem · Medulloblastoma seeds the CSF, so staging requires neuraxis MRI and CSF cytology · Red-flag pediatric headache: wakes from sleep, worse on waking, morning vomiting, progressive over weeks, any focal sign, or a child under six · Peripheral vertigo nystagmus is unidirectional and suppressed by fixation; central nystagmus is direction-changing and unsuppressed
Pairs with Part II Congenital Muscular Torticollis and Plagiocephaly carries posterior fossa tumour as the can't-miss cause of acquired head tilt; this brief supplies the localization that identifies it. Part I Sellar and Suprasellar Masses is the anterior compartment of the same question: which region does the endocrine or visual sign name?
Transferable rule Localization is answered side first and structure second, and the cerebellum is the one place where signs stay on the same side as the lesion, so examiners build their distractors from anatomically respectable options on the wrong side.
Class-vs-memberThe right middle cerebellar peduncle is the right region on the wrong side.
True-fact-wrong-slotPineal masses are common in children but produce Parinaud syndrome, which he does not have.

Cerebral Edema in a Child — Reye Syndrome

The question asks what caused the edema, not what caused the illness

The decision point

The stem hands you Reye syndrome and then refuses to offer it as an answer. Viral prodrome → "over-the-counter medications" (the aspirin, never named) → a biphasic course (better, then vomiting and lethargy) → hepatomegaly without splenomegaly → cerebral edema. But the question asks for the cause of the imaging finding, so it steps one level down, to mechanism.

Every option can cloud consciousness. Only one causes edema. Ammonia entering astrocytes is combined with glutamate into glutamine by glutamine synthetase. Glutamine is osmotically active and cannot leave — water follows, astrocytes swell, and you get cytotoxic cerebral edema. Hypoglycemia, uremia and adrenal crisis produce encephalopathy by other routes and leave the brain the same size.

Option audit — which options cause encephalopathy?
OptionEncephalopathy?Why it fails here
HyperammonemiaYesCorrect — the only one that swells astrocytes
HypoglycemiaYesGenuinely occurs in Reye (failing hepatic gluconeogenesis) but causes no edema — a true fact in the wrong slot
UremiaYesUremic encephalopathy without edema; expect hypertension and peripheral edema, not hepatomegaly
Adrenal insufficiencyYesDysfunction is from hypoperfusion; BP is 98/60 — normal, which kills it outright
HypothyroidismYesMyxedema coma is hypothermic and bradycardic; this child is 36.8 °C with a pulse of 110
The vitals do most of the eliminating BP 98/60 (normal) — kills adrenal crisis, which is a hypotension diagnosis · pulse 110, temp 36.8 — kills myxedema coma, which runs slow and cold · no hypertension, no peripheral edema — kills uremia · hepatomegaly with a normal spleen — points at acute hepatic steatosis, not congestion or storage disease.
Toxic-metabolic encephalopathies & precipitants
Toxic-metabolic encephalopathyPrecipitant
Hypoxic-ischemicNear-drowning, choking episode
Diabetic ketoacidosisPoorly controlled diabetes; edema often follows fluid resuscitation
HyponatremiaSIADH; or rapid correction of hypernatremia
Liver failureViral or autoimmune hepatitis; hepatotoxic drugs such as acetaminophen
Reye syndromeAspirin given for a viral illness in a child
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo F, viral URI treated with an OTC medicine, now vomiting and lethargic with hepatomegaly and cerebral edema → Reye syndrome → supportive care and ICP management
  2. 5 yo F with Reye syndrome; the question asks the cause of the imaging finding → hyperammonemia → astrocyte glutamine draws in water
  3. 5 yo F with Reye syndrome; what was in the over-the-counter medicine → aspirin
  4. 5 yo F, liver biopsy performed → microvesicular steatosis → supportive of the diagnosis but not required
  5. Which children may still receive aspirin → Kawasaki disease and rheumatologic disease such as JIA
  6. 6 yo F, altered after an infection, hypotensive with hyperkalemia and hyponatremia → adrenal crisis → stress-dose hydrocortisone
  7. 12 yo M with type 1 diabetes, glucose 620, becomes obtunded hours into fluid resuscitation → DKA-associated cerebral edema → hypertonic saline or mannitol
  8. 2 yo M with hypernatremic dehydration corrected too rapidly → cerebral edema from the osmotic shift
  9. 3 yo M pulled from a pool, now unresponsive → hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
  10. 3 day old with hyperammonemia, normal LFTs and no hepatomegaly, after feeds began → urea cycle defect → ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency
Trap autopsy Hypoglycemia (9%) — the sharpest trap in the set, because it is true: Reye does cause hypoglycemia through failing hepatic gluconeogenesis. It simply is not what swells the brain. A fact can belong to the disease and still not answer the question. Uremia (11%) — correctly identified as a neurotoxin, then applied to the wrong organ story; nothing here suggests renal failure. Adrenal insufficiency (8%) — plausible until you read the blood pressure. Hypothyroidism (0%) — nobody fell for it, because the pulse and temperature contradict it in the same line.
Paired pearls Aspirin is contraindicated in children except for Kawasaki disease and rheumatologic disease such as JIA — and Kawasaki is the reason the exception exists · the mechanism is mitochondrial injury → impaired β-oxidation → microvesicular steatosis, which is why the liver is big but not scarred · treatment is supportive; there is no antidote · hyperammonemia without hepatomegaly in a neonate is a urea cycle defect, not Reye — same neurotoxin, different tree.
Pairs with Diabetes: the Annual Care Bundle, which turns on reading the outcome noun — morbidity versus mortality. Same discipline: this stem says "cause of this patient's imaging findings," not "cause of this patient's presentation." Store the discriminator as a question: "which effect am I being asked to explain?"
Transferable rule When a stem names a specific finding and asks what caused it, the answer must explain that finding — not the illness. Options that are true of the disease but cannot produce the named finding are the intended traps, and they are the hardest to reject precisely because they are true.
True-fact-wrong-slotSalient decoy

Dermatology & Wounds 6 topics + 1 board-style

Morphology and depth decide these. Exposures and risk profiles suggest; the lesion in front of you decides.

Scaly Rash & Psoriasis

Findings beat exposures

The decision point

Nail dystrophy + extensor-surface scaly plaques together = psoriasis. Distribution does the rest: extensor = psoriasis; flexural = eczema. Occupational "wet work" is bait — though it hides a real pearl, since psoriasis exhibits the Koebner phenomenon and friction can localize it.

Scaly plaques — the differential
DiagnosisDistributionThe tellNails?
PsoriasisExtensor, scalp, trunkSalmon plaques, silvery scale, Auspitz sign, KoebnerYes — pitting, onycholysis
Atopic dermatitisFlexuralPruritus first, rash second; lichenification; atopy triadNo
Nummular eczemaExtremitiesCoin-shaped, intensely pruriticNo
Tinea corporisAnywhereAnnular with central clearing; KOH shows hyphaeSeparate (onychomycosis)
Seborrheic dermatitisScalp, nasolabial, browsGreasy yellow scale; MalasseziaNo
Pityriasis roseaTrunkHerald patch → Christmas-tree patternNo
Lichen planusWrists, ankles, mucosa6 Ps: pruritic purple polygonal planar papules; Wickham striaeCan
Scenario bank
  1. 34 yo M with extensor-surface silvery plaques and nail pitting → psoriasis
  2. 34 yo M with flexural lichenified pruritic patches and a history of asthma → atopic dermatitis
  3. 34 yo M with an annular scaly patch with central clearing and an active border → tinea corporis → KOH preparation
  4. 34 yo M with a herald patch followed by a Christmas-tree truncal eruption → pityriasis rosea
  5. 34 yo M with purple polygonal pruritic papules and oral Wickham striae → lichen planus
  6. 34 yo M whose plaques bleed at pinpoints when the scale is lifted → Auspitz sign
  7. 34 yo M with psoriasis, dactylitis and DIP joint involvement → psoriatic arthritis
Psoriasis facts they attach Pathology: parakeratosis, acanthosis, Munro microabscesses, thinned suprapapillary plates (→ Auspitz) · immunology: Th17 / IL-17 / IL-23 axis — secukinumab (IL-17), ustekinumab (IL-12/23), TNF-α inhibitors (screen for latent TB first) · associations: psoriatic arthritis (DIP joints, "pencil-in-cup," dactylitis), metabolic syndrome and CV risk · ladder: topical steroids + calcipotriene → narrowband UVB → systemics · trap: abrupt steroid withdrawal can trigger a pustular flare · if it were tinea, the answer is a KOH prep — never a steroid (tinea incognito).
Pairs with Part I Patchy Hair Loss in a Child is the scalp version, where follicular invasion changes the therapy from topical to oral.
Transferable rule Exposures suggest; findings decide. When history and exam point in different directions, the exam wins — occupational details are written to test whether a story will overrule a lesion you can see.
Salient decoy

Cellulitis & the Depth Ladder

Border sharpness is a depth readout

The decision point

One adjective decides it: flat border = cellulitis; raised, sharply demarcated border = erysipelas. And the buzzword has a mechanism — superficial infection is contained by tissue planes and stops at a sharp edge, while deeper infection diffuses through fat and fades into an indistinct one.

Skin & soft-tissue infections by depth
LayerInfectionThe tellOrganism
Epidermis / superficial dermis + lymphaticsErysipelasRaised, sharply demarcated, intense erythema; rapid onset, early feverS. pyogenes
Deep dermis + subcutaneous fatCellulitis (nonpurulent)Flat, poorly demarcated; indolent over days; fever laterBeta-hemolytic strep, MSSA
Same, with drainageCellulitis (purulent) / abscessPurulent drainage; furuncle → carbuncleS. aureus incl. MRSA
FasciaNecrotizing fasciitis EmergencyPain out of proportion, crepitus, hemorrhagic bullae, necrosis, anesthesia over the lesion, hourly progressionPolymicrobial (type I) or GAS ± Clostridium (type II)
The treatment fork is purulent vs. nonpurulent Nonpurulent → cover streptococci → cephalexin or dicloxacillin (penicillin for erysipelas). Purulent → cover MRSA → incision and drainage plus TMP-SMX, doxycycline, or clindamycin. Necrotizing → emergent surgical exploration, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic — never wait for imaging.
Mimics — roughly 30% of "cellulitis" is misdiagnosed
MimicThe tell
Stasis dermatitisBilateral, chronic, hemosiderin staining, afebrile — the single most common misdiagnosis
DVTSwelling without a sharply defined rash; recent surgery or immobility
Contact dermatitisItchy, geometric border, afebrile
Erythema nodosumBilateral tender nodules on anterior shins; sarcoid, IBD, strep
Erythema migransExpanding with central clearing, minimally tender
Ruptured Baker cystPopliteal fossa and posterior calf
The bilateral rule Cellulitis is nearly always unilateral. Bilateral lower-extremity erythema is stasis dermatitis until proven otherwise — treat with compression, not antibiotics.
Scenario bank
  1. Raised, sharply demarcated, intensely erythematous, rapid onset with early fever → erysipelas → penicillin
  2. Purulent drainage or a fluctuant abscess → I&D + MRSA coverage
  3. Pain out of proportion, crepitus, hemorrhagic bullae, hourly progression → necrotizing fasciitis → emergent surgical exploration
  4. Bilateral, chronic, hemosiderin staining, afebrile → stasis dermatitis → compression
  5. Saltwater exposure + cirrhosis + hemorrhagic bullae → Vibrio vulnificus → doxycycline + ceftriaxone (high mortality)
  6. Cat bite with cellulitis within 24 hours → Pasteurella multocida → amoxicillin-clavulanate
  7. Dog bite in an asplenic or cirrhotic patient → Capnocytophaga → fulminant sepsis risk
  8. Clenched-fist human bite → Eikenella corrodens
  9. Rose gardener with nodules ascending the lymphatics → Sporothrix → itraconazole
  10. Aquarium exposure with nodular lesions → Mycobacterium marinum
  11. Recurrent cellulitis in the same leg → find and treat the portal of entry — usually tinea pedis with toe-web maceration, or lymphedema
Transferable rule Buzzwords that describe morphology usually encode an underlying anatomic fact. "Sharply demarcated" isn't arbitrary — it's telling you how deep the process is.

Diabetic Foot Ulcer

Findings beat the risk profile

The decision point

Three findings each independently exclude arterial disease: painless, plantar over a bony prominence, and warm feet. "Warm and dry" does double duty — warm means perfused, dry means autonomic denervation. That's a neuropathic ulcer, and the most common cause is diabetes. Note the verb: "diagnose the underlying cause" — a culture characterizes the wound, an ABI characterizes perfusion, only the A1c names the disease.

Foot ulcer typesneuropathic vs arterial vs venous
TypeLocationPainBed & surrounding skinPulsesTest
Neuropathic / diabeticPlantar, over pressure points (1st/5th MT head, heel)Painless"Punched out," necrotic base, surrounding callus; skin warm, dry, fissuredNormalA1c; 10-g monofilament
Arterial / ischemicTips of toes, lateral malleolus, dorsumPainful — worse elevated, better danglingDry, pale, minimal granulation; cool, shiny, hairless, dependent ruborDiminished / absentABI
Venous stasisMedial malleolus (gaiter area)Mild ache, better elevatedShallow, irregular, wet; hemosiderin staining, edemaNormalDuplex ultrasound
Pressure / decubitusSacrum, heel, trochanterVariableStaged by depth; immobile patientNormalClinical
Pyoderma gangrenosumLower legVery painfulViolaceous undermined border, rapid; IBD, RANormalBiopsy — do not debride (pathergy)
Marjolin ulcerChronic wound or scarVariableRolled everted edges, non-healing >3 months—Biopsy
ABI values & neuropathy mechanism >1.4 noncompressible, calcified (diabetes, ESRD) → use the toe-brachial index (<0.7 abnormal) · 1.0–1.4 normal · 0.5–0.9 claudication · <0.4 critical limb ischemia. Small-fiber neuropathy → pain, burning, autonomic dysfunction. Large-fiber neuropathy → sensory loss, which is what lets injury go unrecognized. Peripheral neuropathy can be present at the time of type 2 diabetes diagnosis.
Scenario bank
  1. Painful ulcer at the toe tips, cool pale foot, absent pulses → arterial → ABI
  2. ABI 1.5 in a diabetic → noncompressible vessels → toe-brachial index
  3. Medial malleolar wet ulcer + hemosiderin + edema → venous → duplex + compression
  4. Same ulcer but probe-to-bone positive → osteomyelitis → MRI + bone biopsy (plain films insensitive early; ESR >70 supports it)
  5. Warm, swollen, erythematous foot in a diabetic with no ulcer, no fever, normal WBC → Charcot arthropathy → immobilize; "rocker-bottom" deformity
  6. Rapidly enlarging painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border in a patient with IBD → pyoderma gangrenosum → steroids, never debride
  7. Chronic non-healing ulcer with rolled edges → biopsy for Marjolin ulcer
Management once diabetes is confirmed Off-loading (total contact cast) is the single most important intervention · debride callus and necrotic tissue · glycemic control · culture only if clinically infected, and take deep tissue rather than a swab · check the ABI anyway, since mixed neuroischemic ulcers are common · annual 10-g monofilament exam in every diabetic.
Transferable rule Risk factors set a prior; physical findings set the posterior. When the exam contradicts the risk profile on three separate axes, the exam wins.
Salient decoy

Eczema Herpeticum

The PMH is the precondition

The decision point

Atopic dermatitis + vesicles = eczema herpeticum until proven otherwise. The atopic dermatitis isn't background color — it's the precondition. A disrupted barrier plus local immune dysfunction is what lets HSV spread across skin instead of staying a single cold sore. Treatment is immediate systemic acyclovir, because it can disseminate to liver and brain.

The two assassins "Conjunctiva and oropharynx are clear" kills the drug reaction — SJS/TEN requires mucosal involvement (classically ≥2 sites) plus symmetric target lesions. "Progressive worsening on TMP-SMX" kills impetigo — that drug covers staph including MRSA, and failure on appropriate antibacterial therapy eliminates the bacterial hypothesis, exactly as a failed antihistamine eliminates upper airway cough syndrome.
Atopic dermatitis complications
Complication of atopic dermatitisPathogenPresentationTreatment
Eczema herpeticum Can't missHSV-1Painful monomorphic vesicles → punched-out erosions, hemorrhagic crusting; fever, lymphadenopathySystemic acyclovir immediately
ImpetigoS. aureus, S. pyogenesHoney-colored adherent crustMupirocin or oral cephalexin
Molluscum contagiosumPoxvirusSkin-colored papules with central umbilicationSelf-limited; curettage/cantharidin
Tinea corporisT. rubrumAnnular, central clearing, raised scaly borderTopical azole or terbinafine
Eczema coxsackiumCoxsackie A6Vesicles concentrated in eczematous skinSupportive
Morphology tell & workup Herpes makes monomorphic vesicles evolving into "punched-out" erosions with hemorrhagic crust and scalloped coalescing borders. Impetigo makes honey-colored crust — hemorrhagic ≠ honey. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed with HSV PCR of vesicle fluid (Tzanck shows multinucleated giant cells, less sensitive). IV acyclovir if widespread, ill-appearing, or a young infant; ophthalmology consult if periocular.
Scenario bank
  1. Same child with periocular lesions → emergent ophthalmology (HSV keratoconjunctivitis threatens vision)
  2. Widespread, ill-appearing, poor oral intake → admit for IV acyclovir
  3. Honey-colored crust, afebrile, no vesicles → impetigo → mupirocin
  4. Fever + mucositis at two sites + targetoid lesions after a new drug → SJS → stop the drug, admit
  5. Nikolsky positive with spared mucosa in a toddler → SSSS → IV anti-staph; culture the distant focus, not the skin
  6. Lesions in different stages simultaneously → varicella
  7. Umbilicated papules in an eczematous child → molluscum → observe
  8. Eczema + recurrent skin and lung infections + very high IgE + retained primary teeth → hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome
Transferable rule The past medical history is where the deciding fact hides. Sometimes it's a risk factor overriding a benign read (prior cancer → spinal mets), sometimes a risk factor masquerading as an explanation (Klinefelter → gynecomastia), and sometimes the precondition that makes the right diagnosis possible at all. Read the PMH as enabling information, not biography.
True-fact-wrong-slotTest-overrides-findings

Patchy Hair Loss in a Child

the scalp surface and the nodes decide · board question · Is the patch scaly, and are the draining nodes enlarged?

The decision point

Two findings settle this and both are on the examination rather than in the history. The patch carries overlying scale, which means an inflammatory or infectious process in the skin rather than a hair that is simply being pulled or shed; and the occipital and posterior auricular nodes are enlarged and tender, which is regional lymphadenopathy draining an infected scalp. Together they name tinea capitis — a dermatophyte that, unlike tinea of the body, invades the hair follicle and shaft, so the hair breaks and the patch expands centrifugally over weeks. The recent school change and the anxiety are the stem's deliberate offer of trichotillomania, and neither scale nor tender nodes belongs to that diagnosis.

Defining criteria Tinea capitis — scaly erythematous patch with hair loss and localized lymphadenopathy, with or without black dots (broken hairs at the follicle) and with or without a tender boggy kerion · Why systemic therapy is required — the organism invades the follicle and shaft, which topical agents penetrate poorly, so oral griseofulvin or terbinafine is needed · Confirmation — the diagnosis is clinical; KOH examination of proximal hair shafts or fungal culture confirms it
Pertinent positives & negatives Scale over an enlarging bald patch — an inflammatory or infectious scalp process; scale is what separates infection from every non-inflammatory alopecia · Tender occipital and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy — the nodes that drain the scalp; expected in tinea capitis and absent in traction alopecia and trichotillomania · Frequent scratching — pruritus, an inflammatory feature that argues against a purely mechanical cause · Recent school change with anxiety — the planted psychosocial cue for hair-pulling, which the scale and the nodes exclude · Age 8, previously healthy — the peak age; tinea capitis is predominantly a disease of children and the immunocompromised
Patchy hair loss in a child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Tinea capitisTrichophyton or Microsporum acquired from a contact or a fomite — shared comb, hat, pillowcase; invades follicle and shaftScaly patch with hair loss plus regional lymphadenopathy; black dots; kerion— (the answer)
Alopecia areata ⚠︎ (not on the option list)Autoimmune, non-scarring; abrupt, sharply circumscribedSmooth, scale-free patch with no lymphadenopathy; exclamation-point hairs; nail pitting ⚠︎The patch is scaly and the nodes are enlarged
TrichotillomaniaRepeated plucking, often stress-relatedBroken hairs of varying lengths in an irregular pattern, no scale, no nodesScale and tender lymphadenopathy
Traction alopeciaProlonged pulling from bands or braidsGeometric loss along the traction sites (temporal, along braids); no scale, no nodesNo hairstyle history; scale and nodes present
Seborrheic dermatitisScalp scaling, i.e. dandruff, with pruritusScale without hair lossIt cannot explain the alopecia or the nodes
Discoid lupus erythematosusCutaneous lupus; scarring, well-demarcated inflammatory plaquesAdult women, with face and neck lesions, and the alopecia scarsAge 8 and no facial or neck involvement
Management, in one line Management is not this question's fork, so in one sentence: oral griseofulvin or terbinafine is required, because topical antifungals do not reach the organism inside the hair follicle.
Decision spine Is there scale on the patch? — Yes → an inflammatory or infectious cause, not a pulling one · Are the draining nodes enlarged? — Yes → infection, and trichotillomania and traction alopecia are finished · Are the remaining hairs broken? — Black dots are shafts snapped at the follicle — the fungus is inside the hair · Any traction history or geometric pattern? — No · Confirm and treat — KOH of the proximal shafts; oral, never topical alone
Scenario bank
  1. 8 yo with an enlarging scaly bald patch, pruritus, and tender occipital and postauricular nodes → Tinea capitis → Regional lymphadenopathy plus scale
  2. Child with clinically confirmed tinea capitis; appropriate treatment → Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine → Topicals cannot reach the follicle
  3. Child with tinea capitis; which therapy will not clear the infection → Topical antifungal shampoo used alone → Adjunctive at best
  4. 8 yo with a smooth, scale-free, sharply demarcated bald patch, no lymphadenopathy, and nail pitting → Topical or intralesional glucocorticoid → Alopecia areata
  5. 10 yo with irregular patches of broken hairs of varying lengths, no scale, no lymphadenopathy, after a recent stressor → Habit-reversal behavioral therapy → Trichotillomania
  6. 12 yo with symmetric temporal thinning along tightly pulled braids, no scale and no lymphadenopathy → Loosen the hairstyle → Traction alopecia is reversible if caught early
  7. Child on oral antifungal therapy for tinea capitis who develops a boggy tender scalp mass with pustules → Continue systemic antifungal therapy → A kerion is the same infection
  8. Child with a scaly patch of alopecia and regional lymphadenopathy; confirming the diagnosis → KOH examination of proximal hair shafts or fungal culture → The diagnosis is otherwise clinical
  9. Why tinea capitis requires oral therapy while tinea corporis responds to topical treatment → It invades the hair follicle and shaft → Body lesions remain in the epidermis
  10. Household management after a child is diagnosed with tinea capitis → Examine close contacts and stop sharing combs, hats and pillowcases → Fomite transmission
Decoy note The psychosocial sentence is the whole trap: a new school and anxiety about teachers and friends is a complete, plausible causal story, offered one line before the examination that refutes it. "Frequently scratches at the area" reinforces it, since scratching sounds like a behavior — but it is pruritus, an inflammatory symptom, and it points the other way. The stem also says the patch is nontender, which is easy to misread as a general absence of tenderness; it is the nodes that are tender, and that is the finding.
Pearls A scaly, enlarging bald patch with tender occipital nodes in a child is tinea capitis, and it needs an oral antifungal. · Scale plus regional lymphadenopathy converts "alopecia" into "infection"; the two pulling alopecias, traction and trichotillomania, have neither. · Tinea capitis invades the follicle and shaft, so it needs an oral antifungal — the single most tested management point on the topic. · Black dots are hair shafts broken at the follicular orifice; a boggy tender mass is a kerion, which is the same infection inflamed, not a bacterial abscess to drain. · The mimic this option list omitted is alopecia areata: a smooth, scale-free, sharply circumscribed patch with no lymphadenopathy, sometimes with nail pitting ⚠︎. · Fomites carry it — combs, hats, pillowcases — so the household is examined rather than treated blindly. · A scaly scalp plaque that scars, in an adult woman with facial lesions, is discoid lupus rather than tinea.
Pairs with Verified: Part I Scaly Rash & Psoriasis owns the scaly-plaque differential of the body and the rule that a scaly annular lesion earns a KOH preparation rather than a steroid; this brief is the scalp version, where the follicle changes the therapy. Store the discriminator as a question: is there scale, and are the draining nodes up?
Transferable rule In hair loss, the surface of the patch is the diagnosis — scale with regional nodes means infection, a smooth patch means an autoimmune or traction cause, and broken hairs of unequal length mean the hair is being pulled — so read the scalp before you accept a psychosocial story the stem has helpfully supplied.
Class-vs-memberTraction alopecia — Traction produces geometric loss along the sites of pulling — temporal areas, along braids — with no scale and no lymphadenopathy
Salient decoyTrichotillomania — Hair-pulling leaves broken hairs of varying lengths in an irregular pattern, without scale or nodes
Class-vs-memberCutaneous candidiasis — Candida causes intertrigo in warm moist skinfolds; it does not scale the scalp or take hair
True-fact-wrong-slotSeborrheic dermatitis — It explains the scale and the pruritus and nothing else — not the hair loss, not the nodes
True-fact-wrong-slotDiscoid lupus erythematosus — It occurs mostly in adult women, involves the face and neck, and scars

Benign Neonatal Rashes

Sort by onset · reassurance vs. removable cause

The decision point

Benign + self-limited + no modifiable cause → reassure. Benign + an identifiable, removable trigger → remove the trigger. Miliaria rubra has its cause in the history — onesies under pajamas under a fleece swaddle. You don't wait it out; you unwrap the baby.

Benign neonatal rashes
RashOnsetAppearance & distributionManagement
Pustular melanosisAt birthNonerythematous pustules → hyperpigmented macules with collarette; neutrophils; includes palms and solesObserve; pigment lasts months
MiliaAt birthFirm white keratin papules, faceResolves in a month
Erythema toxicumDays 0–3Papules → pustules on erythematous base; eosinophils; spares palms/solesResolves within a week
Miliaria rubraAny age, never at birthFine erythematous papules in occluded and intertriginous areasThin cotton, cool environment; low-potency steroid if severe
Cephalic pustulosis~3 weeksPapules/pustules, face and scalp onlyObserve ± ketoconazole
Seborrheic dermatitis2–6 weeksGreasy yellow scale, scalp and foldsEmollient, gentle brushing
Scenario bank
  1. 2 wk M, erythematous macules with central pustules on the trunk, well-appearing → erythema toxicum neonatorum → reassurance
  2. 2 wk M dressed in a onesie, pyjamas and a fleece swaddle, with tiny clear vesicles → miliaria rubra → remove the extra layers
  3. Newborn with pustules rupturing to hyperpigmented macules with a collarette of scale → transient neonatal pustular melanosis → reassurance
  4. 2 wk M with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base and irritability → neonatal herpes simplex → PCR and IV acyclovir
  5. 6 wk M with greasy yellow scale on the scalp → seborrheic dermatitis → reassurance with an emollient
  6. Newborn with 1 mm white papules across the nose → milia → reassurance
Can't-miss neonatal rashes Neonatal HSV — clustered vesicles on an erythematous base, days 5–14 → PCR + IV acyclovir. Any vesicular rash in a neonate is HSV until proven otherwise · staph pustulosis / bullous impetigo — honey crust or flaccid bullae · congenital syphilis — palms/soles rash, snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly · blueberry muffin rash — TORCH · Langerhans cell histiocytosis — looks seborrheic but is petechial and doesn't resolve.
Diaper rash rule Candida involves the inguinal creases (beefy red + satellite papules → nystatin). Irritant contact dermatitis spares them (convex surfaces only → barrier cream).
Pairs with Part I Maternal Hormone Effects in the Newborn covers the non-cutaneous half of the same principle: transplacental hormone, physiologic, self-limited.
Transferable rule Before choosing pure reassurance, scan the history for a modifiable exposure — bundling, a soap, a detergent, a medication, a position. If the stem spent a sentence describing the environment, that sentence is the treatment.
1 briefBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Dermatology & Wounds

Scabies

A close contact with the same rash outranks morphology

The decision point

A roommate with the identical itchy rash makes this transmissible by prolonged skin contact — that single fact eliminates contact dermatitis, drug eruption, and every non-communicable itch. Add the distribution and the timeline and nothing else fits. Treatment: permethrin 5%.

Stem findings & their diagnostic weight
FindingWhy it matters
Severe itchMost pruritic common dermatosis; classically worse at night
Hands/wrists → other hand → waistlineTextbook map: finger web spaces, flexor wrists, axillae, belt line, periumbilical, genitals. Spares head and neck in adults
"Spots turned into scabs"Excoriations, not vesicular crusts
Roommate moved in a few weeks agoMatches the 3–6 week incubation on first infestation — a sensitization delay, not a replication delay
Trap autopsy Oral acyclovir — zoster is dermatomal, unilateral, painful, doesn't migrate hand→hand→waist, and doesn't infect a roommate. Oral cephalexin — "no crusting or spreading erythema" exists solely to kill this; impetigo means honey-colored crust. Oral prednisone / topical triamcinolone — both treat the itch, not the mite, and steroids produce scabies incognito: a masked, worsening infestation. The pruritus is a type IV hypersensitivity to mite antigen; suppressing the response doesn't touch the organism.
Treatment specifics that get tested separately Permethrin 5%, neck-down (whole body in infants), left on 8–14 hours, repeated in 1 week — the first application doesn't kill eggs · treat all household and close contacts simultaneously, symptomatic or not · wash bedding and clothing hot, or bag 72 hours · oral ivermectin (200 mcg/kg, repeat day 8) for crusted scabies, outbreaks, or adherence problems — avoid in pregnancy and under 15 kg.
The pearl that generates its own question Post-scabetic pruritus persists 2–4 weeks after successful treatment — the leading reason therapy is thought to have failed. That's when triamcinolone and antihistamines become correct: after the mite is dead, not instead of killing it.
Scenario bank
  1. 63 yo M, web-space papules, roommate with the same rash → permethrin ×2 a week apart, treat contacts, launder linens
  2. 63 yo M, still itching 3 weeks after permethrin, no new burrows → post-scabetic pruritus → topical steroid, not re-treatment
  3. 78 yo M in a nursing home, thick hyperkeratotic plaques, minimal itch, immunosuppressed → crusted (Norwegian) scabies → oral ivermectin + topical, contact isolation
  4. 6 mo F, itchy vesicles on palms, soles, scalp, face → infantile scabies — apply including the head
  5. 28 yo M, new apartment, itchy welts on exposed skin in linear clusters, no web-space lesions → bedbugs
  6. 63 yo M with honey-colored crust and surrounding erythema → impetiginized scabies → permethrin plus cephalexin
  7. 34 yo pregnant woman with scabies → permethrin is safe; avoid ivermectin
  8. 63 yo M whose rash returns at 6 weeks → contacts untreated, or the second application skipped
Transferable rule A close contact with the same condition outranks morphology — it converts the differential to transmissible causes before you interpret a single lesion. And when the loudest symptom is itch, check whether the offered drug kills the cause or only the sensation.

Obstetrics & Gynecology 8 topics + 3 board-style

Interval arithmetic and eligibility rules. The physiologic state of the patient decides which explanations are even permitted.

Vaccines & Timing in Pregnancy

Which one is due today?

The decision point

These stems stack several things the patient will eventually need, so the question is really "which one is due today?" — and the deciding variable is a date, a gestational age, or a serology, not a symptom. In the classic version the answer is signaled by "mid-September" in the first sentence: influenza vaccine, given as soon as it becomes available, in any trimester.

Option analysis — why each fails
ChoiceWhy it temptsWhat kills it
Anti-D immunoglobulinShe is Rh-negative with a negative screenTiming — routine prophylaxis at 28 weeks
MMRShe is non-immune to rubellaLive — contraindicated; give immediately postpartum
TdapIndicated in every pregnancyTiming — but as an optimization, not a gate. 27–36 weeks maximizes transplacental IgG transfer; Tdap is safe at any gestational age and is given off-window for wound prophylaxis or an outbreak. See Tdap in Pregnancy at 10 Weeks
Varicella vaccineRecent exposureLive — contraindicated, and she is already immune
VZIGExposure + pregnancy is the classic PEP settingVaricella IgG positive = immune; PEP is for the non-immune

Two killed by timing, two by live-vaccine status, one by serology. Each distractor fails for a different reason — you eliminate them on their own terms rather than comparing them.

Vaccines in pregnancyroutine / high-risk / contraindicated
Recommended for allIf high-riskContraindicated
Inactivated influenza (any trimester) · Tdap every pregnancy, 27–36 wk · COVID-19 · maternal RSV (32–36 wk) · anti-D at 28 wkHepatitis A, hepatitis B, pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal, VZIG if exposed AND non-immuneMMR · varicella · LAIV · zoster · BCG · oral polio — all live. HPV is not live but is deferred
Rh immunoglobulin timing 28 weeks routinely · within 72 hours of delivery if the newborn is Rh-positive · any sensitizing event (vaginal bleeding, spontaneous or threatened abortion, ectopic, molar pregnancy, amniocentesis/CVS, external cephalic version, abdominal trauma) · and the trap — a positive antibody screen means she is already alloimmunized, so anti-D is useless and you switch to titers and MCA Doppler.
Varicella in pregnancy Non-immune + exposed → VZIG within 10 days (ideally 96 hours) · maternal varicella → varicella pneumonia, high mortality → IV acyclovir · congenital varicella syndrome at 8–20 weeks: limb hypoplasia, cicatricial dermatomal scarring, chorioretinitis, cataracts · neonatal varicella if maternal rash occurs 5 days before to 2 days after delivery → VZIG to the newborn.
Scenario bank
  1. Same patient but varicella IgG negative → VZIG within 10 days
  2. Same patient at 28 weeks → anti-D immunoglobulin
  3. Same patient at 30 weeks → Tdap
  4. Same patient postpartum → MMR (safe while breastfeeding)
  5. Rh-negative with vaginal bleeding at 14 weeks → anti-D now, regardless of gestational age
  6. Rh-negative with a positive antibody screen → already alloimmunized → titers + MCA Doppler
  7. Varicella rash with dyspnea in pregnancy → varicella pneumonia → IV acyclovir
  8. Maternal rash 5 days before to 2 days after delivery → VZIG to the neonate
  9. MMR inadvertently given during pregnancy → counsel and reassure; not an indication for termination
  10. Pregnant patient asks about HPV vaccine → defer to postpartum
Transferable rule When several choices are all things this patient will eventually need, scan for the number — date, gestational age, titer — before weighing the indications.

Cervical Cancer Screening

Intervals, abnormal results, special populations

The decision point

Each negative test starts its own clock, the test type sets the length, and you're due when your longest valid coverage expires. Negative cytology = 3 years of coverage from that date. Negative HPV-containing test = 5 years.

Cervical screening schedule
Age / situationTestInterval
<21None — regardless of sexual debut, partners, or vaccination—
21–29Cytology aloneEvery 3 years
30–65Primary HPV alone (preferred, clinician- or self-collected)Every 5 years
30–65 alternativesCytology alone · or co-testing3 years · 5 years
>65Stop if adequate prior screening and no CIN2+ in 25 years—
Scenario bank
  1. 26 yo F whose cytology was negative 2 years ago → return in 1 year
  2. 34 yo F whose co-test was negative 3 years ago → return in 2 years — the 5-year clock governs
  3. 34 yo F with negative cytology and HPV 16 positive → colposcopy
  4. 26 yo F with ASC-US and a negative reflex HPV → resume routine screening
  5. 34 yo F with HSIL on cytology → colposcopy, or immediate excision
  6. 34 yo F with AGC on cytology → colposcopy with endocervical and endometrial sampling
⚠︎ Primary HPV start age — the ledgers split Exam ledger (USPSTF, what the bank scores): primary HPV testing begins at age 30; 21–29 is cytology alone.
Clinic ledger (ACS 2020): primary HPV begins at age 25, every 5 years, preferred — which removes the 25–29 cytology block entirely.
Answer 30 on the exam. The age-21 floor is identical in both and is not in dispute — see Cervical Screening: the Age-21 Floor.
Abnormal result management by age
ResultAge ≥25Age 21–24
ASC-USReflex HPV: positive → colposcopyRepeat cytology in 1 year
LSILColposcopy if HPV+ or unknownRepeat cytology in 1 year
ASC-HColposcopy regardlessColposcopy
HSILColposcopy or immediate excision (see-and-treat LEEP)Colposcopy only
AGCColposcopy + ECC, plus endometrial biopsy if ≥35 or AUBSame
Cytology negative, HPV 16/18+Colposcopy now—
Colposcopy outcomes SCJ not fully visualized → endocervical curettage · CIN1 → observe · CIN2 → treat (observation acceptable if fertility-desiring) · CIN3 → treat · adenocarcinoma in situ → cold knife conization (LEEP fragments margins) · invasive cancer → staging, not LEEP · post-treatment surveillance for 25 years.
Special populations HIV — start within 1 year of sexual debut (the one exception to "never before 21"); cytology annually ×3 then q3y; never stop at 65 · total hysterectomy for benign disease → stop · cervix retained → continue · hysterectomy for CIN2+ → vaginal cuff cytology 25 years · HPV-vaccinated → same intervals · pregnant → colposcopy safe, ECC and endometrial biopsy contraindicated, defer CIN2/3 treatment to postpartum.
Two decoys A female partner does not lower risk — HPV transmits between women and screening is identical. Obesity is a real endometrial risk factor but does not trigger endometrial biopsy without AUB.

Postmenopausal Bleeding

One line decides it

The decision point

"No menstrual period for over a year" makes her postmenopausal, and any bleeding after 12 months of amenorrhea is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Amount and duration are irrelevant; a single episode of spotting counts. ~90% of endometrial cancer presents this way; ~9–10% of PMB is cancer.

Postmenopausal bleeding workup
StepFindingAction
Endometrial evaluation — TVUS or EMBStripe ≤4 mmNo further workup unless bleeding recurs
Stripe >4 mmEndometrial biopsy
On tamoxifenBiopsy regardless — the threshold doesn't apply
Biopsy insufficient or bleeding recurs—Hysteroscopy with D&C
Results → management Hyperplasia without atypia → progestin (oral or LNG-IUD) · atypical hyperplasia / EIN → hysterectomy (up to 40% harbor concurrent carcinoma) · carcinoma → surgical staging with TAH-BSO + nodal assessment. Risk factors are unopposed estrogen: obesity, nulliparity, late menopause, PCOS, tamoxifen, granulosa cell tumor, Lynch syndrome. Combined OCPs and multiparity are protective.
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo F with no period for 18 months, now spotting → endometrial cancer until proven otherwise → transvaginal ultrasound or biopsy
  2. 58 yo F with postmenopausal bleeding and an endometrial stripe of 3 mm → reassuring — atrophy is the likely cause
  3. 58 yo F with postmenopausal bleeding and an endometrial stripe of 8 mm → endometrial biopsy
  4. 58 yo F with an insufficient biopsy sample and continued bleeding → hysteroscopy with dilation and curettage
  5. 58 yo F with postmenopausal bleeding while taking tamoxifen → still requires full evaluation → tamoxifen raises endometrial cancer risk
  6. 58 yo F with light postmenopausal bleeding lasting only one day → amount and duration are irrelevant — evaluate
The two traps in one stem Fibroids cause bleeding in premenopausal women; after menopause they involute. Atrophy is the most common cause of PMB (~60%) — but it is a diagnosis of exclusion, so "pale vagina with minimal rugation" does not license reassurance. And a progestin IUD is contraindicated in undiagnosed bleeding.
Pairs with Part I Familial Adenomatous Polyposis holds the hereditary colon cancer differential in which Lynch syndrome — the endometrial-cancer pedigree — is the polyp-poor row. Store the discriminator as a question: is there an endometrial cancer in the family?
Transferable rule When a stem offers a familiar benign explanation, check whether the patient is still in the physiologic state where that explanation applies.
True-fact-wrong-slot

Ectopic Pregnancy

Location questions need imaging, not numbers

The decision point

Pregnancy is already confirmed by the urine test. The question is no longer "is she pregnant?" but "where is the pregnancy?" — and only one tool answers a location question: transvaginal ultrasound. A single serum β-hCG localizes nothing.

Defining criteria Methotrexate eligibility — unruptured, hCG <5,000, <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, reliable follow-up · Unstable ectopic — hypotension, rebound, or shoulder pain → emergent laparoscopy/laparotomy
Where β-hCG actually belongs
  1. Symptomatic + positive pregnancy test → TVUS now
  2. Intrauterine pregnancy seen → done (heterotopic is rare outside IVF)
  3. Adnexal mass or free fluid → ectopic, treat
  4. TVUS indeterminate → now β-hCG earns its keep: above the discriminatory zone (~1,500–2,000) with an empty uterus = presumed ectopic; below it → serial hCG q48h (normal IUP doubles; ectopic rises <35–50%; miscarriage falls)
Stability picks the branch Hypotensive, rebound, or shoulder pain (diaphragmatic irritation from hemoperitoneum) → skip everything, emergent laparoscopy/laparotomy. Stable ectopic workup = image; unstable = operate — the same logic as PE.
Pearls Biggest acquired risk factor is prior PID (tubal scarring); also prior ectopic, tubal surgery, IUD in place, smoking (impairs ciliary transport) · half of ectopics have no palpable adnexal mass · methotrexate if unruptured, hCG <5,000, <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, reliable follow-up · Rh-negative mother with any bleeding in pregnancy → RhoGAM.
Transferable rule When two tests both seem reasonable, choose the one whose result forks the management tree. A single hCG changes nothing tonight; the ultrasound changes everything.

HPV Vaccination & Series Rules

A two-lock door

The decision point

Two independent facts: (1) age at first dose sets the series length — under 15 → 2 doses; ≥15 → 3 doses (immunocompromised → 3 regardless. (2) Never restart a vaccine series — delayed doses are simply given late. Minimum intervals matter; maximum intervals don't exist.

Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo F receiving her first HPV dose → two doses
  2. 17 yo M receiving his first HPV dose → three doses
  3. 13 yo M with HIV receiving his first dose → three doses regardless of age
  4. 15 yo F who received one dose 14 months ago → continue the series — never restart
  5. 28 yo F asking about catch-up vaccination → shared decision-making through age 45
  6. 12 yo F who had dose one at age 11 and dose two 4 months later → repeat the second dose → doses less than 5 months apart do not count
Bankable rules "Do not restart, do not repeat" applies to every vaccine series — a gap just means resume where you left off · catch-up HPV vaccination is recommended through age 26, with shared decision-making 27–45 · sexual activity, prior HPV exposure, and abnormal Pap results do not change the recommendation — vaccinate anyway, because it still protects against strains not yet acquired.
Transferable rule When a guideline stem includes lifestyle color, ask whether it actually changes the algorithm. Usually it's there precisely because it doesn't.
Salient decoy

Adolescent Abnormal Uterine Bleeding

Reassurance needs a benign cause AND an acceptable consequence

The decision point

Anovulatory cycles from an immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis are genuinely normal in the first 1–2 years after menarche — which is why most people choose reassurance. But reassurance requires two things: a benign cause and an acceptable consequence. Anemia is a consequence. The physiology being normal doesn't make the outcome acceptable.

Mechanism: immature axis → no LH surge → anovulation → no corpus luteum → no progesterone → unopposed estrogen drives continuous proliferation with no secretory differentiation → the lining outgrows its blood supply and sheds unpredictably. Progesterone converts proliferative to secretory endometrium and produces organized withdrawal bleeding.

Defining criteria Normal adolescent cycle — length 21–45 days (adults 24–38), duration ≤7 days, ≤3–6 products/day · Reassurance requires — a benign cause AND an acceptable consequence; anemia is not an acceptable consequence
The detail most people skip "Nonpainful." Ovulatory cycles are crampy — painless heavy irregular bleeding is the anovulatory signature. Normal adolescent parameters: cycle length 21–45 days (adults 24–38), duration ≤7 days, ≤3–6 products/day.
Adolescent AUB — clue → diagnosis → workup
ClueDiagnosisWorkup
Irregular, heavy, painless, within 2 yrs of menarcheAnovulation from an immature axisClinical
Heavy since the very first period, bruising, epistaxis, family historyvon Willebrand disease — up to 20% of adolescents with heavy mensesvWF antigen, ristocetin cofactor, factor VIII — PT/aPTT are often normal and do not exclude it
Hirsutism, acne, obesity, acanthosis nigricansPCOSAndrogens, glucose
GalactorrheaProlactinomaProlactin → MRI
Weight loss, athlete, low BMIFunctional hypothalamic amenorrheaFemale athlete triad
Any sexually active patientPregnancyPregnancy test before anything else
Scenario bank
  1. Same girl with hemoglobin 13 and not bothered → reassurance + menstrual calendar
  2. Heavy since menarche + easy bruising + family history → von Willebrand panel (normal PT/aPTT doesn't rule it out)
  3. Hirsutism, acne, BMI 34, acanthosis → PCOS → androgens + combined OCP
  4. Hemodynamically unstable acute heavy bleeding → IV conjugated estrogen, high-dose OCP taper, tranexamic acid, transfusion, admit
  5. Galactorrhea + amenorrhea → prolactin → pituitary MRI
  6. Sexually active → pregnancy test first, always
  7. Athlete with weight loss and amenorrhea → functional hypothalamic amenorrhea
  8. Wants a non-hormonal option for heavy bleeding → tranexamic acid
  9. Adolescent with obesity and prolonged anovulation not responding to medical therapy → now endometrial biopsy is reasonable
  10. Woman ≥45 with AUB → endometrial biopsy regardless
The IUD pairing The copper IUD makes menses heavier and longer — contraindicated in heavy bleeding with anemia. The levonorgestrel IUD makes them lighter and is a legitimate treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding.
Transferable rule "This is physiologically normal for her age" answers the diagnosis, not the management. Before choosing reassurance, check whether the stem gave you a consequence — anemia, growth failure, functional impairment. A consequence converts a normal variant into something you treat.
Uniform-answer doubt

Contraception & DMPA

A pregnancy test precedes every contraceptive decision

The decision point

When two explanations produce identical symptoms, test for the one that changes management and can't be missed. DMPA side effects — breast soreness, weight gain, fatigue, amenorrhea — are indistinguishable from early pregnancy. And the arithmetic assassin: DMPA is due every 13 weeks; her last injection was 4 months ago, so she has been uncovered.

The structural rule: a pregnancy test precedes every contraception decision, every amenorrhea workup, and absolutely every IUD placement — inserting an IUD into an established intrauterine pregnancy can disrupt it.

Defining criteria DMPA dosing window — every 13 weeks with a ~2-week grace period · Return to fertility — delayed up to 10 months · Before any contraceptive decision — a pregnancy test
DMPA facts Suppresses GnRH → no LH surge → no ovulation; thickens cervical mucus · every 13 weeks with a ~2-week grace period · irregular bleeding early, then amenorrhea in ~50% at 1 year · weight gain from appetite stimulation · reversible loss of bone mineral density (boxed warning) · the unique one: delayed return to fertility up to 10 months · no estrogen, so safe in smokers ≥35, migraine with aura, VTE history, and immediately postpartum.
Contraception rules by situation
SituationRule
Smoker ≥35Avoid estrogen (WHO category 4) → progestin-only, IUD, implant
Migraine with auraAvoid estrogen — stroke risk
VTE history, uncontrolled HTN, SLE with antiphospholipid antibodiesAvoid estrogen
<21 days postpartum (or <42 if breastfeeding / VTE risk)Avoid estrogen; progestin-only and IUD are fine
Heavy menstrual bleedingLNG-IUD — copper makes bleeding worse
Emergency contraceptionCopper IUD most effective (up to 5 days); ulipristal > levonorgestrel, especially if BMI >30
Enzyme-inducing antiepilepticsCOC and implant efficacy drops → DMPA or IUD
Wants pregnancy soonAvoid DMPA
Secondary amenorrhea framework Defined as no menses >3 months with previously regular cycles (or >6 months if previously irregular). Pregnancy test first, then TSH, prolactin, FSH. FSH high → primary ovarian insufficiency · FSH low/normal → hypothalamic or pituitary · prolactin high → prolactinoma, dopamine blockers, or hypothyroidism · no withdrawal bleed even to estrogen + progesterone after a D&C → Asherman syndrome.
Scenario bank
  1. Negative pregnancy test → now offer copper IUD, COC, or implant by preference
  2. Positive test → prenatal care; DMPA exposure is not teratogenic
  3. Same patient wanting to conceive within a year → avoid DMPA (fertility return up to 10 months)
  4. 38-year-old smoker requesting contraception → progestin-only or IUD, not estrogen
  5. Migraine with aura → no estrogen-containing method
  6. Needs emergency contraception 4 days after unprotected sex → copper IUD (or ulipristal)
  7. On DMPA 3 years, concerned about bone density → counsel that loss is reversible, ensure calcium and vitamin D, consider alternatives
  8. Amenorrhea 4 months with a negative pregnancy test → TSH, prolactin, FSH
  9. Amenorrhea after a D&C → Asherman syndrome
  10. Exclusively breastfeeding, <6 months postpartum, amenorrheic → lactational amenorrhea method requires all three; formula-feeding voids it
Transferable rule When a stem offers a plausible drug-effect explanation for symptoms that overlap a can't-miss diagnosis, the drug effect is a diagnosis of exclusion — especially when a date in the stem shows the drug wasn't actually working.

Uterine Fibroids

Treat consequences, not findings

The decision point

Fibroid size does not drive treatment — symptoms do. Stems front-load "markedly enlarged," "multiple," "intramural and pedunculated" to make impressive anatomy feel like it demands action, then explicitly negate every symptom domain. Asymptomatic fibroids get observation.

Findings audit — benign or consequential?
FindingConsequence?Answer
Benign rash (miliaria)No, but a removable causeRemove the cause
Normal anovulation (adolescent AUB)Yes — anemiaTreat
Impressive fibroid anatomyNoneReassure and observe
Indications for treating fibroids — the entire question
  • Heavy or prolonged menses, especially with anemia
  • Bulk symptoms — pressure, urinary frequency, constipation, hydronephrosis
  • Pelvic pain or dyspareunia
  • Infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss (submucosal)
  • Rapid growth, or any growth after menopause → leiomyosarcoma concern
Location determines the symptom Submucosal → heavy bleeding and infertility (most symptomatic despite often being smallest) · intramural → bleeding and bulk · subserosal / pedunculated → pressure, and can torse · cervical → obstruction. Fibroids are estrogen- and progesterone-dependent, so they regress after menopause — which is why they can never explain postmenopausal bleeding.
The enlarged uterus — the differential
Enlarged uterusUterusThe tell
LeiomyomaIrregular, firm, lumpy, mobileHeavy menses; regresses after menopause
AdenomyosisGlobular, symmetric, boggy, tenderSevere dysmenorrhea; MRI shows a thickened junctional zone
PregnancySymmetric, softAmenorrhea → β-hCG
Endometrial cancerNormal or enlargedPostmenopausal bleeding → biopsy
LeiomyosarcomaRapidly enlarging, especially postmenopausalDoes not arise from a leiomyoma; avoid morcellation
Scenario bank
  1. Menorrhagia with hemoglobin 9 → LNG-IUD first-line medical therapy
  2. Hydronephrosis on imaging → now symptomatic → surgical management
  3. Submucosal fibroid with recurrent pregnancy loss → hysteroscopic myomectomy
  4. Large fibroid with anemia before planned surgery → GnRH agonist short-term (osteoporosis risk beyond 6 months; use add-back)
  5. Globular tender uterus with severe dysmenorrhea → adenomyosis → LNG-IUD or hysterectomy
  6. Postmenopausal rapidly enlarging uterine mass → leiomyosarcoma workup, avoid morcellation
  7. Heavy bleeding, declines hormones, wants to preserve fertility → tranexamic acid
  8. Completed childbearing, severe symptoms, failed medical therapy → hysterectomy (definitive)
  9. Pedunculated subserosal fibroid with acute severe pain → torsion or degeneration → imaging
A detail that was bait in one stem and signal in another A same-sex relationship appeared in the cervical cancer stem as a decoy (implying low risk — wrong, screening is identical). Here it functions as valid reasoning: low pregnancy risk means the contraceptive benefit of a COC or IUD doesn't offset their risks. Details aren't inherently bait or signal — what the detail is being asked to decide determines which it is.
Transferable rule Treat consequences, not findings. Anatomic impressiveness on a CT report is not clinical significance — it's treat-the-number in imaging clothing.
Treat-the-number
3 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Obstetrics & Gynecology

Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

Treat on the exam finding, not the culture · Aquifer · the threshold is low by design

The decision point

The stem has already met the diagnostic threshold. PID is a presumptive clinical diagnosis, and the gate is deliberately low: a sexually active young woman with pelvic pain, no other identified cause, and any one of cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness. She has cervical motion tenderness, and the purulent discharge plus fever above 38.3 C are supporting criteria.

The threshold sits there because treatment prevents the sequelae and delay causes them. Managing the alternatives — ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, ovarian cyst, torsion — is not impaired by starting antimicrobials. There is no diagnostic penalty for treating early and a permanent one for treating late: infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain.

Defining criteria Minimum criteria — pelvic or lower abdominal pain with no other identified cause plus at least one of cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness · Additional criteria — temperature above 38.3 C, mucopurulent cervical discharge or friability, abundant WBCs on saline microscopy, raised ESR or CRP, documented gonococcal or chlamydial infection · Negative predictor — normal cervical discharge with no WBCs on wet prep makes PID unlikely
Acute pelvic pain in a young woman - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Pelvic inflammatory diseaseAscending gonococcal, chlamydial or vaginal-flora infectionCervical motion tenderness with mucopurulent discharge
Ectopic pregnancy Can't missAmenorrhea then unilateral painPositive hCG with an empty uterus; a pregnancy test is always mandatory
Tubo-ovarian abscessA complication of PID rather than a separate diseasePalpable or sonographic adnexal mass; admit
Ovarian torsionSudden severe unilateral pain with an ovarian massNausea and vomiting, usually afebrile, absent Doppler flow
AppendicitisPeriumbilical pain migratingMcBurney point tenderness, no cervical findings
PyelonephritisAscending urinary infectionCostovertebral angle tenderness with pyuria
Management ladder — pelvic inflammatory disease
TierInterventionEscalate when
PresumptiveStart empiric antibiotics as soon as the clinical diagnosis is madeAny hospitalisation criterion below
OutpatientCeftriaxone 500 mg IM once, plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 14 daysNo improvement within 72 hours means admit and reconsider the diagnosis
InpatientCeftriaxone 1 g IV daily with doxycycline and metronidazole, or cefoxitin or cefotetan with doxycyclineTubo-ovarian abscess failing medical therapy means drainage
TransitionOral doxycycline and metronidazole after 24 to 48 hours of improvement, completing 14 days—
Follow-upRetest for gonorrhea and chlamydia at 3 months—
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo F, sudden pelvic pain, T 39 C, cervical motion tenderness, purulent cervical discharge, no adnexal mass → start empiric antibiotics now → PID is a presumptive clinical diagnosis
  2. 19 yo F meeting PID criteria with a 6 cm tubo-ovarian abscess on ultrasound → admit for intravenous antibiotics → drainage if no response
  3. 22 yo F meeting PID criteria with a positive pregnancy test and an intrauterine gestation → hospitalize for intravenous antibiotics → doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy
  4. 24 yo F meeting PID criteria with a copper intrauterine device in place → treat and leave the device in place → reconsider removal only if no improvement at 48 to 72 hours
  5. 18 yo F on outpatient PID therapy with no clinical improvement at 72 hours → admit for intravenous therapy and reassess the diagnosis → consider diagnostic laparoscopy
  6. 20 yo F diagnosed with PID whose last sexual intercourse was 3 weeks ago → evaluate and presumptively treat partners from the last 60 days → for chlamydia and gonorrhea regardless of her results
  7. 17 yo F with pelvic inflammatory disease and new right upper quadrant pleuritic pain → Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome → perihepatitis with violin-string adhesions
  8. 16 yo F with sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, vomiting, an adnexal mass and no fever → ovarian torsion → Doppler ultrasound then laparoscopy
  9. 17 yo F newly diagnosed with pelvic inflammatory disease, what else to test for → HIV and syphilis → plus gonorrhea and chlamydia, retesting at 3 months
When to admit Surgical emergency cannot be excluded, tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, severe illness or vomiting or temperature above 38.5 C, inability to tolerate oral therapy, or no response to oral therapy. Adolescence is not itself a criterion — the same thresholds apply as for adults. All contraceptive methods can be continued during treatment, and an intrauterine device does not need removal.
Pearls The low threshold is the guideline, not a shortcut — clinical diagnosis carries a positive predictive value of only 65 to 90% for salpingitis, and that is accepted deliberately · Only about half of acute PID has a positive gonorrhea or chlamydia test, so a negative test never excludes it · Metronidazole joined the routine regimen in 2021 for anaerobic coverage; older item banks may key ceftriaxone plus doxycycline alone · Quinolones are no longer recommended because of gonococcal resistance · Fitz-Hugh-Curtis is PID that reached the liver capsule, with right upper quadrant pleuritic pain
Pairs with Part I Ectopic Pregnancy is the mandatory partner: both present as acute pelvic pain in a reproductive-age woman, and the fork is settled by one test. Store the discriminator as a question: what is the pregnancy test?
Transferable rule When a diagnosis is defined as presumptive and clinical, the arrival of its confirmatory test is documentation rather than management, so ask what the pending test could change today and treat if the answer is nothing.
Sequencing trapUltrasound is normal in uncomplicated PID and delays the only intervention that prevents sequelae.
Class-vs-memberUrine culture is the right class of test on the wrong compartment.
True-fact-wrong-slotContraception is appropriate care but is prevention, not treatment of an established infection.

Cervical Screening: the Age-21 Floor

An eligibility gate, not a risk calculation

The decision point

A 20-year-old is below the screening floor. Sexual debut at 15, five partners, inconsistent condoms — every one of those raises HPV exposure and none of them lowers the starting age. The answer is no cytology; screening begins at 21.

The rule is deliberately risk-blind. HPV in adolescents is near-universal and clears in ~90% within 2 years; progression to cancer takes a decade-plus. Screening early finds transient infection and produces excisional procedures (LEEP) that raise preterm-birth risk in women who were never going to develop cancer. That's why cervical cancer under 21 is rare — and why screening her would harm without benefit.

Cervical screening — age gates
AgeScreen withInterval
<21Do not screen — regardless of sexual history, partners, or STI history—
21–29Cytology aloneEvery 3 years
30–65Cytology q3y · co-testing q5y · primary HPV q5y3 or 5 years
>65Stop if adequate prior negative screening and no CIN2+ in 25 years—
⚠︎ Primary HPV start age — the ledgers split Exam ledger (bank/USPSTF): primary HPV testing from age 30.
Clinic ledger (ACS 2020): primary HPV from age 25, q5y, preferred.
Answer 30 on the exam. Know 25 exists so a clinic attending's answer doesn't unseat you.
Exit ramps — where the age floor genuinely moves HIV infection → screen at diagnosis (or within 1 year of sexual debut if younger), then annually × 3, then q3y — this is the one exception that beats age 21 · other immunocompromise (transplant, chronic steroids) → same accelerated schedule · in-utero DES exposure → annual · prior CIN2+ → surveillance q3y for 25 years, including past 65 · hysterectomy with cervix removed for benign disease → stop entirely; cervix retained (supracervical) → keep screening · vaccinated → schedule unchanged.
Scenario bank
  1. 20 yo F, debut at 15, five partners → no screening — begin at 21
  2. 18 yo F newly diagnosed with HIV → screen now, then annually × 3
  3. 21 yo F, virgin, never sexually active → screen anyway; the recommendation is age-based, not activity-based
  4. 24 yo F with ASC-US cytology → reflex HPV; if negative, resume routine
  5. 28 yo F, normal cytology 2 years ago → return in 1 year (q3y from the last test)
  6. 33 yo F, cytology negative / HPV positive, not 16 or 18 → repeat co-test in 1 year
  7. 33 yo F, cytology negative / HPV 16 positive → colposcopy — genotype escalates
  8. 67 yo F, three consecutive negatives, no CIN history → stop screening
  9. 67 yo F with CIN2 treated 10 years ago → keep screening — the 25-year clock overrides age 65
  10. 42 yo F, hysterectomy for fibroids, cervix removed → stop · hysterectomy for cervical cancer → continue vaginal cuff cytology
  11. 20 yo F with visible cervical lesion or postcoital bleeding → biopsy the lesion — that's diagnostic, not screening
Trap autopsy The stem's entire risk paragraph is a salient decoy constructed to make "no screening" feel negligent. Colposcopy is the sequencing trap — it's for an abnormal result, and she has no result. HPV vaccination counseling is a true-fact-wrong-slot: she's 20, catch-up runs through 26, so it's genuinely indicated — just not what the question asked.
Pairs with Part I Cervical Cancer Screening (interval mechanics when cytology and co-testing fall out of sync) and HPV Vaccination. Store the discriminator: "Is she eligible yet?" — asked before "is she at risk?"
Transferable rule Screening guidelines are population rules with age gates. Individual risk factors adjust intensity within the eligible window; they rarely move the floor. Check eligibility before you calculate risk.
Salient decoySequencing trapTrue-fact-wrong-slot

Tdap in Pregnancy at 10 Weeks

A window that optimizes, not a gate that excludes

The decision point

She is 10 weeks pregnant and asks about vaccines. Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy, but the antibody transfer that protects the newborn is maximized when it's given at 27–36 weeks, preferably early in that window. So at 10 weeks the answer is administer Tdap in the third trimester — schedule it, don't decline it.

Correction to an earlier framing in this document The Part I pregnancy-vaccine brief listed Tdap's trap as "Timing — 27–36 weeks," which reads like an eligibility gate. It isn't. Tdap is safe at any gestational age, and if a pregnant woman has a wound requiring tetanus prophylaxis, or is caught in a pertussis outbreak, you give it then. 27–36 weeks is an optimization of transplacental IgG transfer, not a permission window. Gate vs. optimization is exactly the distinction NBME builds a question on.
Vaccine rules in pregnancy
VaccineIn pregnancyThe tell
TdapEvery pregnancy, ideally 27–36 weeksRepeat each pregnancy even if given last year — it's for this fetus
Influenza (IM, inactivated)Any trimester during seasonNo timing window — 10 weeks in flu season → give today
RSV (RSVpreF, Abrysvo)32–36 weeks, seasonalMaternal vaccine or infant nirsevimab — generally not both
COVID-19Recommended, any trimester—
MMR · VaricellaContraindicated — livePostpartum, before discharge; non-immune rubella is a classic stem
Live attenuated influenza (nasal)ContraindicatedThe class-vs-member trap: "influenza vaccine" is right, that influenza vaccine is wrong
HPVDefer to postpartumNot teratogenic — deferred for lack of data
Scenario bank
  1. 26 yo F at 10 weeks asking about vaccines → Tdap in the third trimester (+ influenza now if in season)
  2. 26 yo F at 30 weeks, Tdap in a prior pregnancy 2 years ago → give Tdap again
  3. 26 yo F at 12 weeks in October → inactivated influenza vaccine today — no window
  4. 26 yo F at 14 weeks with a dirty puncture wound, last Td 12 years ago → Tdap now — the window doesn't apply to prophylaxis
  5. 26 yo F at 34 weeks in November, no RSV vaccine → RSVpreF, or plan nirsevimab for the infant
  6. 26 yo F, rubella non-immune on prenatal labs → MMR postpartum before discharge, not now
  7. 26 yo F who received MMR then discovered she's pregnant → counsel and monitor; not an indication for termination
  8. 26 yo F at 10 weeks, offered the nasal influenza vaccine → refuse the live formulation, give IM
  9. Household members and the partner of a newborn, no prior Tdap → cocooning — vaccinate ≥2 weeks before contact
  10. 26 yo F postpartum, breastfeeding → all vaccines including live ones are permitted
Paired pearls Maternal Tdap is for the infant, who can't be vaccinated until 2 months — the deadliest pertussis window is the first 3 months · antibody transfer needs ~2 weeks to develop and time to cross, which is what makes late-third-trimester dosing suboptimal and preterm delivery the reason to dose at 27, not 36 · breastfeeding lifts every restriction; pregnancy is the constraint, lactation is not.
Pairs with Part I Vaccines in Pregnancy — this brief supersedes its Tdap timing row. Store the discriminator: "Is this window a gate or an optimization?"
Transferable rule When a recommendation carries a time window, ask what the window protects. If it optimizes an effect (antibody transfer), you can move outside it when the indication changes. If it defines eligibility (age 21 for cytology), you cannot.
Class-vs-memberSequencing trap

Preventive Medicine & Ethics 5 topics + 2 board-style

Ranking questions and eligibility questions. Capacity determines the reporting path.

Ranking Preventive Interventions

"Most beneficial" is a magnitude question

The decision point

When every option is guideline-supported, the question is asking you to rank by magnitude of benefit. Nothing beats quitting a pack a day: smoking cessation reduces all-cause mortality more than any drug on the list, cuts CV risk substantially within 1–2 years, and approaches never-smoker risk over ~15 years.
